**Left behind.** **A fee charged on an ENDED lease is not collected by autopay** — `collectDueInvoices` filters `lease.status in OCCUPYING_LEASE_STATUSES`, correctly, since a moved-out tenant's card should not be charged automatically; the move-out settlement and the final statement are what collect it, and a fee posted after a move-out completes leaves the tenant a second statement. **No approval workflow for an over-limit override** — it refuses and names the rank that could carry it, which is the same posture `waiveFeeInvoice` has had since B-047; the approval queue is still nobody's item. **The charge control is not on the walkthrough or unit board**, where a lock cut is also discovered — two screens was the row's scope. **`auction_cost` still has no automatic poster**: advertising and auctioneer costs are genuinely ad hoc, but the auction pipeline could post the ones it knows about, and nothing owns that. **B-168 still has to unpick the promotional recapture**, which is a raw `ledgerEntry` rather than a fee invoice — this item deliberately did not touch it, but `raiseFeeInvoice` is now the shape it should move onto.

## B-168 — A promotional recapture you can argue down without forgiving the arrears

`f661a45`

**What it built.** B-145 posted the recapture as a bare `type: 'charge'` ledger row, so `waivableFees` could not list it, `waiveFeeInvoice` could not void it, it never aged, it never dunned, and autopay never collected it. The only lever `CompleteMoveOutInput` offered was `writeOff?: boolean` — **all or nothing across the entire residual**, so forgiving a disputed $60 recapture also forgave $400 of genuine arrears under one reason code. It now posts through B-167's `raiseFeeInvoice` as its own `kind: 'fee'` invoice, and reducing or waiving it is a lever of its own with a reason code and the fee-waiver ladder behind it. `PromoRedemption` gains `recaptureChargedCents`, `recaptureWaivedCents` and `recaptureInvoiceId`, and the promotions report gains three columns off them.

**What it decided.**

**The authority is measured on the amount FORGIVEN, not the amount charged.** The discretion being exercised is the gap — the same rule B-167 settled for a fee override against its schedule, applied to the rule's figure here. It goes through `fee_waiver` rather than riding on `leases:move_out`, which every counter staffer completing a move-out already holds; without that, the term the business advertises could be given away at the desk by anyone.

**The reduction flows through the SETTLEMENT, not around it.** `previewMoveOut` takes the override and hands the reduced figure to `settleMoveOut`, so `amountDueCents`, the write-off threshold and the manager-override decision all see the same number. Subtracting afterwards would have left the screen demanding a manager for a debt that no longer existed.

**A reduction rewrites the sentence, and the sentence stays on the ledger row.** B-145's rule is that the ledger description — which is what the tenant's own statement renders — must not be a different form of words from the screen that got their consent. `raiseFeeInvoice` appends the invoice number to whatever it is given, so the full reason is passed as the ledger description, and `applyRecaptureOverride` extends it with "— reduced by $79.00" or "— waived in full". The figure and the words move together.

**Clamped to the ruled amount: an operator may forgive a recapture, never invent one.** Charging more than the promotion actually gave away would bill money nobody saved, which is the same reasoning `recaptureFor` already uses for refusing to bill back a discount that was never delivered. Over-charging is clamped rather than refused, and needs no reason, because nothing was forgiven.

**Three report columns, not one.** A minimum stay that bills $4,000 and **waives** $3,800 at the counter is not a term; one that bills $4,000 and **collects** $600 from tenants who have already left is a different failure. Charged and waived are stored on the redemption; collected is read through `recaptureInvoiceId` to the invoice's own `amountPaidCents`, because a decision and a payment are different facts. All three are **null on a redemption whose lease is still live** — "not decided yet" must not report as "recovered nothing".

**Its own audit action, `promo.recapture_reduced`.** Filed under `fee.waived` it would be one row among every waiver ever made, and the question it exists to answer — is the minimum stay real — could not be asked of it.

**D-89 is untouched.** A transfer still recovers nothing; there is nothing to reduce, and the existing test still says so.

**Test verification.** Full unit suite **3,678 passed, 8 skipped of 3,686** (220 files passed, 1 skipped), **exit 0**, and run twice. Typecheck, lint, `next build` and `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` clean. Seven new tests: five in `tests/move-out-db.test.ts` — the invoice's shape, date and line text plus its reachability by `waiveFeeInvoice`; a counter reduction recording both halves and its audit row; a full waiver leaving $400 of arrears **untouched**, which is the defect in one assertion; the three refusals (no reason, over limit, no authority) each leaving the lease open; and the clamp — and two in `tests/promo-roi-db.test.ts` wiring the redemption columns through to the report, including the null case. `tests/promo-roi.test.ts`'s empty-totals assertion had to grow the three new keys, which is exactly what that test is for.

**A fixture that had to change, and why it is worth naming.** `tests/move-out-db.test.ts`'s teardown deleted leases but never invoices, because until this item a move-out created none. It now does, so the FK held every lease down and seven tests failed at cleanup rather than at their assertion. The redemption is deleted first — it points at the invoice.

**Left behind.** **A write-off still leaves the recapture invoice open.** `writeOff` posts a `write_off` ledger entry for the whole residual and leaves every invoice behind it `open` — true of rent invoices since B-047 and now true of this one too. The ledger nets correctly and the invoice list does not, which is a pre-existing shape this did not widen and nobody owns. **The move-out screen does not re-preview as you type.** It is a server component, so the settlement shown is the ruled figure until you submit; the fieldset states the entitlement and what forgiving costs, which is enough to decide, but the total above does not move under your hands. **The report's date range still filters on when the promotion was REDEEMED**, not when the recapture happened, so a recapture billed this month against an eight-month-old redemption sits in that cohort — right for "is this promotion's term working", wrong for "what did we recover in March". **No partial payment of a recapture invoice is surfaced anywhere but the report.**

## B-169 — The backstop that could not reach the units it was built for

`7631936`

**What it built.** B-151's release backstop lived inside `runDelinquencyTimeline`, **after** the guard that returns `skippedNoTimeline` for a facility with no configured timeline — so the sites most likely to have locks stuck on ended leases were the only ones it could never reach. It is now its own nightly job step, `delinquency.stuck-overlocks`, unconditional on timeline configuration. The removal task's label stopped asserting a payment, the reason moved into a new `Task.detail`, the reconciliation list gained a `stuck_no_lease` state, and the units board says a lock-with-no-tenant is not rentable.

**What it decided.**

**A sweep, not the one-off repair the row asked for.** B-151's own reasoning — quoted back at it — is that a nightly job that fixes what it finds cannot be forgotten the way a script can. `releaseStuckOverlocks` is idempotent and runs every night, so its first run **is** the repair and there is nothing to remember to run twice.

**The backstop was moved, not copied.** Left in the engine as well it would be a second copy of one rule with two places to drift; the engine's `continue` now carries a comment pointing at the job and saying why it could not work from there.

**The label states the fact; `Task.detail` states the reason.** B-058 wrote "the tenant has paid" for the cure path and it was true of it. B-151 then raised the same task after a lease ended, after an auction sale and after an abandonment — so the card asserted a payment that had not happened on the two paths where the tenant most certainly had not paid, and a staffer walked out expecting a grateful customer. The type cannot know which of five reasons produced it; the caller always does. `Task.detail` is generic rather than overlock-shaped for the same reason B-115's `subject` was: this is the second instance of "a card with nothing on it that its own creator could have supplied".

**The sweep reads the lease's own `moveOutReason`** rather than saying a blanket "lease ended", so a lock left after an abandonment says so. `UnitOverlock.removalReason` records it on the lock itself — "was this removed because they paid, or because we sold their things" is a question the record has to answer without a join.

**`stuck_no_lease` is flagged immediately, not after 24 hours.** Every other mismatch on that screen is a staff member not having got there yet. This one is a unit that has fallen out of sellable inventory with nothing in any queue about it, and waiting a day to say so is the same silence the state exists to break. It sorts above `awaiting_removal`, and a lock whose removal HAS been asked for is not stuck — it is already visible and already ageing.

**The units board derives it from two facts it already had.** `status === 'overlocked' && !occupant` needed no fifth query: a unit reading `overlocked` with nobody in it is not a tenant behind on rent, and the board previously showed the ordinary delinquency badge for it. All three layouts (table, grid tile, mobile card) say it in words, linked to the removal task list.

**Test verification.** Full unit suite **3,687 passed, 8 skipped of 3,695** (220 files passed, 1 skipped), **exit 0**, and run twice. Typecheck, lint, `next build` and `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` clean. Nine new tests: two in `tests/overlock-reconciliation.test.ts` pinning the new state and that a requested removal is not "stuck"; seven in `tests/overlock-db.test.ts` — the reason on the card for an auction sale and for a cure, and five on the sweep including **a facility with no delinquency timeline at all**, which is the case the whole item exists for.

**A fixture bug found and fixed.** `tests/overlock-db.test.ts` shares one lease row across the file and its `beforeEach` never reset the lease status, so the sweep's tests — the first in the file to END the lease — leaked `ended` into "leaves a live lease alone". It passed or failed on run order. The reset is now in `beforeEach` beside the unit's.

**Left behind.** **`deriveUnitStatus` still returns `overlocked` for a unit with no lease**, ahead of the `maintenance` a move-out sets. Changing that is an occupancy-math change with reporting consequences well beyond this row, so the board and the reconciliation screen NAME the state instead; the number in the occupancy denominator is unchanged and still correct per B-151 (there is a real lock on the door). **The sweep is per-facility and nightly**, so a lock stuck this morning is queued tonight rather than immediately — the three lease-ending paths still release in their own transaction, and this only catches what they miss. **`Task.detail` has exactly one writer.** Every other task type still says only what its type means, and several of them (`gate_manual_action`, `settling_payment_failed`) have a creator who knows more than the label does. **No e2e spec** covers the stuck state or the new banner.

## B-170 — Two of four proof fields, and an announcement that died with the row it reported on

`dedbc57`

**What it built.** `TaskCompleteForm` renders one labelled control for **every** field the task's own gate requires, from one label map; the gate itself now reads the configured delinquency step as well as the catalog; and the four task queues, the promotions list and the tenant page's returned-payment list announce their outcomes from a live region **above** the list, which the outcome cannot unmount.

**What it decided.**

**The gate and the form read one list, resolved in one function.** `requiredProofFieldsFor` unions the catalog's fields with the configured step's for a `delinquency_step` task, and `facilityTasks` and `completeTask` both call it. This was the actual defect under the row's first finding: both shipped certified-mail steps require `tracking_number` and `delivered_on`, `completeTask` gated only on the catalog's `['note']`, so those tasks closed on a note and `auctionReadiness` — which reads the STEP's fields against `Task.proof` — then blocked the sale for ever on evidence no screen in the product could record. A form that asks for less than the gate demands is a task nobody can close; one that asks for more is a refusal nobody can act on. One function is the only way they cannot drift.

**`PROOF_FIELD_LABELS` is typed `Record<ProofField, …>`, so a fifth proof field is a build failure.** `TaskTypeSpec.requiredProofFields` was widened from `readonly string[]` to `readonly ProofField[]` to make that reach the catalog too. The two hand-rolled label maps on the delinquency settings screen and the notices screen now read the shared one — the notices screen keeps `email_address`, which is a delivery proof and not a member of `PROOF_FIELDS`. The raw-enum refusal (`` `${field} is required.` ``) is gone: every message is built from the map.

**The announcement is pushed from the action, not from an effect.** `AnnounceRegion` holds the message and the focus; `AdminForm` gains an opt-in `announceOutside` that calls into it from inside `rememberSubmission`, **after `await action(...)` and before returning**. An effect on `state` would not do: by the time the success state commits, the `revalidatePath` it triggered may already have unmounted the form, and an effect that never runs announces nothing. The push happens while the form is still mounted and lands in state owned by a component the revalidation does not touch. This is `components/marketing/form-result.tsx`'s structural move — put the region where the outcome cannot remove it — applied to the admin side, which B-148 never reached.

**Opt-in, not product-wide.** Every other admin form stays mounted through its own success and is right to keep the message where the reader already is. Six forms take it: the shared `TaskCompleteForm` (four queues), promotions' status buttons, and the tenant page's "Record the return".

**The success message names its subject.** `Task completed: Returned mail — contact info may be stale, Dana Delinquent`, from a hidden field the card already had for its button's `aria-label`; the promotion status message names the promotion. Not decoration: a live region rewritten with **identical** text is no DOM mutation and therefore no announcement, so two completions in a row would have announced once. It also makes the message useful after the card is gone.

**The idle region is `sr-only`, never `empty:hidden`.** `display: none` takes the element out of the accessibility tree until the moment it has text, which is the same "region that appears with the event" failure one layer down — the failure `AdminForm`'s own comment documents and B-111 fixed product-wide. `sr-only` is `position: absolute`, so an empty region also contributes no `gap` to the flex column these pages lay their sections out with.

**Test verification.** Full unit suite **3,688 passed, 8 skipped of 3,696** (220 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0. Typecheck (including `tests/` and `e2e/`), lint and `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` clean; the e2e run's own production build succeeded. `e2e/admin-tasks.spec.ts`: **15 passed, 3 skipped, exit 0** — the returned-mail flow now also asserts the visible `<label>`, that the announcement survives the card (`role="status"` contains the named message) and that focus did not fall to `<body>`; four new tests assert the page-level region is mounted and empty at load on each queue.

**A test bug found and fixed.** `admin-tasks.spec.ts` asserted the completion by `getByText('Returned mail — contact info may be stale')` on the whole page. Now that the message names the task it completed, that string is still on the page — in the announcement. Scoped to the card, which is what "it cleared the list" actually means.

**Left behind.** **`Task.detail`-style per-task proof is still catalog-plus-step only** — a caller that knows a task needs something the step did not configure has no way to say so. **The e2e refusal test still self-skips against an empty queue**: the freshly seeded demo carries no open tasks, so `a refused completion says why` ran on neither project this session; the refusal itself is pinned by `tests/tasks-db.test.ts`. **Completion is only driven end-to-end on `/admin/tasks`** — the other three queues get the structural assertion, because completing a delinquency or keypad task mutates shared demo fixtures with none of B-120's three disciplines available. **The promotions and returned-payment announcements have no e2e of their own.** **B-176 owns the `aria-label`s on the promotions status buttons** and B-178 the returned-payment form's controls; this row touched neither beyond adding the hidden field the message needs.

## B-171 — Both public marketing forms were silent on the error path

`91f99d4`

**What it built.** `FormResult` writes its live region on the **error** branch as well as the success one, moves focus to it either way, and renders a refusal in red rather than in the hardcoded green of a confirmation. Both public forms — the sold-out waitlist notify-me and the quote/callback — get an e2e test of their refused state, including the first axe scan either has ever had.

**What it decided.**

**One component, both branches, no new region.** `{success ? state.message : ''}` was the whole defect: the region stayed empty on `status: 'error'`, so the summary was discarded and focus stayed on the submit. The only evidence of a refusal was a `<span>` beside the field, reachable by swiping backwards — so a screen-reader user could not tell "we refused this" from "we accepted it and said nothing", on **every** error path of both forms (`joinWaitlistAction` always sets `fieldErrors.email`; `submitLeadAction` always returns a `fieldError`). B-148 fixed the success branch only, and `e2e/smoke.spec.ts` tested only success, which is why it survived.

**The focus effect keys on `state`, not on a boolean.** A second refusal is a new state object but the same `error === true`, so an effect keyed on the boolean would not re-fire: a visitor who fixes one field and is refused for another would be left standing on the submit. This is the same class of bug as B-170's identical-text-no-announcement, one layer up.

**The summary wording is left as each action already writes it.** The waitlist announces its actual problem ("Enter an email address we can reach you at."); the lead form announces `fieldError`'s "There is a problem with one field." Converting the waitlist to `fieldError` for symmetry would have made its announcement strictly less useful — a one-field form whose region says only that one field is wrong.

**A field-naming bug found by the new test, not by review.** The lead form's `Field` wrapped its hint **and** its error inside the `<label>`, so both became part of the field's accessible NAME as well as its description: the phone field was named `Phone Required if you would like a call back.` at rest, and a refused email field was named `Email An email address or a phone number — we need one way to reply.` — the refusal read out as the field's identity and then again as its description (2.4.6). Fixed to `htmlFor` plus siblings, which is the shape `WaitlistForm` beside it already used. axe does not flag this; the test caught it because `getByLabel('Email', { exact: true })` stopped matching.

**A test trap worth naming.** The first version of the waitlist spec submitted before React had hydrated, which posts the form **natively** — the page navigates, the disclosure collapses and the inline state is lost, leaving an empty green region. That reads exactly like this item's bug. The spec now mirrors the success test's opening sequence (`toBeHidden` → `expectPreexisting` → open → `toBeVisible`) so the interaction cannot outrun hydration.

**Both refusals write nothing to the database**, so neither needs any of B-120's three disciplines: the waitlist is refused by `isPlausibleEmail` before any row, and the lead is refused before any `Lead` is written — which also means it never walks toward US-8 AC4's five-per-ten-minutes limit the way a successful submit would.

**The accessibility statement was re-read and deliberately not strengthened.** Its bullet claims a rejection's message is tied to the field and that a successful save is announced; both were true before and are still true. It never claimed that a *rejection* is announced, and it still does not — that would be a claim about every public form, and only these two are built on `FormResult`; checkout's steps render their own refusals. The re-verification is recorded in the page's comment chain with the reasoning.

**Test verification.** Full unit suite **3,688 passed, 8 skipped of 3,696** (220 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0. Typecheck, lint and `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` clean. `e2e/smoke.spec.ts` filtered to the four marketing-form tests plus the sold-out flow: **12 passed, exit 0**, both projects.

**Left behind.** **The `type="email"` refusal is only reachable with a domain that has no dot** (`someone@localhost`), because the browser blocks anything less plausible before the server sees it — the spec says so where it does it. **Checkout's own refusals are untouched** and are not on `FormResult`; making the statement's bullet claim announced rejections everywhere waits on that. **No unit test for `FormResult`** — the repo has no component-test harness, and the e2e covers both branches on both forms. **The refused states are scanned but the route-versus-state gap is still B-184's**: two states are now covered, the general problem is not.

## B-172 — Checkout's unit-lost branch stops being a display

`4d181cd`

**What it built.** `relockAtSize` — the branch's way forward when the size itself has gone. Each alternative size is now a submit that re-points the session onto it, re-quotes the rate, re-evaluates the promotion and returns the renter to the step they were on. The branch also stopped quoting a unit the renter no longer has, stopped reading as glyph noise to a screen reader, and got the first axe scan it has ever had.

**What it decided.**

**Three things are re-derived, not carried, because this is a different product.** The **rate** comes from `currentRateForUnitType` — carrying the locked one would sell a 10×15 at a 10×10's price. The **promotion** is re-evaluated through `offerFor`, because a promotion can be scoped to unit types (`not_for_this_size`) and carrying the snapshot would apply an offer to a size it was never valid for; a code the renter typed rides along and is re-judged rather than trusted, exactly as `applyPromoCodeAction` re-judges it. The **unit** is claimed with the same `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` every other path uses.

**Both the session columns AND the basket line move.** The basket is what the money path sums; a session whose columns moved and whose line did not would summarise and charge the size that had gone. The primary line is identified the way `removeUnitFromBasket` identifies it.

**Refused from the payment step onward, in the service rather than only in the UI.** `createChargeIntent`'s idempotency key is `charge:v2:checkout:<sessionId>`, and Stripe remembers the parameters a key was first used with for 24 hours — so an intent already made for the old size comes back at the **old amount** however the basket changes. Moving a size under it would charge the renter for the unit they lost. The panel's copy and the server's guard read the same condition, so the screen never offers a button the server would refuse.

**The copy only claims the answers are reusable when they are.** "Everything you have entered is still here" was true and unusable — B-149 shipped it beside a control that could only re-claim the size that had just gone. It now branches: the same-size relock, the size move, or (when neither is possible) a sentence that says so and sends them to the phone or the facility page instead.

**No second live region.** The first cut added an `AnnounceRegion`, since a successful move removes the panel that would report it — B-170's failure exactly. But `CheckoutAnnouncer` already exists for this transition, already survives it and already moves focus to the step heading. It only needed to learn that the size can change as well as the unit: "we found you another unit **the same size**" would otherwise be the announcement contradicting the screen. One prop, no new mechanism.

**The button is named on the button.** `aria-label` on the wrapping `AdminForm` buys nothing — no screen reader composes a form's label into its descendants' names, which is the rule `task-complete-form.tsx` states in a comment on the component created to fix it. Caught by the e2e, having made the same mistake the codebase documents.

**The price summary and the code box are suppressed while the lock is lapsed**, rather than restated in the past tense. The figure is void either way, and the price of every size the renter CAN take is on the button beside it.

**Deliberately out of scope:** a recommender, as B-149 already ruled. The facility's own ordering is the ordering.

**Two real bugs found along the way.**

**The lapsed panel rendered on a COMPLETED checkout.** `session.lockLapsed` is derived from the clock alone, so a renter who had paid and came back to their link half an hour later was shown "We couldn't keep that unit" and a "Find me another unit" button — while the "You are moved in" confirmation, which lives inside the `!lockLapsed` section, was hidden from them. The page now derives `lockLapsed` with `step !== 'provisioned' && status !== 'completed'`, and `relock` — which had no status guard at all and would have re-claimed a unit for a finished checkout — refuses a completed session.

**A fixture reading a different clock from the code it asserts against.** `tests/rate-increase-db.test.ts`'s `daysFromNow` used `now.getUTCDate()` while `renoticeRateIncrease` uses `businessDateFor(new Date(), facility.timezone)`. The two agree only until 19:00 CDT; after that the helper is a day ahead and the suite fails as "expected 1790121600000 to be 1790208000000", which reads like broken arithmetic. Latent since the file was written, surfaced at 23:41. The same trap CLAUDE.md records for quiet-hours messaging, one module over.

**Test verification.** Full unit suite **3,693 passed, 8 skipped of 3,701** (220 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0. Typecheck, lint and `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` clean. Five new `relockAtSize` tests in `tests/checkout-db.test.ts` pin the re-point, the re-quote, a sold-out target, a foreign facility's unit type, the payment-step refusal and that neither relock path revives a completed checkout. New `e2e/checkout-unit-lost.spec.ts`: **6 passed, exit 0**, both projects; the whole public suite (`smoke.spec.ts` plus the new file) **148 passed, 4 skipped, exit 0**.

**The new e2e builds its own facility.** Reaching this branch means taking a whole size to zero available, and doing that to shared demo inventory is exactly the unscoped mutation B-120 forbids — every other checkout spec would then fail with "sold out" for a reason unrelated to the code. Isolated, it needs none of B-120's three disciplines and is repeatable against an un-reseeded database. Three fixture traps cost it four runs and are named in the file: both browser projects race on one slug unless it is per-project; two unit types cannot share a name at one facility; and the serial tests must reset the size they just sold out.

**Left behind.** **Only the primary basket line moves.** A multi-unit basket keeps its other lines pointed at their original units, which is `relock`'s existing behaviour and not a regression — but `expireCheckoutSessions` releases only `session.unitId`, so a lapsed multi-unit basket has line units nobody released. That is a pre-existing gap and wants its own row when N > 1 is real. **A renter at the payment step cannot move size** and is told to call or start again; making that possible needs the charge reference to carry the quote, which is a payments change well beyond this row. **Two live regions carry overlapping text** on a successful move — the announcer's sentence and `PriceSummary`'s change note — because explaining why the figures moved is a different job from reporting the action. **The branch is scanned in one STATE, not in general**: B-184 still owns route-versus-state.

## B-173 — One form, one truth: the date you typed is the date that posts

`67f874d`

**What it built.** All four move-out and transfer screens — `/admin/tenants/[id]/move-out`, `/admin/tenants/[id]/transfer`, `/portal/move-out`, `/portal/transfer` — had the same shape: a `method="GET"` form whose only submit was "Recalculate", and a separate committing form carrying a hidden date built from the URL. Changing Sep 1 to Sep 5 and pressing **Complete move-out** closed the lease on Sep 1, silently, after showing the tenant a Sep 5 settlement. Nothing on any of the four screens said the picker was inert until a second button had been pressed. The preview control now lives inside the committing form, and `stalePreview` refuses the commit while it and the priced value disagree.

**What it decided.**

**The row offered the two fixes as alternatives; both were needed.** "Either the date control lives inside the committing form, or the commit re-reads it" — but moving the control alone only mirrors the defect. What posts becomes the typed date, and the figures above it were still worked out for the old one: the same lie with the operands swapped, on the screen that ends a tenancy. So the control is a field of the committing form **and** `stalePreview` (`lib/admin/form-state.ts`) compares it against a `previewed_<name>` hidden twin and returns a `fieldError` naming the value now in the control.

**A missing `previewed_` twin refuses rather than passes.** Absent both fields the comparison would be `'' === ''` and every commit would sail through — so the twin is rendered as a hidden input beside its control on every screen and never derived anywhere else, and a control with no twin is treated as moved. A unit test pins that specifically, because it is the failure mode that would make the guard decorative without anything going red.

**Recalculate stayed one control, not two.** One HTML control cannot feed two forms, and the obvious workarounds (duplicating the picker, a client-side `onChange` navigation) either put two dates on screen or make the guard depend on JavaScript. The native answer is that a submit button whose `formAction` is a **string** is the one case React hands back to the browser: `react-dom`'s form plugin takes the submitter's `formAction` over the form's function action, and only calls `preventDefault` when what it ends up with is a function. So "Recalculate" / "Update" / "Show me what it costs" is a `formMethod="get"` submit of the committing form. Verified in the built app, not assumed — the three existing round-trip specs are what prove it.

**The guard covers the unit and the rate, not just the date.** Same form, same mechanism, same silence: the transfer screens committed the previously-previewed **unit** if the picker moved after pricing, and the admin one the previously-previewed **rate**. Guarding only the date the row named would have left two live instances of the defect one field over.

**Enter re-prices instead of committing.** The pricing submit is first in DOM order in the merged form, so it is the implicit submitter — pressing Enter in the date field can no longer commit money. Not designed for; worth keeping deliberately.

**The commit button restates the day in its own accessible name** ("Complete move-out on Sep 5, 2026", "Transfer to unit 104 on Sep 5, 2026", "Request Unit 104 from September 5, 2026"), because 2.4.6 is about the control, and the subject was several fields further up the page.

**The charge-fee disclosure moved above the picker** on `/admin/tenants/[id]/move-out`. The committing form now starts at the picker and a `<form>` cannot nest inside another one. B-167's property is unchanged — it is still above the settlement, so posting a fee and reloading shows it in the figures underneath.

**The two portal pickers became `Field`s**, so a refusal carries `aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` rather than only appearing in the summary. The portal transfer unit **fieldset** was deliberately left raw: `FieldSet`'s legend drops `text-sm`, and `e2e/portal-transfer.spec.ts` asserts no horizontal overflow at 200% text zoom — a styling change to buy an `aria-invalid` the error summary already announces was not worth putting that at risk.

**The accessibility statement was re-read and needed no change.** It has never made a claim about error prevention on the money path — worth recording rather than quietly fixing. What it does say about forms (a rejection is tied to its field, a save is announced) was true before and is still true.

**Test verification.** Full unit suite **3,697 passed, 8 skipped of 3,705** (220 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0. Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`), lint and `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` all clean. Four new `stalePreview` tests in `tests/form-state.test.ts`. E2E over the four affected specs: **34 passed, 2 skipped of 36, exit 0**, both browser projects, run twice.

**One test bug found along the way, mine.** The new regression spec located the refusal with a bare `getByRole('alert')`, which on Dana's over-threshold lease resolves to three elements — the manager-override panel, Next's route announcer, and the summary being looked for — so strict mode failed it before the summary had rendered. It reads exactly like "the guard did not fire". Filtered by text now, with the reason in a comment.

**Left behind.** **The refusal is a STATE and no axe scan reaches it** — B-184's route-versus-state gap, and unlike B-171 and B-172 this row does not close it for its own states: the guard is asserted end-to-end on the admin move-out screen only, and the two portal refusals rest on `stalePreview`'s unit tests. **A GET submit now serializes the whole committing form into the URL** (`writeOff`, `reason`, the recapture figure), which is ugly and harmless — the pages read only `lease`, `date`, `unit` and `rate`. **B-174's holes in `/portal/move-out` are untouched** — the preview panel that vanishes with no message, and the date picker with no ceiling — and are still B-174's, one row down.

## B-174 — The portal move-out preview stops vanishing in silence

`00ec8a4`

**What it built.** `/portal/move-out` kept only the `ok` branch of its preview, so a refused date rendered a blank where the settlement had been while "Request this move-out" stayed live and pressable beside it — a page byte-identical to a working one except for the missing money (3.3.1). B-142 fixed exactly this on the sibling transfer screen and the fix never crossed one file. The refusal is now a `role="alert"`, the figures and the submit are gone together, the picker has a ceiling on both sides of the wire, and a dead field is deleted.

**What it decided.**

**`noticeShortfallDays` was deleted, and the reason matters more than the deletion.** The row offered "shown to the tenant or deleted". `noticeGivenAt` is written in exactly two places in the whole codebase, both in `lib/portal/move-out.ts` — stamped by `requestMoveOut`, cleared by `cancelMoveOutRequest` — and the picker only renders when there is no request outstanding. So on this screen the field is **always null**, and `noticeShortfallDays(null, …)` returns the full required notice by design. The figure was a constant equal to `moveOutNoticeDays`, not a measurement of anything: rendering it with the admin screen's sentence would have told a tenant picking a date at or beyond the floor that they were ten days short of notice they were in the act of giving. The notice rule lives in the floor on this screen — `min` on the picker, `date_too_soon` on the server — and that is the right place for it.

**The ceiling is 365 days, a module constant rather than a facility column.** The longest thing a tenant can legitimately be giving notice against is a twelve-month term ending; past that it is a mistyped year. A column that configures behaviour has to ship with an operator control in the same item (CLAUDE.md's own rule, learned from `billingPolicy` and four siblings), and nothing has asked for this to vary by site — when something does, that item adds the column and the field together.

**Both bounds moved into one `moveOutDateProblem`, shared by the preview and the write.** A screen that refuses what the write accepts (or the reverse) is how the two drift, and this defect is what that drift looks like: the floor was checked in `requestMoveOut` only, the ceiling in neither, and the preview refused nothing at all. That last part is why the alert had nothing to say — there was no refusal to render, only figures for an impossible date.

**The submit is hidden, not disabled, when there is nothing priced behind it.** A disabled button is not focusable and announces nothing, so a keyboard or screen-reader user meets silence where a sighted one at least sees something greyed out. The `role="alert"` above already says why the figures are missing. The reassurance sentence goes with the button, because it promises a date the server has just refused.

**One copy map for the screen.** The action carried a four-entry near-duplicate of the refusals the lib now owns; it spreads the shared map and adds only `already_requested`. A refusal worded one way when the preview says it and another when the submit does is two answers to one question.

**The refused state is scanned.** `e2e/portal-move-out.spec.ts` drives it straight off the URL — no interaction, no mutation, repeatable against shared demo data — and runs axe on it. One more of B-184's route-versus-state gaps closed for one state, the way B-171 and B-172 closed theirs. B-173, one row up, did not close its own; this one does.

**A real bug found, and deliberately not fixed here.** Because nothing outside the portal ever writes `noticeGivenAt`, the **admin** move-out screen reports the full notice period as a shortfall for every walk-in tenant. Someone who gave thirty days' notice at the counter has none recorded, there is no control anywhere that records it, and the screen says "This is 10 days short of the notice the lease asks for. Recorded, not blocked." It is defensible as "no notice on record" and it is still a figure that is wrong for most tenants who ever move out. Wants its own row rather than a quiet fix inside this one.

**Test verification.** Full unit suite **3,701 passed, 8 skipped of 3,709** (220 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0; `tests/move-out-request-db.test.ts` run twice, 23 passed both times. Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`), lint and `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` clean. Five new cases pin both bounds on both the preview and the write, plus the boundary day itself — an off-by-one there refuses a tenant giving notice against the end of a twelve-month term, which is the exact case the ceiling was sized for.

**A test bug found, mine, and the second instance of it.** Two existing preview tests passed a fixed calendar date (`2026-12-01`) to a function that had no bounds; adding bounds would have made them go red on a date nobody chose. They compute from the real clock now. And both new e2e cases first located the refusal with a bare `getByRole('alert')`, which is a strict-mode violation on **every page in the product** — Next renders an always-present `role="alert"` route announcer outside `<main>`. It fails before the refusal has rendered, which reads exactly like the refusal not firing. Scoped to `<main>`, with the reason in a comment, after making the same mistake in B-173 one hour earlier.

**Left behind.** **The ceiling does not vary by facility** — a module constant, for the reason above. **The walk-in `noticeGivenAt` gap** described above is untouched and belongs to a row of its own. **B-182 still owns the wording** of the lien-pipeline refusal this screen renders ("Please ring them"), which is on its list already.

## B-175 — The lease says what a broken minimum stay costs

`424c30f`

**What it built.** The signed agreement stated the minimum stay and stopped there. `lib/lease/build.ts`'s `termSummary` was deliberately silent on consequence — B-144's choice, and correct at the time, because nothing recovered anything and a signed promise to claw a discount back would have been a term the operator did not do. B-145 then built `recaptureFor` and the charge became real; the sentence stayed silent. The word "recovered" first reached the tenant on the move-out screen, with the amount already computed and the tenant already leaving. It now names the consequence, branched on the facility's `promoRecapturePolicy`.

**What it decided.**

**The wording moved to sit beside the arithmetic.** `minStayTermSummary` lives in `packages/core/promotions/recapture.ts`, not in `lib/lease/build.ts` where the sentence has always been. The row's acceptance criterion is that the lease and the arithmetic "move together or not at all", and where a function lives decides which test is the obvious one to write: sharing a file with `recaptureFor` makes "assert the sentence and the number under the same policy" the natural thing, where a sentence three modules away makes it a thing somebody has to remember. The gap this row closes is precisely a thing somebody did not remember, twice, across B-144 and B-145.

**`none` is left exactly as B-144 wrote it, and that is not an oversight.** At a facility that recovers nothing, a sentence saying we will charge the discount back is the same defect mirrored — a signed term the operator does not do. The minimum stay is a condition with no consequence there, which is its own problem and B-176's, one row down.

**Two tests, because they fail for different reasons.** The pure one pins each policy's sentence against the amount `recaptureFor` returns under it: `full` promises the whole discount and charges exactly `discountGivenCents`; `prorated` promises the unserved share and charges a third of it for two of six months unserved, asserted as both the exact figure and as strictly less than the whole — which is the entire difference the two sentences describe. The DB one pins the **wiring**: that the facility's own column is what reaches the signed document. `minStayTermSummary` could be correct while `buildLease` passed it a hardcoded `none`, and that is the exact shape of the bug being fixed.

**The DB test restores the policy in a `finally`.** The facility is shared with every other test in that file, and a policy left flipped would charge recaptures in suites that never asked for one — B-120's discipline applied to a unit fixture rather than an e2e one.

**PRD 02 US-10 gained the acceptance criterion.** It had one requiring the minimum stay be *stated* on the lease (B-144's) and none requiring the consequence, which is how the sentence stayed silent through B-145 without anything going red.

**Test verification.** Full unit suite **3,707 passed, 8 skipped of 3,715** (220 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0; the two touched files run twice, 37 passed both times. Typecheck, lint and `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` clean.

**A test bug found along the way, mine.** The first cut of the DB test invented a `startCheckout({ promotion: … })` shape that does not exist — the real key is `promo`, and it carries `terms` and `promoCodeId` as well — and called `offerFor` without `isNewTenant`, so no offer was returned and it died on `null.promotionId` rather than on anything to do with leases. Mirrored on the sibling test in the same file, which had it right all along.

**Left behind.** **No e2e.** Reaching the changed sentence means a facility whose recapture policy is not the `none` default, and flipping the shared demo facility is the unscoped mutation B-120 forbids; the DB test covers the wiring instead. **The `none`-with-a-minimum-stay case is untouched** — a term stated on a signed lease that nothing enforces — and is B-176's, which is the row that makes the two settings mention each other.

## B-176 — The screen that sets a minimum stay now says whether anything enforces it

`cef567c`

**What it built.** `minStayMonths` is set on `/admin/settings/promotions`; `promoRecapturePolicy` is set on `/admin/settings`; neither screen mentioned the other. The promotions field hinted that the minimum stay "is stated on the lease and in checkout" and said nothing about whether anything is recovered, while the policy defaults to `none` — "Nothing — the discount is theirs to keep". An operator could therefore run a six-month minimum for a year in the belief it was enforced, and it was decoration. Three things close it: the field states the facility's **current** policy with a link to the setting; submitting a minimum stay at a `none` facility returns a confirm-and-echo step naming the consequence before anything is created; and any minimum stay the facility does not recover is appended with "· not recovered on early move-out" in the list.

**What it decided.**

**The operator's sentence lives beside the arithmetic, exactly as B-175's does.** `minStayEnforcementSummary` sits in `packages/core/promotions/recapture.ts` next to `minStayTermSummary` and `recaptureFor`, and the page hint and the confirm echo both read it. Two screens describing the same policy in two hand-written strings is the shape of the defect this row fixes, one layer up; and putting it there makes "assert the sentence beside the amount `recaptureFor` returns under that policy" the obvious test rather than a remembered one.

**The confirm step exists because a promotion cannot be edited after creation.** `createPromotion`, `setPromotionStatus` and `addPromoCode` are the only writers — there is no update path. So the operator who believes the term is enforced cannot correct it later, only end the promotion and start a new one, and the ordinary 3.3.4 reasoning about irreversible money settings applies exactly as it does to a tax component. The create form now says so in a line of its own, which was missing and read as a draft you could come back to.

**The confirm waits for a name.** `createPromotion` refuses a nameless promotion anyway, and echoing "(unnamed)" back is a confirmation of nothing — that refusal goes first, and the confirm is what the second submit meets.

**A per-row control is named by its row, not by its form.** The three status controls render once per promotion, so a rotor heard "Make live, Pause, End, Make live, Pause, End…" with nothing saying which promotion (2.4.6). Both the visible text and the accessible name now come from one `statusAction` helper, so they cannot disagree. The wrapping `AdminForm`'s `label` was carrying `${status} ${promotion.name}` — "active Summer Special", not a sentence — and it bought nothing either way: **no screen reader composes a form's label into its descendants' accessible names**, the rule stated in a comment on `task-complete-form.tsx`, the component created to fix this same defect on the task queues.

**`Field`'s `hint` is a `React.ReactNode` now.** A hint whose whole job is to point at the setting it depends on has to be able to carry the link there. `label` was already a node for the same class of reason, and the prop is still serializable across the server/client boundary.

**Test verification.** Full unit suite **3,711 passed, 8 skipped of 3,719** (220 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0. Production build, typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`), lint and `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` clean. Four new pure cases in `tests/promo-recapture.test.ts` pin each policy's operator sentence against what `recaptureFor` charges under it, and one asserts the half that matters: the `none` sentence is the only one that must not read as an enforcement.

**Left behind.** **The link points at `/admin/settings`, not at the field.** The recapture control is deep in that page and `Field` generates its id with `useId`, so there is no stable anchor to link to; the hint names the setting's exact label instead. A stable id per settings field is worth doing when something else needs one. **No e2e.** Reaching the interesting branch means a facility whose policy is not `none`, and flipping the shared demo facility is the unscoped mutation B-120 forbids. **Nothing warns retroactively:** a promotion created before this shipped, carrying a minimum stay at a `none` facility, is flagged only in the list line — there is no task, no report row and no prompt to fix the policy.

## B-177 — The rate screen names the tenant instead of asking for a cuid

`2fca73d`

**What it built.** Both money forms on `/admin/rate-increases` took a free-text **"Lease ID"** with the hint "From the tenant's lease page", while the eligible table directly above them already listed every tenant, unit and current rate and offered no action at all. So the workflow was copy a cuid, paste a cuid — and a mistyped one permanently reduced a **different** tenant's rate, with a reason code recorded against them and nothing between the paste and the commit. B-153 shipped that as its own named left-behind and B-166's re-notice made it worse by requiring the same paste again. Both forms now take a picker of the facility's occupying leases, the eligible rows carry links that prefill it, and both return a confirm step before anything is written.

**What it decided.**

**A native `<select>`, not a combobox.** Every option is a real lease with the tenant, the unit and what they pay now on it, so there is no id to mistype and nothing on offer that a rate change is illegal on — an ended lease is refused by both services, so listing one is offering a dead end. It is linear in units, which is marked with a `ponytail:` comment: a facility large enough for that to bite wants a typeahead over a search endpoint, not a longer `<select>`.

**The per-row links are plain links, and the prefill is a query parameter.** `?raise=<leaseId>&rate=129.00#oneoff-heading` and `?lower=<leaseId>#decrease-heading` — no client JS, no state to keep in sync, and the form still refuses everything the service refuses. A prefill is only honoured when it names a lease that is actually in the picker, so a `rate` cannot render into the form beside no tenant at all.

**The confirm echo is read from the database, never from the form.** The current rate is the figure the operator is being asked to agree the change *against*; echoing back a number the browser supplied would confirm whatever the page happened to be showing rather than what is true. The helper returns `null` when the lease is missing or belongs to another facility, and the action then falls through to the service, which owns that refusal's wording — the echo describes, it never duplicates a rule.

**Nothing pre-flights the service's own refusals.** A rate that is not higher, an effective date inside the notice period, or a lease that already carries a live increase are still reported after the confirm rather than before it. Re-checking them in the action is exactly the "screen refuses what the write accepts" drift B-174 fixed by moving both bounds into one function, and the alternative — a dry-run flag through both schedule paths — buys ordering for a case the prefilled defaults make rare.

**`confirmLabel` was added to the confirm state.** The button was hardcoded "Yes, add it", which is right for an append-only tax component and wrong here; it now reads "Yes, lower this rate". Naming the act is most of what the step is for.

**The retention-save section is gated on `credits:manual` at this facility.** It rendered for anyone who reached the page and was refused on submit. Hoisting the gate the service already applies is what lets the picker require one of the two authorities *at this facility* without turning a graceful refusal into an error page for a manager whose authority is at another site.

**Per-row controls are named by their row.** "Approve" and "Cancel" rendered once per increase with identical accessible names and identical styling side by side, so the rotor read "Approve, Cancel, Approve, Cancel…" and the destructive one was a row-misread away (2.4.6). Each now carries an `aria-label` with tenant and unit, Cancel is visually destructive, and the batch pair is named by what the batch holds ("Cancel 12 increases effective Sep 23, 2026"). The wrapping `AdminForm`'s label bought nothing — no screen reader composes a form's label into its descendants' names, the same rule B-176 applied to the promotions screen an hour earlier.

**Test verification.** Full unit suite **3,715 passed, 8 skipped of 3,723** (220 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0; `tests/rate-increase-db.test.ts` run twice, 64 passed both times. Production build, typecheck, lint and `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` clean. Four new cases pin the picker: it offers the tenant, unit and current rate; it never offers an ended lease; it is reachable on the retention-save authority alone; and it refuses an actor holding neither.

**Left behind.** **No test on the confirm steps themselves.** They live in server actions behind `requireStaffActor`, which nothing in `tests/` currently stands up; the axe pass over `/admin/rate-increases` covers the screen but not the second submit. **The "Lower this rate" link only appears where the eligible table does**, which needs `rates:tenant_increase` — a manager holding only `credits:manual` reaches the same form through the picker, one section down. **`Field`'s `hint` became a `React.ReactNode` in B-176 and is used as one here**; no other caller has been converted, and none needs to be.

## B-178 — The fee question says what it charges, and its answer matches its value

`c349796`

**What it built.** The returned-payment control on the tenant profile was a dropdown headed "Charge the fee?" whose first option read "Yes — charge the configured fee" and carried the value `"no"`, because the field was named `waiveFee`. The displayed answer was the opposite of the stored one on the one screen where a bank return is recorded, and it never stated the amount. It is now `chargeFee`, yes/no, rendered from one table the action reads back — and the facility's own configured figure is in the option text. Where the facility has priced no returned-payment fee there is no control at all, only a sentence. Same session, same class: the refund form's cheque-number input renders only for a cheque refund, and the four screens that printed raw reason-code keys ("collections uneconomic") read an operator label map instead.

**What it decided.**

**Label and stored value live in the same row, in `RETURN_FEE_CHOICES`.** Nothing could have caught the inversion, because the words and the value it submitted were two unrelated expressions in the same JSX — one careless edit from waiving every returned-payment fee at the counter, silently and permanently. They are now one table in `lib/billing/reversals.ts`, beside `returnPayment` itself, and `waiveFeeFromForm` is what the action reads. The test is the coupling: the option whose label starts with "Charge" must be the option that does not waive.

**An absent field waives, never charges.** `waiveFeeFromForm` returns `true` for null and for anything unrecognised. That is the only safe default given the second half of this row — the control is not rendered when the facility has priced no fee, so the field genuinely is absent on that submit.

**No fee configured is a sentence, not a dropdown.** A control offering to charge nothing is a question with no answer, and answering it wrote a `feeWaived: true` audit context that reads identically to a deliberate waiver. The paragraph says what will happen instead.

**The amount goes IN the option, not in a hint beside it.** The amount is the decision this screen is taking. `{amount}` in the label is substituted at render from `scheduledFeeCents(facilityId, 'nsf')` — the same schedule `assessNsfFee` reads inside the transaction, so the figure shown is the figure that posts. Two facilities on one profile get their own price each, which is why it is a map keyed on the returnable payment's facility rather than a single lookup.

**The control is named after its subject.** "Returned-payment fee", not "Charge the fee?" (2.4.6) — the action is in the options. The outcome still announces through B-170's page-level region, which matters more here than on most forms: recording the return removes the payment from `profile.returnable`, so the row reporting the outcome is the row the outcome deletes.

**The cheque number renders only for a cheque.** It was permanently visible under a hint reading "Cheques only." — a field inapplicable four fifths of the time on a form that moves money, with the instruction to skip it delegated to a hint. `RefundMethodFields` is a small client component holding the method select and the conditional field, the same disclosure `ChargeFeeForm` uses and for the same reason. **The spelling stays "Cheque"** — the product-wide D-15 pass to "check" is B-182's, and doing half of it here would hide the rest from that row's grep.

**`REASON_CODE_LABELS` went to the source, not to the screen the row named.** The backlog names `move-out/page.tsx`, which printed `code.replace(/_/g, " ")`. Two more screens — `/admin/units` and `/admin/units/setup` — passed the same codes through `labelForStatus`, whose fallback sentence-cases but cannot know that `collections_uneconomic` is "Not worth collecting". One exhaustive `Record<ReasonCode, string>` in `packages/core/audit/actions.ts`, beside `REASON_CODES`, read by all four; `labelForStatus` is no longer imported by either units page. A new reason code now fails to compile until it has words, which is the property `PROOF_FIELD_LABELS` (B-170) has and the reason this is the same device.

**`WAIVER_REASONS` on the tenant profile was deliberately left alone.** It is a narrowed list with context-specific wording — "Duplicate charge", "Other (explain in the note)" — and collapsing it into the shared map would make both worse.

**Test verification.** Full unit suite **3,720 passed, 8 skipped of 3,728** (221 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0. Production build, typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`), lint and `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` clean. Five new cases in `tests/return-fee-choice.test.ts`: the label/value coupling, exactly one charging option and one waiving one, the amount present in the charging label, the absent-field default, and an operator label for every reason code with no underscores left in any of them.

**Left behind.** **No e2e on either form.** `profile.returnable` needs a succeeded payment with a posted ledger entry and `profile.refundable` needs one too, and the demo seed creates no payments at all — so neither section renders on a seeded database and neither is reachable from a spec without the unscoped mutation B-120 forbids. The unit test covers the coupling; the rendering is covered by nothing, which is exactly the route-versus-state gap **B-184** owns. **The audit context still records `feeWaived`**, so a no-fee facility and a deliberate waiver remain distinguishable only by `feeCents: 0` versus the absence of a choice — the control's disappearance is not itself recorded. **Nothing back-fills.** Returns recorded before this shipped carry whatever the inverted control submitted, and there is no report that would show which. **The tenant profile is still seventeen stacked sections** — that is B-181, which depends on this row precisely because it is about to hide these controls behind disclosures.

## B-179 — A returned payment offers the pay route, not a phone number

`646e34e`

**What it built.** `/portal/documents` listed a bounced payment with the sentence "Returned unpaid by the bank. This amount is owed again — please call us" beside an amount column still showing the full payment as though it had landed, while `PayNowButton` sat one tap away on the dashboard. The tenant was asked to queue on a phone line to do what the next screen does in three taps, and the only signal the money was owed again was a sentence contradicting the figure next to it. The row now names the returned-payment fee if one was charged, marks the amount **in words** as returned, and offers the same `/portal/pay` route the dashboard uses — with the **facility's** line via `phoneFor` as the secondary route rather than the org number.

**What it decided.**

**The fee is read from the audit log, because nothing else ties it to the payment.** `assessNsfFee` raises an ordinary fee invoice through `raiseFeeInvoice`; `Invoice` has no column pointing back at the payment that caused it, and the ledger entry it posts carries no `paymentId` either. The one record that connects them is the `payment.returned` audit entry, whose context has held `feeCents` and `feeInvoiceNumber` since B-146 — indexed on `(entityType, entityId)`, one query for every returned payment in the list. Matching on the line-item description instead ("Returned payment fee — …") would be guesswork, and this figure is what decides whether the tenant understands a balance thirty dollars larger than the payment they are looking at.

**The pay link carries no amount of its own.** `/portal/pay?lease=X` sums the whole ledger through `payableLease`, so the reversal *and* the fee are already in the figure it prepares — the link text shows that same balance rather than the returned payment's amount. A link offering to pay $129 against a $159 balance would be a third number on a screen whose whole defect was numbers disagreeing.

**A lease that cannot take an online payment gets the phone, not a dead link.** `payableLease` requires an occupying lease, so a moved-out tenant following the link would land on "We couldn't find that unit on your account" — and a settled lease on "there's nothing to pay right now". `portalPayments` resolves both conditions itself and returns `payableCents: null`, which is what selects the `CallLink` branch. The tenant who most needs an explanation is the one whose account has already closed.

**The state is on the figure, in words.** "$129 / returned" under the amount, not a strikethrough and not a colour (1.4.1). B-146 put the sentence in the date column and left the money column saying the opposite; the two columns now agree without either relying on the other being read first.

**The pay link is named by its unit.** Several returned rows would otherwise offer links reading "Pay $159 now" with nothing distinguishing them in a rotor (2.4.4/2.4.6); the `aria-label` adds "on unit 12" where the unit is known.

**The enrichment costs nothing on an ordinary list.** `returnedPaymentContexts` is passed only the returned rows and returns an empty map before issuing a query when there are none — which is nearly every tenant. The three reads it does make run in parallel, and the lease read is scoped by `tenantId` as well as by id, per this file's rule that a read never relies on an earlier one having been scoped.

**Test verification.** Full unit suite **3,724 passed, 8 skipped of 3,732** (221 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0. Production build, typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`), lint and `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` clean. Four new cases in `tests/refunds-db.test.ts`, in the file that already stands up a real returned payment: the fee named and the balance offered (with the facility's own phone, not the org line); zero fee reported when the return was waived, so the tenant is never shown a charge nobody made; `payableCents: null` when the reversal left the lease settled; and no return context at all on an ordinary payment. Run twice, 33 passed both times.

**Left behind.** **The returned row is a state no scan reaches.** `/portal/documents` is in `SCANNED_ROUTES` and is scanned on every push, but the demo seed creates **no payments at all**, so the axe pass covers the ordinary rows only and the new links have never been scanned in place. That is the route-versus-state gap **B-184** owns, and it is now named on the accessibility page rather than left to be inferred from a green run. **The bottom-of-page "Need a receipt? Call…" paragraph still uses the org line**, deliberately: it is about the whole list, and a tenant with units at two facilities has no single facility line to give. **Nothing tells the tenant *when* the bank returned it** — the row still shows the date the payment was taken, which is the date on the receipt they hold, and the return date is not surfaced anywhere on the portal.

## B-180 — One email field for the whole quote table, and a confirmation that names the size

`f13465a`

**What it built.** The lead screen's waitlist capture rendered an email input **per size row**, labelled by nothing but a placeholder reading "Email" — which disappears the moment anything is typed, is unavailable to speech input, and asked a caller who wanted a 10x10 *and* a 10x20 for the same address twice. There is now one labelled field above the quote table, and each full size's **Join waitlist** button submits it. The confirmation names the size and the address it recorded instead of "On the waitlist."

**What it decided.**

**The per-row field was deleted, not relabelled.** Six visible labels reading "Email for waitlist alerts" down one column is a worse screen than the placeholder was, and the finding's real complaint — typed once per size — survives any amount of labelling. One field above the table is the fix; the labels follow from there.

**The buttons reach the form through the native `form=` owner attribute.** The email field lives in an `AdminForm` above the table and every "Join waitlist" button lives in a row, carrying its own `unitTypeId` as `name`/`value` on the submitter. No client component holds the address in state and no hidden input is mirrored into six forms. **This is why `AdminForm` gained an `id` prop and why the prop is not decoration:** React's `createFormDataWithSubmitter` copies the submitter's name and value into the submission by inserting a temporary input beside the submitter and tagging it `form="<id>"` — with no id on the form, that temp input is not owned by it, and every button still renders, still submits, and carries **no size at all**. That failure is silent, which is what the e2e spec exists to catch.

**`joinWaitlist` returns what the confirmation says.** The ok branch now carries `unitTypeName` and the **normalised** email, so "Added to the waitlist for the 10x20. We'll email ada@example.com…" reports what was recorded rather than echoing the box — an address typed as `ADA@Example.com` is stored, and confirmed, lowercased. The public form's copy is untouched: it deliberately gives the same words whether the visitor was already on the list or not, because that distinction is ours and not theirs.

**The success sentence says what a waitlist is not.** "…as soon as one is free — it is not a hold, and the first to complete a rental gets it." D-87's honest-copy obligation at the counter: a staffer reading "Added" to a caller must not leave them believing a unit is set aside.

**The empty-size case is refused by name.** The email field is `required`, so native validation covers an empty address across the form boundary. What it does not cover is a submission with no submitter — implicit submission from the field itself — so the action refuses an empty `unitTypeId` with "Press 'Join waitlist' on the row for the size they want" rather than passing it to `joinWaitlist`, which would report "That unit is no longer listed" and send a staffer looking for a delisted size.

**Test verification.** Full unit suite **3,724 passed, 8 skipped of 3,732** (221 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0. Production build (via the e2e `webServer`), typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`), lint and `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` clean. New `e2e/admin-leads.spec.ts`: an axe pass on the lead screen, and the wiring check — fill the one field, press one row's button, and assert the message names that row's size and that address. Run twice, 6 passed both times; the waitlist address is **fixed rather than unique per run** so the second sweep takes `joinWaitlist`'s idempotent "already on" branch (whose sentence names the same two things) instead of leaving a second row behind, which is B-120's discipline (2). `tests/inquiries-db.test.ts` asserts the returned name and email match what was recorded.

**Real bug found, not fixed here.** The full sweep failed once, on `comms-observability-db.test.ts > alertOwner > emails the owner and records the send`, expecting its own owner and getting `owner-case-…@example.com` — another suite's fixture. `ownerEmail()` in `apps/web/lib/comms/alerts.ts` is a `findFirst` for **any** active owner with no ordering, so under a parallel run it can resolve to a concurrent suite's owner. It passed alone and passed on the re-run, and the database held zero leftover `owner-*` rows afterwards, so this is a live race between suites rather than accumulation — a sibling of what **B-185** owns, and worth naming there.

**Left behind.** **The success message renders above the table.** It is inside the one form, which is above the quote list, so a staffer who pressed a button at the bottom of a six-size table hears it (`role="status"`) before they see it. B-170's page-level announce region is the mechanism if that proves to matter; it is not obviously better here, since the message would still be nowhere near the button. **The spec's "e.g. IMG_4471" placeholder has no counterpart on this screen** — it belonged to the task-form half of the finding, which is B-170's, and an email field prefilled with the lead's own address needs no example. **The e2e depends on the demo seed's `5x15 Climate` having no units** to have a full size to wait for, and self-skips with a named reason rather than failing if that ever changes.

## B-181 — The tenant profile reads before it writes

`686b3cc`

**What it built.** `admin/tenants/[tenantId]/page.tsx` was seventeen stacked sections in a single scroll with nothing collapsible, and the units, rates and balances a staffer is being asked about were the **ninth** thing down — behind a support-session form, a contact form and an address form, none of which is touched more than a few times a month. The banner stack is unchanged. Under it now: **Leases**, Outstanding fees, Contact, Address of record, Referrals, Notes, Documents, Recent gate activity, Communication history — then one **Actions** region holding every occasional write, all closed. Contact and address render as text with an Edit disclosure. The two long logs show five with the rest behind a named disclosure. No new data and no new queries: the same seventeen sections, reordered and disclosed.

**What it decided.**

**The order was the owner's call, and it was taken rather than assumed — D-95.** The row inherited its reviewer's MEDIUM confidence and asked for an operator pass before the order was committed to. Two alternatives were put up and refused, and the reasons are in D-95 so they are not re-argued: money near the top (buys a shorter reach for the commonest write, costs a longer read stack before the contact details) and disclosure-in-place with no Actions region (smaller diff, fixes how deep the leases are without fixing that there are seventeen headings to pass, and leaves the controls scattered).

**`Flag as returned mail` stayed in the open, and the reason is a rule, not a preference.** It is one click and the counterpart to the returned-mail alert directly above it — filed under "Edit address of record" it would be filed under the wrong verb. It also had a test consequence worth naming: `admin-tasks.spec.ts` waits for that button and **`test.skip`s** when it is not visible, so hiding it would have made that spec skip forever rather than fail. A control that turns a suite green by disappearing is the worst kind of regression, and it was found by asking why the test skipped rather than by the test failing. Proved reachable by clearing `returnedMailAt` on the demo tenant and running the flow end to end; the run re-set the flag, so the fixture is exactly as it was.

**`Outstanding fees` stayed in the read stack.** A figure owed is a reading, not an act — its waive control is attached to a row a staffer is already looking at, and a balance hidden behind a disclosure is a balance nobody quotes.

**Every disclosure is a native `<details>`.** No script, so the collapsed state is exposed by the platform (4.1.2), and each `<summary>` names what it opens rather than the act (2.4.6): "Edit contact details", not "Edit"; "Show 12 older messages", not "Show more". Two identical "Show more" controls on one page tell a rotor nothing about which list they open.

**The axe pass now opens disclosures before it scans.** Everything behind a closed `<details>` is invisible to axe, so scanning this page as shipped would have moved half its controls **out** of the audit rather than into it — the row would have made the scan greener by making it cover less. `the tenant profile has no WCAG 2.1 AA violations, with a disclosure open` opens one write form and one long-log disclosure first. That is FR-25 (1) and one more of **B-184**'s route-versus-state gaps closed for one route.

**Both long logs render their row through a function, not a copied block.** `gateEvent` and `commsItem` are declared in the component and typed off the data the page already loaded (`(typeof profile.accessHistory)[number]`), because each row is now rendered in two places — the first five and the disclosure holding the rest — and naming the two element types would mean exporting two more types for no reader's benefit.

**Test verification.** Full unit suite **3,724 passed, 8 skipped of 3,732** (221 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0. Production build (via the e2e `webServer`), typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`), lint and `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` clean. e2e across the five specs that reach this page — `admin-tenants`, `impersonation`, `admin-tasks`, `admin-move-out`, `admin-transfer` — **72 passed, 6 skipped, run twice**. Four existing specs were updated to open the disclosure they now need (military service, add a note, log a document, the support session): Playwright refuses to fill a control inside a closed `<details>`, and that refusal is the proof the form is actually hidden — a spec that still passed unchanged would have meant it was not. One new spec asserts the order by **position** (`Leases` before `Contact` and before `Actions`) rather than by presence, because the section was always present and being ninth was the defect, and that the support-session form is still on the page reporting its own collapsed state.

**Real bug found in the new test, worth recording because it would have passed for the wrong reason.** The first draft waited on `getByRole('main')` before reading the headings — but the tenant **list** has a `main` too, so the wait was satisfied before the navigation and the assertion read the list's headings, of which there are none at level 2 inside `main`. It failed rather than passing, but the same mistake against a `toContain`-shaped assertion would have passed on the wrong page. It waits on the level-1 tenant name now.

**Left behind.** **Two fields labelled `Reason`** now sit in the same region — the support session's and Place a hold's — distinguishable only by their enclosing form's accessible name. That was true before this row and is not made worse by it, but they are neighbours now where they were sections apart, and a rotor hears them as a pair; renaming one is a copy question for whoever next touches D-15's lexicon. **No in-page navigation.** The row asked for ordering and disclosure only; whether a profile this long wants a jump list is its own question and nobody has asked for one. **The disclosures do not remember.** A staffer who opens "Record a returned payment", acts, and is revalidated back gets it closed again — native `<details>` has no persistence and adding it would mean state, which this row deliberately does not introduce.

## B-182 — Customer-facing copy: "ring" → "call", "cheque" → "check"

`13fb9ff685b1ed6a2b53b84de6d361b0bbe2c508`

**What it built.** D-15 lexicon cleanup across three unrelated defects the 2026-08-24 UX review grouped as one row. (1) British register ("ring", "cheque") on a Texas product, product-wide. (2) `date_too_far_out`'s copy arguing its own reasoning at the tenant rather than stating the rule. (3) One checkout screen able to show two different phone numbers depending on which branch rendered.

**"Ring the office" → "call the office", and the transfer screen's fix went past the word swap.** `portal/transfer/page.tsx` built its own "ring the office on {phone}" text in four places, from raw `lease.facilityPhone`, with no fallback when a facility has none on file and no real `tel:` link — the exact defect the sibling move-out screen already has a fix for (`lienMoveOutRefusal()` + `phoneFor`/`CallLink`, B-142). A word-only fix would have shipped "call the office on" with the same missing-number hole. Instead: a new `lienTransferRefusal()` in `lib/portal/transfer.ts` mirrors `lienMoveOutRefusal()`, and all four spots — the unschedulable-lease list item, the full-page lien refusal, both halves of "transfer requested" (hold expiry, "call sooner"), and "nothing else free" — now render the number through `phoneFor`/`CallLink`. `PORTAL_TRANSFER_PROBLEM_COPY.lien_pipeline` and `PORTAL_MOVE_OUT_PROBLEM_COPY.lien_pipeline` both got "ring" → "call".

**`date_too_far_out`.** `lib/portal/transfer.ts` read "Pick a date within 60 days — the same window the public site holds a unit for"; trimmed to "Pick a date within the next 60 days." `lib/portal/move-out.ts`'s copy was already in that shape — nothing to change there, a fact worth recording since the row named both files.

**Checkout's two-number problem.** `(public)/checkout/page.tsx`'s `provisioned` step ("your gate code will be texted... if it has not arrived") rendered `SITE.phone` — the org line — unconditionally. The unit-lost branch on the same page already computes `lostPhone = phoneFor(inventory?.facility.phone ?? null)` for exactly this reason (one page, one number). The gate-code fallback now reuses the same `lostPhone` via `CallLink`, so a renter cannot see the facility's own number in one branch and the org line in another within a single checkout. `SITE.phone` stays as the org line on the "we couldn't find that checkout" branch — no session, no facility, nothing for `phoneFor` to prefer.

**"Cheque" → "check", product-wide, closing a named deferral.** `components/admin/refund-method-fields.tsx` (built in B-178) carried the spelling deliberately, with a comment naming this row: "the product-wide D-15 pass to 'check' is B-182's."
