That pass: the tenant profile's refund and returned-payment panels, its refund/return actions, the delinquency grace-period hint, both POS screens (drawer and merchandise — labels, hints, options, success and error copy) and their actions, and the deposits report and CSV export.

**What it decided.** No scope beyond what the row named — no lexicon lint (the row's own "leaves behind" already says this is a review-enforced rule, not a build-enforced one, and that stands). Source comments using "cheque"/"ring" as history (e.g. `refund-method-fields.tsx`'s own B-178 note, `lib/billing/refunds.ts`'s reasoning comments) were left as prose, not user-facing copy — updated only where the comment was itself now stale (the refund-method-fields deferral note, since this row executes it).

**Test verification.** Typecheck and lint clean (lint's 7 warnings are pre-existing and unrelated — unused `_prev` params, one unused seed-script variable). Full unit suite **3,724 passed, 8 skipped of 3,732**, exit 0. Schema-drift check clean — no schema touched. Production build via `build:test` clean. e2e — `portal-transfer`, `portal-move-out`, `admin-transfer`, `admin-move-out`, `checkout-unit-lost`, `admin-pos`, `admin-tenants` — **96 passed, 2 skipped, run twice**, no failures either run.

**Left behind.** No lexicon lint, as the row itself notes — D-15 stays review-enforced. Grep confirms no remaining customer- or staff-facing "cheque"/"ring the office" text outside history comments.

## B-183 — AR aging sits under a month picker that does not govern it

`157cb68d02fc57ae7babdce6a9715037b9cbb1f5`

**What it built.** B-150 answered "does the AR aging table obey the month picker above it?" in prose — a paragraph explaining the range does not apply, reasoning included. Two problems with that: the reasoning argued where a reader needed a fact, and the same "this ignores the picker" idea had no consistent visual treatment, so a reader who skipped the paragraph read four wrong numbers with nothing to stop them. `arAgingNote()` dropped its "because how old a debt is describes one instant rather than a range" clause — it now states the fact and stops. Both the AR aging section and the occupancy section (`admin/reports/page.tsx`) got an "As of right now" `<h3>` immediately above their as-at paragraph, visually detaching the caveat from the period-scoped sections around it — unconditional for AR aging (D-65: it never answers for the period), conditional on `reason !== 'as-at-period-end'` for occupancy (a table that DOES answer for the month picked gets no caveat heading).

**Same file, merged in, per the row:** `/admin/reports/waitlist`'s column headings "Been told" → "Notified" and "Free now" → "Units free now"; a row with people waiting **and** a unit free right now is now surfaced with its own inline label ("waiting + free — call somebody") and a light row highlight, rather than left to be spotted by comparing two columns; the `<summary>` disclosures on that page's contact rotor now carry `aria-label={`Contacts waiting for ${w} foot by ${l} foot`}` so a rotor can tell "3 people" apart across rows.

**What it decided.** The occupancy note's other three branches (`period-not-ended`, `before-history`, `no-units`) were left as-is — they state a fact each ("has not ended yet", "was not recorded before X") rather than arguing one, so B-150's earlier phrasing there didn't have the defect this row was fixing. Only AR aging's sentence carried the extra justification clause.

**Test verification.** Typecheck and lint clean (lint's 7 warnings are pre-existing and unrelated). Full unit suite **3,724 passed, 8 skipped of 3,732** (221 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0 — `tests/ar-aging-note.test.ts` still passes unchanged (it asserts substrings, not the full sentence). e2e: `e2e/admin-reports.spec.ts` — 78 passed; 6 pre-existing failures reproduced identically on unmodified `main` (confirmed by stashing this row's diff and re-running), so they are not this row's regression.

**Real bug found, not fixed here.** Three of those six pre-existing failures are a stale spec: `e2e/admin-reports.spec.ts:253` asserts the duplicate-content report's size-intro row header reads `'City page intros'`, but `apps/web/lib/marketing/content-corpus.ts:33` has read `'City/size page intros'` since B-134 shipped per-size intros — the spec was never updated for that label split, and a second assertion two tests later (`:273`) expects the old drill-through URL shape for the same reason. The other three (`:267` and the rent-roll CSV-vs-screen occupancy mismatch, `:48`) look like demo-data drift rather than a copy defect and were not investigated further here — out of this row's scope, but worth a look before either spec is trusted again.

**Left behind.** No new note was written for the waitlist page itself — it carries no month picker and nothing on it currently implies an answer for a period it doesn't have, so there was no "ignores the picker" confusion to fix there; only the merged copy/a11y fixes applied.

## B-184 — The scan contract III: states the route list cannot express, and the assertions that were only ever run on public routes

`c3aa355`

**What it built.** Six sub-items from the fourth review block, T1–T6. **T1**: a second exported pair in `lib/a11y/scan-coverage.ts` — `SCANNED_STATES` (route, state, spec) and `STATE_EXCEPTIONS` (route, state, audience, reason) — the same route/exception shape `SCAN_EXCEPTIONS` already used, one level down from a route to a state reached only by an interaction. Nine `SCANNED_STATES` rows, each tied to a `// a11y-state: <route> | <state>` comment beside its actual scan and cross-checked by two new unit tests: one confirms the named spec still runs axe and still carries that exact comment, the other walks every `e2e/*.spec.ts` file for `a11y-state:` comments and fails if one exists with no matching list entry (the same "coverage grew by accident" trap B-119 closed for whole routes, one level down). Seven `STATE_EXCEPTIONS` rows for states genuinely blocked on live data (`/portal/pay/done`'s four settled-payment outcomes, `/portal/documents`'s returned-payment row, `/portal/transfer`'s `pending_auction` refusal) or on a mismatch the form no longer lets a visitor reach (see below). The public accessibility page renders `customerFacingStateExceptions()` in a second list beside the route one, replacing the sentence that used to just assert "some states aren't covered" with the actual list. **T2**: the incomplete-filtering block that lived only in `e2e/a11y.spec.ts`'s public-route loop moved to `assertNoAxeViolations` in `e2e/a11y-helpers.ts`, and every ad hoc `const { violations } = await new AxeBuilder(...)` in the suite — eleven files, not just the eight the row named, once `admin-tasks.spec.ts` and the two portal transfer/move-out specs were counted — now calls it. **T3**: `assertNoAxeViolations(page)` after the existing focused-alert assertion in `admin-tasks.spec.ts`'s refused-completion test. **T4**: `expectAnnounced` takes an optional `{ focused: true }`; used on the task-completion test, where `AnnounceRegion` already moves focus once it has a message. **T5**: `AdminForm`'s confirm-and-echo step announces from the same pre-mounted `role="status"` paragraph the success branch already used (extended to cover `confirm` too, rather than adding a second region — see "What it decided"), and the bordered echo box drops its own `role="status"` for the confirm branch so the two don't announce the same sentence twice; `admin.spec.ts`'s tax-rate confirm test now asserts the region pre-exists, is written into, and the page passes `assertNoAxeViolations` in that state.

**Three new states found genuinely reachable, not exempted.** B-173's `stalePreview` guard (type a new value, skip the explicit recalculate control, submit directly) turned out to be an ordinary path on all three screens it protects, not just the admin one — `/portal/move-out` and `/portal/transfer` both have their own recalculate button (`Update`, `Show me what it costs`) rather than auto-syncing as you type, so the mismatch is as reachable there as on the staff side. All three got a real scan (`e2e/admin-move-out.spec.ts`, `e2e/portal-move-out.spec.ts`, `e2e/portal-transfer.spec.ts`) instead of the two portal ones going into `STATE_EXCEPTIONS` on an assumption that turned out to be wrong on inspection.

**What it decided.** **The confirm region reuses the success paragraph rather than mounting a second one.** The first pass added a dedicated `sr-only` `role="status"` paragraph for `confirm`, pre-mounted alongside the existing success one — which put two `role="status"` regions in the same form and broke every `form.getByRole('status')` locator in the suite with a strict-mode violation (5 of the 8 e2e failures the first full run found). Since a form is never in both `success` and `confirm` at once, one paragraph now carries either message, styled per state; the bordered box keeps its role for `error` (an alert announces fine even freshly inserted) and drops it for `confirm` (a status region does not, which is the whole reason the paragraph exists). **T4's `{focused: true}` is demonstrated on task completion only, not on `/portal/contact` as the row also named.** Making `/portal/contact`'s plain address-save take focus on success would have meant focusing `AdminForm`'s success paragraph on EVERY form in the product that doesn't opt into `announceOutside` — a behavior change to a shared component used by dozens of screens, validated in this session only by the specs it happens to touch. Reverted in favor of the narrower, already-true case (`AnnounceRegion`'s own focus effect, unchanged) rather than shipping an unvalidated product-wide change to hit both examples the row named.

**Two real, previously-unchecked findings, both exempted by hand rather than fixed or ignored.** Turning on `incomplete` outside the public route loop (T2's whole point) immediately found two: `UnitStatusBadge`'s `unrentable` state layers a translucent hatch pattern over `bg-gray-100` (1.4.1 — colour is never the only signal across the six unit statuses), and axe cannot compute a background through a CSS gradient; the checkout stepper's `✓`/step-number glyph is `aria-hidden` with no colour override, so it inherits the same text-on-background pairing `contrast-tokens.test.ts` already asserts meets AA, and axe's "only non-text characters" is a font-metrics limitation on the character itself, not a real ambiguity. A third — Stripe's own `__privateStripeFrame…` iframes all sharing the title "Secure payment input frame" — is squarely third-party and matched on the frame's `target` selector rather than the generic wording, so a real duplicate title on a frame we control still fails. `HAND_CHECKED_INCOMPLETE` in `a11y-helpers.ts` now documents all three alongside the two the public-route loop already had.

**Test verification.** Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`) and lint clean (lint's 7 pre-existing warnings, unrelated). Full unit suite **3,728 passed, 8 skipped of 3,736** (221 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0 — `tests/a11y-scan-coverage.test.ts`'s new describe block, 4 tests. Schema-drift check clean (no schema touched). Production build via `db:migrate:e2e` + `test:e2e`'s own `webServer`. e2e across the twelve touched specs (`a11y`, `smoke`, `portal`, `admin`, `admin-transfer`, `admin-tenants`, `admin-move-out`, `admin-pos`, `pay-link`, `admin-tasks`, `portal-move-out`, `portal-transfer`) — **559 passed, 6 skipped, run twice against the same un-reseeded database**, no failures either run. The first full run found 8 failures (5 from the confirm-region regression above, 3 from the two new incomplete findings); each was root-caused rather than worked around, and none reappeared once fixed.

**Left behind — T6, and it is not done.** The row names three manual passes as part of its own definition of done, and none of the three happened in this session: a VoiceOver pass over the money path (checkout 1→4, `/portal/pay`, the tenant profile's returned-payment and refund forms), a keyboard pass over the four task queues and the promotions list, and the live-map pass owed since the B-093 entry. All three need a person — an agent session has no screen reader and no eyes on a live map — and the row's own rule applies without exception: a pass not written down did not happen. The public accessibility page already states this plainly ("Neither a full screen-reader pass nor a recorded keyboard pass has been carried out yet") and that sentence is unchanged by this row. Marked ✅ for T1–T5, which are built, tested and the only parts a coding session can close; T6 stays open until a person runs it and records the date here.

## B-185 — The unit test database accumulates fixtures until the sweep stops being trustworthy

`68ce711a166a8990850caaafaad23e325006c769`

**What it built.** `storage_test` held 13,106 facilities and 8,276 units, all created in August 2026, none by design — only 28 of 106 `*-db` suites currently call `facility.deleteMany`, so the rest leave fixtures behind on every run. The row's own two ideas for fixing this — a shared `afterAll` cleanup helper, or a truncate-between-files hook — were tried in that order and both turned out to be impossible, not just undesirable. `audit_log`'s append-only migration (`20260730174727_audit_log_append_only`) gives it a RESTRICT foreign key to `facility` and `staff_user`, and a statement-level trigger that raises on UPDATE, DELETE, *and* TRUNCATE against itself — "deliberately no in-band escape hatch," per that migration's own comment. Building the truncate hook first and running it proved this directly: `TRUNCATE facility CASCADE` forces Postgres to also truncate `audit_log` (CASCADE follows every incoming foreign key regardless of RESTRICT), and the trigger refuses with `audit_log is append-only: TRUNCATE is not permitted`. Any fixture a suite ever audit-logged against — leases, tenant edits, impersonation, most real admin actions — is therefore permanently unwipeable by row-level cleanup, however disciplined the suite is; `access-service-db.test.ts` already carries a comment naming exactly this ("Not the facility: revealCode's audit entries hold a Restrict FK to it"). So per-suite discipline can only ever reclaim what `audit_log` hasn't pinned, which is not the accumulation this row measured.

**What actually shipped: `npm run db:reset-test`.** `scripts/reset-test-schema.mts` drops and rebuilds the `storage_test` schema in one command — the same "drop and re-migrate" recipe that already fixed the 2026-08-24 incident, now a real script instead of the "local command nobody is told to run" the row named as the actual problem. It reuses `db:migrate:test`'s own schema-create + migrate + seed logic rather than duplicating it. Deliberately not wired into `npm test`: replaying ~30 migrations against a remote Neon database on every run is the same cost `db:migrate:test`'s own comment already rules out for that reason. Verified end-to-end: dropped the schema, ran it, confirmed migrations reapplied and roles/permissions/comms reference data reseeded (`Seeded 7 roles, 35 permissions, 100 grants. Seeded 40 org-default templates, 33 org-default rules.`).

**A second, unrelated bug found in the same investigation, found while building B-180 (2026-08-25), got its own fix.** `ownerEmail()` in `apps/web/lib/comms/alerts.ts` was an unordered `findFirst` for any active 'owner'-role staff user — fine in production (there is only ever one), but a genuine race in a shared test schema, where at least 11 DB suites bootstrap their own transient 'owner' concurrently. `alertOwner`/`ownerEmail` now take an optional `Prisma.StaffUserWhereInput` (`ownerWhere`) narrowing which staff row counts as "the" owner; all four production call sites (three in `comms/detectors.ts`, one in `jobs/registry.ts`) omit it and are unaffected — only `comms-observability-db.test.ts` passes one, scoped to its own fixture's email. **Caught mid-fix, not in review:** the first version hoisted `const ownerWhere = { email: ownerEmail }` to the `describe` body, which runs during collection — before `beforeAll` sets `ownerEmail` — so it froze on the empty string and both `alertOwner` tests failed with `sent: false`. Rebuilt as a function (`ownerWhere()`) re-evaluated inside each `it()`.

**What it decided.** The two originally-reported failing assertions (`marketplace-db.test.ts`'s `marketplaceFeed` connection-pool timeout under a 13k-row table; `admin-tenants-db.test.ts`'s `searchTenants` 25-result cap) were not independently patched. Both are symptoms of the same accumulation `db:reset-test` now has a one-command fix for, not defects in the assertions: `searchTenants`'s "Ada Renter" search there is already suffix-scoped (`Ada Renter-${suffix}`, written at B-114, before this row existed) and would not have been affected by pollution under that name; `marketplaceFeed` itself is correct production behaviour (a real deployment never has 13,106 stray facilities). Patching either against a symptom that a clean database no longer produces would have been solving the wrong layer.

**Test verification.** Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`) and lint clean (lint's 7 pre-existing warnings, unrelated). Full unit suite **3,728 passed, 8 skipped of 3,736** (221 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0 — same totals as the B-184 baseline, since this row changed no test count, only two existing assertions' arguments. Schema-drift check clean (no schema touched). Production build via `build:test` clean. No e2e run: nothing customer-facing or UI-reachable was touched (a test-infra script, an npm script, and an optional parameter on a server-side comms helper four production call sites already don't pass).

**Left behind.** No enforcement exists yet to stop a new `*-db` suite from leaving fixtures behind the way ~78 of 106 already do — the row's "cannot be silently skipped" bar is still unmet. Building that enforcement honestly requires telling "genuinely audit-pinned, can't clean up" apart from "just forgot to," which this session did not attempt; a naive lint (e.g. "every `*-db.test.ts` must call `facility.deleteMany`") would false-positive on every suite like `access-service-db.test.ts` that already knows it can't. `db:reset-test` is the mitigation until that exists, and it is a manual one — nobody is currently told to run it periodically, only pointed at it once the suite is already slow.

## B-186 — Every walk-in tenant is recorded as having given no notice at all

`f59f6a18ce70e14f49374f5425e9aec21ba6d719`

**What it built.** `Lease.noticeGivenAt` gained its second writer. Before this row it had exactly one — `requestMoveOut`/`cancelMoveOutRequest` in `lib/portal/move-out.ts`, the tenant's own portal request — so `noticeShortfallDays(null, …)` returned the full required notice for every walk-in, and the move-out screen told staff that constant as if it were a measurement. `recordNoticeGiven` in `lib/admin/move-out.ts` is the admin-side writer: gated on `leases:move_out`, refuses a future date, refuses on a lease that has already ended, audits as `lease.edited` with the old/new value in context. Two entry points call it, each a self-contained `<form>` with its own visible submit rather than a field folded into an existing one — neither the move-out screen's completion form nor the profile's other forms can take a second nested `<form>` (illegal HTML, and B-173's own comment already says so), so notice recording is its own act, not a side effect of a different one. On the move-out screen it sits directly above the shortfall message it feeds and redirects back to the same preview URL, so saving it is what makes the figure below recompute. On the tenant profile it is a new "Notice given" column on the leases table, settable per active lease, so notice given at the counter can be recorded the moment it's given rather than only once someone opens a move-out.

**What it decided.** The row's own two sub-problems are not both this row's job, and only one was built. (1) — no way to record off-platform notice — is the control above. (2) — the shortfall message promises a charge ("the lease's remedy is a charge, not a refusal") that nothing posts, since `settleMoveOut` takes no shortfall input — was left alone on purpose. The row itself frames this as a lease-terms/per-state question (D-10), not a UI defect, and says building the charge or rewriting the sentence is follow-up work rather than something to settle here. Blank clears `noticeGivenAt` back to `null` rather than stamping today's date — confirmed by a test, not just asserted in a comment, since a default of today would recreate the same lie in the other direction for every walk-in staff haven't gotten to yet. No schema change: the column already existed, unused by the admin side; `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` confirms no drift.

**Test verification.** Typecheck clean. `tests/move-out-db.test.ts`'s new `describe("off-platform notice (B-186)")` — four cases: shortfall recomputes from a recorded date, clearing goes back to `null` rather than today, a future date is refused, an ended lease is refused — run twice, both green, no flakiness. Full unit suite **3,732 passed, 8 skipped of 3,740** (221 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0. Schema-drift check clean. No e2e run: nothing on the public/customer side was touched, only two admin (staff-facing) screens.

**Left behind.** Item (2) above — the "the lease's remedy is a charge, not a refusal" sentence and the missing charge behind it — stays open, exactly as the row said it should. Whoever picks it up needs a D-10 per-state policy answer before it's a coding task.

## B-090c — Delinquency payment plans and self-cure (B-090 part 3): a hold with no schedule behind it

`dc9e09b`

**What it built.** The `payment_plan` `LeaseHold` type has existed since B-096 and halts dunning, late fees and access suspension the moment it's placed — but it was a forbearance switch, not a plan: no schedule, no amounts, no breach detection, and nothing a tenant could see. `PaymentPlan` and `PaymentPlanInstallment` are new, and neither carries a `facilityId` of its own — both are scoped through the lease, the same reasoning `LeaseHold` already uses (added to `tests/schema-invariants.test.ts`'s exemption list alongside it). Creating a plan (`createPaymentPlan` in `lib/admin/payment-plans.ts`, gated on `delinquency:execute_step` — manager and above, not the `tenants:edit` a bare hold needs, because agreeing a schedule is a financial commitment the business is making) places the SAME `payment_plan` hold through the existing `placeHold`, in one transaction with the schedule — `placeHold` gained an optional trailing `client` parameter (mirroring `leaseHasEffect`'s own) so the hold and the installments write together rather than leaving a hold with no plan behind it on a crash between two writes, which was the exact defect this row exists to fix, one layer up. A second audit entry, `payment_plan.created`, carries the schedule itself (`hold.placed`'s own entry only ever carried a one-sentence reason).

**No stored per-installment "paid" flag — deliberately, and it is the design's load-bearing decision.** `PaymentPlanInstallment` carries only a date and an amount. Whether one is paid, missed, or still ahead is derived every time it's read (`installmentViews` in `packages/core/payment-plans/schedule.ts`) by allocating whatever has actually been paid against the lease — read straight from `LedgerEntry`, `type: 'payment'`, since the plan started — oldest installment first, the same D-65 reasoning that keeps occupancy and every other historical figure in this codebase recomputed rather than stored: a payment applied through ANY path (autopay, a counter payment, a waived fee freeing up room) is reflected without a second write remembering to update a status column too. `isBreached` (an installment's due date passed uncovered) and `isFullyPaid` (cumulative payments reach the total) are the two questions the nightly job asks; `validateSchedule` refuses a schedule that doesn't add up to the amount being put on the plan, has a date not strictly in the future, two installments on one day, or more than `MAX_INSTALLMENTS` (6 — ponytail: a plain fixed-row form rather than a dynamic add/remove list, raise both together if a real plan needs more).

**The nightly check that hold never had.** `evaluatePaymentPlanBreaches` (`lib/delinquency/payment-plan-breach.ts`), registered as `delinquency.payment-plan-breach` at hour 4 — after autopay (3am) has settled the night's payments onto the ledger this reads, and before the dunning ladder (5am) and the delinquency timeline (6am), both of which read `onHold`, so a plan broken tonight resumes collections the SAME night rather than one run late. Breaking a plan marks it `broken`, lifts the hold through a new `systemLiftHold` (no actor, no permission check, no manager gate — the same posture `restoreAccessIfSettled` already takes for an automated consequence nobody is exercising discretion over), and raises a `payment_plan_broken` task (`high` priority, sensitive — the record of why collections resumed against a tenant who was told they were on a plan). Finishing one (every installment covered) marks it `completed` and lifts the hold the same way, closing out the record rather than leaving an indefinitely-open hold on a lease that has actually paid. Both are idempotent by construction: the job only acts on `status: 'active'` plans, so a re-run within a catch-up range or the same night does nothing further — `systemLiftHold` is also a no-op on an already-lifted hold, guarding against a person lifting one in between.

**Staff UI:** a "Payment plans" section on the tenant profile, one lease at a time — an active/past plan's schedule table (mirroring the Holds section's `role="note"` styling), a cancel form for an active one (reuses the ordinary staff-facing `liftHold`, audited as `hold.lifted` with `reasonCode: 'management_approval'`, same as lifting any other hold type by hand — cancelling is a staff decision, unlike a break, so it does not go through `systemLiftHold`), and a `<details>` "Set up a payment plan" builder — `MAX_INSTALLMENTS` fixed date/amount rows, gated on the same permission and only shown for a non-ended lease with no already-active plan.

**Portal UI ("self-cure UX beyond banner", PRD 01 §9's own words).** Before this, a tenant on a plan had no way to know it existed short of calling the office — the dashboard showed the same "past due" banner whether or not staff had agreed a schedule with them. The dashboard card now shows the next installment's amount and date when a plan is active, linking to a new read-only `/portal/payment-plan`, which lists the full schedule per lease with per-installment status. Nothing on either portal surface can change the plan — it's a commitment staff and the tenant agreed to, the same posture `lib/portal/move-out.ts` takes toward what `lib/admin/move-out.ts` decides.

**What it decided.** The row bundles "payment plans" and "self-cure" as one line, and this build reads self-cure as **visibility**, not **tenant-initiated origination** — staff still set up every plan, from the counter or the phone conversation the row's own examples describe. A tenant-facing REQUEST flow (mirroring B-090b's transfer-request pattern: the tenant proposes, staff still commit) is a natural next step but is real, additional scope — a policy question about how far a tenant may self-serve into forbearance, not a UI gap — and was not built here. The schedule's `totalCents` is derived as the SUM of what staff enter rather than cross-checked against the lease's live ledger balance at creation: a plan is specifically for the ARREARS a staffer and a tenant agreed on, and forcing an exact match against the whole balance would conflate that with ongoing rent accruing separately — trusted the same way `placeHold`'s own `reason` field already is.

**Test verification.** Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`) and lint clean (lint's 7 pre-existing warnings, unrelated). `tests/payment-plans.test.ts` — 17 cases on `validateSchedule`/`installmentViews`/`isBreached`/`isFullyPaid`, pure. `tests/payment-plans-db.test.ts` — 10 cases: creating places the hold and writes the schedule in one transaction and halts the pipeline; a schedule with a non-future date is refused and places no hold; counter staff are refused (manager-tier only); a second active plan on the same lease is refused; cancelling lifts the hold and resumes collections; cancelling without a reason is refused; a missed installment breaks the plan, lifts the hold, and raises a `high`-priority task; a plan kept current is not broken; full payment completes the plan and lifts the hold; re-running the breach check after a plan already broke raises no second task — run twice against the un-reseeded database, both green. Full unit suite **3,761 passed, 8 skipped of 3,769** (223 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0 — includes fixing two cross-cutting contract tests the new schema and route tripped: `tests/schema-invariants.test.ts`'s facility-scoping check (both new models added to its exemption list, scoped through the lease like `LeaseHold`) and `tests/a11y-scan-coverage.test.ts`'s route contract (`/portal/payment-plan` added to `PORTAL_SCAN_ROUTES`, its active-plan state — which needs a real plan the demo seed doesn't create — recorded honestly in `STATE_EXCEPTIONS` rather than left silently uncovered). Schema-drift check clean. `e2e/admin-tenants.spec.ts`'s existing "disclosure open" a11y scan extended to open the new "Set up a payment plan" disclosure alongside the two it already opened, rather than added as a separate test — same route, same state, one claim. e2e run: `portal.spec.ts`, `admin-tenants.spec.ts`, `a11y.spec.ts`, production build — **402 passed, 6 failed**, all 6 `mobile-chrome`-only (`the tenant ledger`'s two tests, `lien notices for a lease`'s four) and confirmed pre-existing by stashing this row's whole diff and re-running against unmodified `main`: identical failures, identical tests, and the same four pass cleanly on `desktop-chrome` in the same run. Not this row's regression.

**One real finding along the way, run down rather than routed around.** The extended disclosure test first failed on `color-contrast`, axe's `elmPartiallyObscured` variant, against the "Move out" link in the leases table — nothing to do with any colour this row introduced. Reproduced in isolation (a throwaway spec opening only the new disclosure), confirmed it wasn't a dev-server artifact (reproduces against the production build too), and settled by hand with `document.elementsFromPoint` at the flagged link's centre: a clean `TD → TABLE → MAIN → BODY` stack, nothing actually overlapping it. The tenant profile's `<main>` carries a pre-existing `[contain:layout]` this row didn't add; the new disclosure is simply the first thing on this page tall enough to push it well past one screen, which is what exposes the limitation. Added to `HAND_CHECKED_INCOMPLETE` in `e2e/a11y-helpers.ts` alongside the gradient and glyph exemptions B-184 already carries, with the verification recorded in the comment rather than assumed. A second, smaller thing fixed on the way there rather than left as a maybe: the plan-history card's background used `bg-muted/30` (a partial-opacity class new to this file); swapped for the plain `bg-muted` already used twice elsewhere on the same page, since an alpha-blended background is exactly the kind of thing axe cannot resolve a solid one for.

**Left behind.** No tenant-initiated plan REQUEST — see "What it decided" above. The active-plan schedule state of `/portal/payment-plan` has no e2e scan of its own (recorded in `STATE_EXCEPTIONS`, not silently absent) — the demo seed creates no `PaymentPlan`, and minting one to scan a table is a fixture nobody else needs yet. Breaking a plan raises a staff task and writes an audit entry but sends the tenant no notice — a genuine gap (they find out their plan broke when dunning resumes, not before), left open because building it means a new comms rule and template, which is its own row rather than a tail-end addition here.

## B-187 — The accessibility statement's one strengthened sentence is false again

`0e08180`

**What it built.** Five e2e spec files still called `new AxeBuilder({ page }).withTags([…]).analyze()` directly and destructured only `violations`, discarding `incomplete` — the same pattern B-184 (T2) migrated eight other files off of, onto `assertNoAxeViolations` in `e2e/a11y-helpers.ts`. `e2e/admin-leads.spec.ts`, `e2e/impersonation.spec.ts`, `e2e/admin-reports.spec.ts`, `e2e/admin-billing-runs.spec.ts` and `e2e/checkout-unit-lost.spec.ts` now all route through the shared helper, mechanically — no test assertions changed beyond the axe call itself. `e2e/checkout-unit-lost.spec.ts` was additionally in no coverage list at all: its unit-lost branch is a STATE of `/checkout` no route makes reachable, the same shape as the waitlist-form-opened and stale-preview states already in `SCANNED_STATES`. It gained a `SCANNED_STATES` entry (`route: '/checkout', state: 'unit lost'`) and a matching `// a11y-state: /checkout | unit lost` comment beside its scan, so `tests/a11y-scan-coverage.test.ts` can see it. The public accessibility statement's sentence at `app/(public)/accessibility/page.tsx:556-559` — "they also fail on checks the tool could not decide, everywhere they run" — needed no edit: it was already the strengthened, TRUE version; this row is what makes it actually true rather than retracting it. `LAST_REVIEWED` does not move, per the row's own instruction — one claim corrected, not the "Where we fall short" list re-verified.

**What it found.** Migrating `admin-leads.spec.ts` surfaced exactly the kind of `incomplete` finding the old code was silently discarding: axe's `shortTextContent` check on the lead detail screen's quote table, mobile-chrome only, on the one- and two-digit "Available" column cells (`6`, `0`, `1`, `8`). Reproduced in isolation and checked by hand with `document.elementsFromPoint` at each flagged cell's centre (scrolled into view first — off-viewport coordinates return an empty stack and looked at first like nothing was there): a clean `TD → TABLE → DIV → SECTION → DIV → MAIN → BODY` stack every time, nothing overlapping any of them. The common ancestor is the same `<main class="[contain:layout]">` B-090c already found and hand-verified as a false-positive source on the tenant profile — this is a second, independent page hitting the identical CSS-containment limitation, just surfacing through axe's "content too short to resolve" heuristic instead of its "partially obscured" one, because the flagged text here is single digits rather than a link. Added `/too short to determine if it is actual text content/i` to `HAND_CHECKED_INCOMPLETE` in `e2e/a11y-helpers.ts`, with the verification written into the comment rather than assumed — never both a hand-check and a silent narrowing of the statement's sentence, per the row's own rule.

Lint clean (7 pre-existing warnings, unrelated). `tests/a11y-scan-coverage.test.ts` — all 10 cases green, including the new `/checkout | unit lost` state claim. Full unit suite **3,761 passed, 8 skipped of 3,769**, exit 0 — untouched by this row, run anyway since `a11y-helpers.ts` and `scan-coverage.ts` are both imported by tests. No schema change; drift check not applicable. e2e run of the five touched spec files plus their surrounding suite: **96 passed, 6 failed** — the 6 are `admin-reports.spec.ts`'s CSV-export and duplicate-content tests (both platforms), none of which this row touched. Confirmed pre-existing by stashing this row's whole diff and re-running the same tests against unmodified `main`: identical 6 failures, identical error text (`"5.1"` vs `"4.2"` on the CSV export; `"City page intros"` vs `"City/size page intros"` and a stale URL assertion on duplicate-content), on both `mobile-chrome` and `desktop-chrome`. Not this row's regression, and not filed here since it is not what this row reviewed — worth a future row if nobody has one open for it already.

**Left behind.** The pre-existing `admin-reports.spec.ts` failures above are unrelated to this row and were not investigated further than confirming they predate it.

## B-086 part 1 — Time-boxed shared access, and the scope column that was never enforced

`f78f280`

**What it built.** PRD 03 US-8 ("smart-entry shared access") turned out to be roughly 80% already shipped, and reading it against the code before writing any was the useful part of the session: **AC2** (individual revocation, suspension cascaded with the primary on delinquency) and **AC3** (per-credential event attribution) are US-9's, built in B-029 and completed in B-105, and needed nothing. **AC1's "which unit(s)"** was likewise already answered — an `AuthorizedAccessPerson` hangs off exactly one lease, which is one unit. What was genuinely missing was AC1's other two words, **schedule** and **expiry**, and one of them turned out to be a live defect rather than a gap.

**The expiry.** `AuthorizedAccessPerson.expiresAt` (one additive migration, `20260826042357_shared_access_time_boxing`) stores the **end** of a facility-local day — local midnight beginning the next one, via `zonedMidnight` — because "until the 14th" includes the 14th, which is what a person filling in a date field means. `access.expire-shared` sweeps at `localHour: 0, scope: 'per_facility'`, the same shape and the same DST reasoning `reservation.expire` directly above it uses: a single UTC hour would cut a Texas guest off five hours early or nineteen hours late depending on the season. Storing the instant at the sweep's own boundary means the two are the same moment rather than two approximations of it. **It revokes rather than filtering, and that is the item's load-bearing decision**: a keypad decides from the codes it was last told about and does not stop working because our server is down, so a row hidden only from our own reads still opens the gate — `expireSharedAccess` goes through `revokeAuthorizedPerson`, which transitions the grant and puts a revoke in the outbox that actually reaches the controller. The test asserting `simulatedGateCode.active === false` after a sweep is the one that would catch a regression to a filtered read.

**The defect it fixed on the way.** `AuthorizedAccessPerson.accessHours` has existed since B-029, is written by the staff service and by B-105's portal, and was **read by nothing** — pushed to no controller, rendered on no screen, asserted by no test. A manager who set "weekends only" at the counter had configured precisely nothing, and nothing anywhere said so. The schema comment had even recorded the intention ("Nothing enforces it yet — gate-hours enforcement is FR-5 / B-064's") and B-064 shipped without picking it up. `scheduleForGrant` in `lib/access/time-windows.ts` is now the **one** place that decides which window a grant gets pushed, and both callers route through it — `propagateGateHours` (a settings save) and `pushGateHoursForGrant` (provisioning, and a per-grant override change) — so the three cannot disagree. `narrowSchedule` in `packages/core/access/gate-hours.ts` does the intersection.

**What it decided.** **D-100: a per-person window narrows, never widens.** The naive fix — push the person's schedule instead of the facility's — is a hole: `extendedHours` is 24-hour access the facility **sells as a paid add-on** (US-4 AC3), and a replacing schedule would hand it out free to anyone typing 00:00–23:59 into a portal form, indistinguishable on every screen from a tenant who paid. Intersection is also the only rule right in both directions, since a tenant granting shared access is narrowing their own, never issuing a wider one. **D-101: three presets, not a weekly-schedule editor.** The column stays a full `WeeklySchedule` so nothing is foreclosed; what is refused is a seven-row open/close grid in a tenant portal to express a choice that in practice is "whenever I can get in", "while I'm at work" or "at the weekend". The reverse lookup is **by value** rather than a stored enum beside the JSON, so label and schedule cannot drift; a value matching no preset reads back as "Limited hours — call the office" rather than being mislabelled, because telling a tenant their guest can get in on a day they cannot is worse than telling them to ring. A third, smaller one: `GrantCause` gained `system:shared_access_expired`, and `revokeAuthorizedPerson`'s two-way ternary became three — it previously labelled anything without a `tenantId` as `staff:`, which would have put a manager's name on a gate-log entry nobody was present for.

**Controls in the same item**, per this repo's own rule — both new behaviours are reachable from `/portal/access`, not just from a database client: a "When they can get in" select over the three presets and a native `<input type="date">` "Last day (optional)", whose `min` is **facility-local** today rather than the server's (a browser would otherwise offer yesterday at a site five hours behind). Both default to the unrestricted answer, because the common case is still "my brother, no limits" and a tenant made to answer two questions they did not ask goes back to texting their own code. Each person's row renders its window and its expiry back — **as an absolute facility-local day, never a countdown**, per PRD 01 §6.8.1 and the standing rule B-142 applied to the transfer hold. A past date is refused at the service (`ExpiryInThePastError`), tied to the field, with a suggestion rather than a rejection (SC 3.3.3): issuing a working code that dies on tonight's sweep reads as a broken gate, not as a form that accepted something it should not have.

**Test verification.** Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`) clean; lint clean (7 pre-existing warnings, unrelated). `tests/shared-access-scope.test.ts` — 9 pure cases on `narrowSchedule` and the presets: null on either side, the tighter end winning, **never widening past the facility however permissive the person is**, a day either side closes, non-overlapping windows closing rather than producing an inverted range `parseWeeklySchedule` would reject on the way back in, the narrowed result actually feeding `gateHoursDecision`, and every preset round-tripping to its own name with an unrecognised window reading as `custom`. `tests/shared-access-expiry-db.test.ts` — 9 DB cases: the stored instant is the END of the named day (asserted as a facility-local date **and** as a non-zero UTC hour, which is what a naive conversion would have got wrong); a past date is refused and writes no row; no date means never; nobody expires before their last day is over; **the controller's own row goes inactive**, with the grant at `system:shared_access_expired` and neither `revokedByStaffId` nor `revokedByTenantId` set; a second pass is a no-op so a catch-up run is safe; one person expires without touching another on the same lease; and a "weekends only" person reaches the controller with Monday closed and Saturday at the facility's `06:00–22:00` rather than the preset's `00:00–23:59`. Full unit suite **3,779 passed, 8 skipped of 3,787** (225 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0. Schema-drift check clean (`No difference detected`). e2e `portal.spec.ts`: **126 passed**, exit 0.

**One gap found in this row's own work and closed rather than shipped.** The two new controls sit inside the existing "Add someone" `<details>`, and `/portal/access`'s axe scan runs against the page as loaded — so everything behind a closed disclosure is invisible to axe, exactly the trap D-95 named when B-181 moved half the tenant profile behind disclosures. Without noticing it, this row would have moved two new form controls **out** of the audit rather than into it. Added a disclosure-open scan to `portal.spec.ts` alongside the base loop (the precedent is B-090c's extension of `admin-tenants.spec.ts`), with a matching `SCANNED_STATES` entry so `tests/a11y-scan-coverage.test.ts` holds the claim. It self-skips if the demo tenant is at the facility's cap and the form is therefore not rendered — B-120's second discipline, rather than a failure that reads as a broken page. **The first version of that test was worse than none and only the run revealed it**: located by `getByRole('group', { name: 'Add someone' })`, it matched nothing (Chromium's mapping of `<details>` to `group`, and of `<summary>` to that group's accessible name, is not something to bet a scan on), so the self-skip fired and the test reported green having audited **zero** controls — the exact failure it was added to prevent, wearing a passing tick. Re-located by `summary` text, it now runs and passes on both viewports; the skip is reserved for the cap case it was written for.

**The public accessibility statement was re-read and needs no edit**, checked rather than assumed: this row adds no route (`/portal/access` is already in `PORTAL_SCAN_ROUTES`), and its two claims that bear on the change — form fields having real labels, and a rejection being tied to its field — are both true of the new controls, which go through the audited `Field` component and return a field-scoped error. Scan coverage went **up**, not down, so no sentence moved in either direction. `LAST_REVIEWED` does not move: one row's controls added to a scan is not a re-verification of the "Where we fall short" list.

**Left behind.** **Part 2 is unbuilt and owns AC4 entirely** — `AccessCredentialType.mobile_key` has been in the enum since B-002 with no reader, no writer and no UI; the simulated Bluetooth unlock; and OQ-2's native-app/PWA spike, which part 1 does not touch. The backlog row's accessibility acceptance criteria (added 2026-08-24) are part 2's, with one exception now met: the absolute-facility-local-time rule for a time-boxed credential, which `/portal/access` satisfies for the expiry date. **Staff have no control for either new field** — `createAuthorizedPerson` accepts both from any actor, but only the portal form passes them, so a manager at the counter still cannot set an expiry or a window; US-9 AC4 makes the counter the primary case, so this is a real asymmetry and the natural first thing part 2 (or B-038's screen) picks up. **Neither field can be EDITED after the fact** — changing a window or extending a date means withdrawing the person and re-adding them, which issues a new code; deliberate, because an update path is a second write path into the same grant state and the cap logic, and nobody has needed it yet. **SR-7's "invitations expire and are single-use" is not built**: there is no invitation in this design at all — the tenant types a name and a code is issued immediately — so there is nothing yet for that requirement to attach to. It should be read against part 2, where a mobile key genuinely needs a delivery mechanism.

## B-188 — A payment plan counted money that came back, and money that was never meant for it

`0da24f8`

**What it built.** Three defects in one function, and it was the function the whole feature rested on. `paidSincePlanStart` summed `LedgerEntry` where `type: 'payment'` and `occurredAt >= plan.createdAt`, and that sum WAS progress — `installmentViews` allocated it oldest-first, `isFullyPaid` closed the plan, and `payment-plan-breach.ts` lifted the hold on the strength of it. It is gone, replaced by `planProgressCents(totalCents, invoiceIds)`: **the frozen arrears less what is still outstanding on the invoices the plan covers.** One new column, `PaymentPlan.invoiceIds String[]` (additive migration `20260826204550_payment_plan_covered_invoices`), frozen at creation from the new `arrearsForLease` — every invoice already due and not fully settled at the moment a person agreed to the plan.

**Reading the invoices is what makes the three fixes fall out rather than be built.** (1) **A returned payment no longer stays counted.** `returnPayment` posts a positive `adjustment` and deliberately leaves the original `payment` row standing (its own comment says why), and `refundPayment` posts a `refund` — but both unwind their `PaymentAllocation` rows, and `recomputeInvoices` re-opens the invoice off the back of that. So progress goes backwards without the arithmetic knowing a reversal happened, and a plan can no longer complete itself and lift its own hold on money the bank took back. (2) **Ordinary rent no longer satisfies the arrears**: a rent invoice raised after the plan started is not in the covered set at all. (3) **The plan is checked against what is owed.** `createPaymentPlan` previously computed `totalCents` as the sum of the installments and handed BOTH to `validateSchedule(installments, totalCents, now)`, so the `sum !== totalCents` branch was unreachable from the only production caller and a $50 plan against an $1,800 arrear validated, halted the ladder and completed. `totalCents` is now the lease's actual arrears, which makes that branch live for the first time — no code removed, a referent supplied.

**The derivation stays derived** (D-65, B-090c): no stored per-installment paid flag, no stored progress figure. What changed is what is summed, not where it lives. The nightly breach job recomputes from the covered invoices every run rather than accumulating, so a plan whose progress goes backwards is re-evaluated **that night** rather than at the next installment date, and an installment covered by money since taken back returns to `missed`. Clamped at zero because outstanding can legitimately exceed the frozen total — a payment that part-settled one of these invoices *before* the plan was agreed can bounce afterwards — and a negative figure would read as a credit.

**What it decided. D-96 is resolved: rent first, then the plan.** An installment is satisfied only by money that settles the arrears the plan was agreed over; current rent stays due on its own date on top. **Not per-facility configurable**, deliberately — a rule a tenant can be told only after looking up their site is a rule staff will state wrongly. The two alternatives and why each was refused are in the decision log; the short version is that "any payment counts" lets a plan complete having collected nothing toward the arrears while the tenant sits permanently behind a hold owing more each month, and "any payment minus the month's rent" reaches the same answer from cash while getting none of the reversal netting for free. **The frozen invoice LIST rather than a live `dueDate <= createdAt` filter** is the other decision worth not reversing: a fee invoice raised later the same day carries that day's due date and would silently join the covered set, making progress fall for a charge the plan never promised to clear.

**Controls and copy in the same item, because the rule is now real and a tenant is held to it.** The staff builder states the figure the installments must add up to (`{arrears} is past due on this lease`) instead of leaving a staffer to infer it from the balance beside it — `TenantLeaseSummary` gained `arrearsCents`, which is a smaller figure than `balanceCents` whenever this month's rent is invoiced and not yet due — and says in as many words that paying next month's rent does not count towards an installment. `/portal/payment-plan`'s intro said **"Paying keeps you on track"**, which was true of the code and is now false of the plan; it now tells the tenant that the plan covers what was already overdue and that regular rent is still due on top (D-15, their words). `validateSchedule`'s mismatch message moved from cents to dollars — it said `"5000 cents against 6000 cents"` for as long as it was unreachable, and a staffer reads it on a form. The `totalCents <= 0` case returns its problem **alone** rather than alongside a sum mismatch: "nothing is past due" and "your installments total $300 against $0 past due" are the same fact said twice, and the second reads as arithmetic advice on a plan that should not exist.

**Test verification.** Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`) clean; lint clean (7 pre-existing warnings, unrelated). `tests/payment-plans.test.ts` — 18 pure cases, two new: the mismatch refusal naming both figures in dollars, and the nothing-past-due refusal returning that problem and nothing else. `tests/payment-plans-db.test.ts` — 16 DB cases against real invoices and real allocations, four of them new and each pinning one defect: a plan that does not cover the arrears is refused naming the shortfall (and the same lease succeeds the moment the installments add up); a lease with nothing past due is refused; the covered invoices are frozen on the row; **next month's rent paid in full leaves installment 1 `missed` and the nightly job breaks the plan** rather than leaving the ladder halted on a payment that never touched the arrears; **a payment run back through the real `returnPayment` takes its progress back and breaks the plan that night**; and a plan whose money came back before the nightly run does **not** complete, with the hold staying on. Run twice against the un-reseeded database, both green. Full unit suite **3,786 passed, 8 skipped of 3,794** (225 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0. Schema-drift check clean (`No difference detected`). e2e `admin-tenants.spec.ts` + `portal.spec.ts`: **160 passed, 6 failed**, all 6 `mobile-chrome`-only (`the tenant ledger`'s two, `lien notices for a lease`'s four) — the same six the B-086 entry above records, confirmed pre-existing again here by stashing this row's whole diff and re-running against unmodified `main`: identical six, identical names. The disclosure-open a11y scan of the plan builder passed on both viewports with the new copy.

**One fixture defect found in this row's own tests and fixed rather than worked around.** The suite's `pay()` helper posted a bare `payment` ledger entry, which under the new derivation moves nothing — so it had to settle an invoice through the real `applyPayment`. The first version passed no `explicitInvoiceId`, and three tests failed in ways that looked like the feature was broken. The cause is that **allocation claims run per tenant × FACILITY, not per lease**, and every lease in that file belongs to one tenant at one facility: an unnamed payment settled whichever test's arrears happened to be oldest. Every assertion in the file would have been an assertion about test ordering. `pay()` now names this lease's own oldest unpaid invoice unless told otherwise, with the reason written into the helper.

**The public accessibility statement was re-read and needs no edit**, checked rather than assumed. No new route and no new control: the two screens touched are both already in the scan lists, and the change is copy plus one emphasized figure that is also plainly stated in text. The statement's claim that a rejection is tied to its field is already false for this builder — that is **B-192 finding (3)**, and this row does not make it worse: the two refusals it adds are genuinely schedule-level rather than field-level, and a page-level message is their correct presentation. `LAST_REVIEWED` does not move.

**Left behind.** **A plan that completes and only then has its money returned is not re-opened.** Completion lifts the hold, so collections resume anyway and D-92's reversal handling takes over with its ten days of grace — the residual harm is a plan record labelled `completed` rather than an uncollected debt, and re-opening it would need a status transition and a hold nobody has asked for. Worth a row only if the label turns out to mislead someone. **An invoice VOIDED after the plan started counts as progress** — a waived fee inside the covered set reduces outstanding, so the tenant gets credit toward an installment for money nobody collected. Deliberate: the debt genuinely came down and a manager decided so. **Nothing caps what may be deferred and nothing carries a replacement plan's predecessor forward** — B-190, unchanged by this row, and its `paidSincePlanStart`-resets-to-zero symptom is now a `totalCents`-and-`invoiceIds`-reset-to-the-current-arrears symptom instead. **Autopay still does not know a plan exists in either direction** (B-189). **The tenant is still told nothing when a plan breaks** (B-191). The **remaining-balance column** both schedule tables want is B-192's and B-193's, not added here.

## B-189 — Autopay did not know a payment plan existed, in either direction

`733d444`

**What it built.** Two halves of one defect, both in the money path. **The arrears half:** `packages/core/holds/catalog.ts` gives the `payment_plan` hold `halt_dunning`, `halt_late_fees` and `halt_access_suspension` — not `halt_autopay`, the only effect `runAutopay` checks — so autopay selected every `open`/`partially_paid` invoice with `dueDate <= businessDate` and charged the **full outstanding**, on the retry ladder, for as long as the card authorised. A tenant who agreed to clear $1,800 over six months had their card taken for $1,800 the same night the plan was agreed. **The installment half:** an installment due date was a date on which nothing was charged at all, so a tenant with a saved card had to remember to pay by hand or the hour-4 breach job broke their plan for them.

**The fix for the first half is deliberately not `halt_autopay`.** That effect is all-or-nothing per lease, so declaring it would have stopped collecting current rent too and turned forbearance on what is owed into a rent holiday nobody agreed to. `runAutopay` instead skips exactly the invoices the plan froze into `invoiceIds` at creation (D-96) and charges everything invoiced since on its own due date — reported as its own skip reason (`deferred under an agreed payment plan`) rather than folded into `lease_on_hold`, because the two are different facts on the Billing Runs screen.

**An installment is one charge, not one per covered invoice.** It carries the plan id to Stripe as metadata; the webhook resolves the plan — checking its lease against the payment's own tenant and facility first, the same caution B-045's named invoice already takes — and `applyPayment` narrows the allocation to the covered set, so the money lands on the arrears in the facility's own order and can never drift onto rent the plan never deferred. Two card charges for one agreed payment is how a tenant already in collections reads their statement as a mistake, and a disputed charge is what B-147 had to build handling for. The amount is the **cumulative schedule through that installment less what the plan has retired**, not the face value: `installmentViews` reports partial coverage as uncovered, so the face value would take the same money twice.

**A declined installment is a decline, not a breach (CN-6).** `Payment` gained a nullable `paymentPlanInstallmentId` (additive migration `20260826222437_b189_payment_plan_auto_collect`), and it exists because the ladder has to be countable: an installment charge names no single invoice, so it writes no `PaymentAllocation` until it succeeds and B-045's `declineHistory` — which counts failed allocations per invoice — can see nothing at all. With it, `retryDecision` runs anchored on the **installment's own due date** (never an invoice's, never the last attempt), and `evaluatePaymentPlanBreaches` leaves the plan standing while that ladder is still running. The grace is bounded three ways so that "wait for the retries" can never become "never break": it is the facility's own `paymentRetryDays` rather than a number invented in the breach job, a terminal decline code ends it immediately, and it applies only where collection is genuinely in play.

**What it decided. D-97 is resolved: auto-collect by default, with an opt-out at agreement.** Auto-collection collects more and is kinder to the tenant who wants it handled, which is most of them; but the manual-pay argument is real — "you kept to the plan" should be able to be a statement about the tenant rather than about their card — and a checkbox costs one column and one field, which is cheaper than being wrong for every tenant in either direction. The box is ticked because that is what most plans want. **Three separate things make a plan manual-pay in fact and screens must not conflate them**: the box unticked, autopay off on the lease, or no saved card. `PaymentPlanView` therefore reports both `autoCollect` and `autoCollectEffective`, and every screen states the effective one — a plan agreed as automatic against a card since removed will collect nothing, and telling someone their payment is taken care of when it is not is how they end up in collections believing they kept to the plan.

**The control shipped with the column**, per this repo's own rule. The checkbox is on the agreement form beside the schedule rather than in a settings screen, because it is a term of the conversation being had at that moment; the action reads presence rather than a value, since an unchecked checkbox posts nothing. Both the staff plan card and `/portal/payment-plan` state in words which kind of plan it is, and the builder's existing copy now says that rent invoiced from here on is **still collected** on its own due date rather than only that it is still due.

**Test verification.** Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`) clean; lint clean (7 pre-existing warnings, unrelated). New `tests/payment-plan-autopay-db.test.ts` — 9 DB cases: the arrears deferred while September's rent is still charged; one installment charged on its due date naming the plan and **not** an invoice; nothing charged on a manual-pay plan *and* nothing swept up by the ordinary path either; only the $50 remaining of a $300 installment the tenant part-paid; no second charge while the first is still `pending`; a `card_declined` leaving the plan `active` on the first night it reads `missed` and breaking it once the schedule's last offset has passed; an `expired_card` breaking it at once; a manual-pay plan breaking the same night it always did; and an installment payment landing entirely on the covered arrears with the later rent invoice untouched. Run twice against the un-reseeded database, both green. Full unit suite **3,795 passed, 8 skipped of 3,803** (226 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0. Schema-drift check clean (`No difference detected`). Production build clean.

**One test defect found and fixed rather than shipped.** The two breach tests first asserted on the installment's own due date, and both passed for a reason that had nothing to do with the ladder: `installmentViews` marks an installment `missed` only when its due date is strictly in the past, so on the due date itself nothing can break a plan regardless of what the card did. The terminal-decline case failed, which is what surfaced it; the "ladder still running" case had been passing green while testing nothing. Both now evaluate on the first night the installment genuinely reads `missed`.

**The public accessibility statement was re-read and needs no edit**, checked rather than assumed. The item ships no new customer-facing route: what it adds to `/portal/payment-plan` is one sentence, rendered only for a tenant with an active plan — the exact state `STATE_EXCEPTIONS` already names as unscanned, for the reason it already gives (no demo `PaymentPlan` exists). So the coverage claim goes false in neither direction. The seed row that would close that exception is B-196's. `LAST_REVIEWED` does not move.

**Left behind.** **The tenant is told none of this** — not that a plan was agreed, not that an installment is about to be charged, not that a charge declined, not that the plan broke. That is B-191's CN-24 in full, and this row deliberately does not invent a message ahead of it; the only tenant-facing change here is the sentence saying whether the card will be charged. **A declined installment raises no staff task of its own** — the Billing Runs screen records it, and a person is reached when the ladder is exhausted and the plan breaks, which raises `payment_plan_broken`. Whether the earlier signal is worth a task is a real question and belongs with B-191's comms rather than being guessed here. **Nothing caps what a plan may defer or how many a lease may have** (B-190, D-98 still open), and a chain of plans still reads on every screen as one. **The ladder's grace is measured from the facility's retry schedule, not from attempts actually made**, so a plan whose charge never fires at all — a Stripe outage, a `pending` payment that never resolves — holds open for the length of that schedule and then breaks. The bound is what makes it safe; the reconciliation report is what surfaces the stuck payment. **No report can still say who is on a plan** (B-195). **The autopay run's `payment.failed` event is not emitted for an installment decline**, because its payload is invoice-shaped; B-050's retry reminders therefore do not fire for one, which is the same gap B-191 closes properly.

## B-190 — Nothing capped what a payment plan could defer, or how many times a lease could defer it

`b4f2ee0`

**What it built.** Two holes with one shape, and D-98 answered to close them. **(1) There was no monetary authority anywhere.** `createPaymentPlan` gated on `delinquency:execute_step` and nothing else — no `checkMonetaryAuthority` call existed in the file — so a manager whose fee-waiver limit is $50 could commit the business to deferring any balance over any schedule. **(2) Nothing capped the chain.** A second plan was refused only while one was `active`, so a plan broken last night was replaceable this morning, indefinitely; each replacement re-halted dunning, late fees and access suspension, and the lien clock never ran.

Now: the deferral passes `checkMonetaryAuthority(actor, 'payment_plan', arrears, facilityId)` against a new per-role `maxPlanDeferralCents`, escalating by naming the role that can carry it. A facility configures `planMaxDays` (90), `planMaxPerRollingYear` (2) and `planGraceDays` (3), each with a control on `/admin/settings` in this item. The second plan inside the rolling year is agreed a rank up; the one past the limit is refused with the count named. `paymentPlansForLease` returns the whole chain, each plan carrying `collectedCents`, and the tenant profile states the count and the total in a sentence. Additive migration `20260827051029_b190_payment_plan_limits`.

**What it decided. The authority could not reuse the fee-waiver limit, and that is the one thing the backlog row got wrong.** B-167 settled that a departure from the fee schedule needs authority in either direction, and the row reasoned by analogy from it. The analogy does not hold: a fee waiver in either direction is a **gift**, so the limits are sized for gifts — $50 for a manager, $250 for a regional. A plan defers the **whole arrears**, typically $1,800, and gives nothing away; the money is still owed and the tenant is still on the hook for all of it. Measured against the waiver limit, every real plan on the property would have escalated to the owner, and a gate that fires on every attempt is a gate somebody switches off inside a week. So `maxPlanDeferralCents` is its own column: $0 counter and bookkeeper, $2,000 manager, $10,000 regional, unlimited owner.

**`undefined` is not `null` in a limit, and the difference is the owner's authority.** Making the new field optional on `MonetaryLimits` — so the fifty-odd test fixtures that build a `limits` object by hand did not all have to change — put a `?? 0` within reach that would have collapsed the two: `null` means unlimited by design, and `null ?? 0` caps every owner at zero on **all four** actions. It reads as an equivalent tidy-up and it is a portfolio-wide authority failure. The check is explicitly `=== undefined`, with the reason written above it and a test that deletes the field from a fixture and asserts zero rather than unlimited.

**The escalation floor is read from the role table, not compared against `manager`.** `lowestRankWith('delinquency:execute_step')` is what "a level up" means, so a role inserted between the existing two slots into the ladder without a code change — the rule `nextApproverRole` already follows.

**D-98's grace is a separate window from B-189's retry ladder and is never netted against it.** The ladder asks whether a charge is still coming; the grace asks whether the **tenant** still has time to pay some other way. So a terminal decline ends the ladder immediately and still gets its three days, and a manual-pay plan — which has no ladder at all and used to break at 00:01 over money handed across the counter that afternoon — now gets the window that was the whole point of the question. It is applied by moving the breach clock back rather than by filtering the result, so it lands identically on every path, and deliberately **not** applied to `isFullyPaid`, which has no date in it.

**Carry-forward needed no column and no arithmetic.** The row asked for a replacement plan to carry forward what its predecessor collected. D-96 already measures progress as the frozen arrears less what is still outstanding on the covered invoices, so a replacement is agreed over what was **left** and its progress correctly restarts at zero — nothing was ever discarded except the record. What was missing was legibility, and that is what shipped: the chain, newest first, with `collectedCents` per plan.

**Three numbers, three controls, in the same item** — this repo's own first hard-learned rule. They sit in the billing-policy form directly under dunning, late fees and access suspension, because a plan is the thing that stops all three, and a limit on the brake belongs beside the brake. Their own `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>`, since three fields labelled with bare nouns are otherwise three unrelated fields (WCAG 1.3.1).

**Test verification.** Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`) clean. Schema-drift check clean (`No difference detected`). Six new cases: the day cap in the pure schedule test (refused, inside, and unlimited when no ceiling is passed); `payment_plan` having its own limit in `tests/rbac.test.ts` plus the `undefined`-is-not-`null` case; and four DB cases — an over-limit deferral naming `Regional Manager` from the role table, a schedule past the 90-day ceiling, the second plan escalating and the third refused with `priorCount: 2, limit: 2`, and a two-plan chain reading as a chain with the first plan's $20 still readable beside the second. Full unit suite **3,803 passed, 8 skipped of 3,811** (226 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0, run twice against the un-reseeded database.

**Five existing tests asserted the old break-that-night behaviour and were corrected, not deleted.** Three in `payment-plans-db.test.ts` and two in `payment-plan-autopay-db.test.ts` evaluated the breach one day past the due date. What they assert is now false for a stated reason, so each moved past the grace window with a comment naming D-98, and the one whose **name** had become false — "breaks a manual-pay plan the night the installment is missed" — was renamed rather than left to mislead the next reader. Two of them now also assert the plan is still `active` inside the window, which is the behaviour the row exists to add.

**The public accessibility statement was re-read and needs no edit**, checked rather than assumed. This item ships nothing a customer touches: the two screens are `/admin/settings` and the staff tenant profile, both already in the scan lists, and the portal is untouched. The statement's claim that a refusal is tied to its field is already false for the plan builder — that is **B-192 finding (3)**, unchanged here: the three refusals this row adds are genuinely plan-level rather than field-level, so a page-level message is their correct presentation. `LAST_REVIEWED` does not move.

**Left behind.** **No approval queue for an over-limit plan** — it names who can agree it and stops, the same posture `waiveFeeInvoice` and B-167's charge control already take; inventing a third would be the wrong place to start a queue. **`maxPlanDeferralCents` has no editing surface**, because its three siblings never had one either — B-004's scope claimed "monetary authority limits config" and PRD 02 RBAC-2 asserts the limits "are not hardcoded policy", which is currently false four times over. Raised as **B-197** rather than absorbed. **The rolling year is counted from `PaymentPlan.createdAt` with no history of the facility's own limit**, so lowering `planMaxPerRollingYear` applies to plans already agreed — the same "as of now" property D-65 names, and the right one here, since the limit is about what may be agreed next. **The tenant is told nothing about any of this** (B-191), **the builder's refusals still land page-level and the section still sits where D-95 says it must not** (B-192), and **no report can say who is on a plan** (B-195).

## B-191 — A payment plan told the tenant nothing, and went quietest at the moment it broke

`6e3c9aa`

**What it built.** PRD 05 **CN-24**, in full: four messages, plus the dashboard card that was the entire tenant-facing signal before them and was wrong in two ways.

Four new events (`payment_plan.agreed`, `.installment_due_soon`, `.broken`, `.completed`), each with a seeded template and rule, all on entity `Lease` with `planId` in the payload — a lease can have a chain of plans (D-98) and the message is about one of them. **Agreed** is emitted inside `createPaymentPlan`'s own transaction and lists every installment with its date and amount, the total, what the plan pauses and what happens if a payment is missed. **Installment due** is raised by a new `emitInstallmentReminders` sweep riding with the hour-4 payment-plan job. **Broken** is emitted in the same beat that lifts the hold, so the tenant hears it from us at hour 4 rather than from the dunning ladder at 5 or the keypad. **Kept** is emitted on completion.

**What it decided. The reminder's lead time is the facility's existing `invoiceLeadDays`, not a fifth number beside it.** CN-24 asks for "a per-facility configurable number of days ahead", and this facility already has a setting whose meaning is exactly that — how many days before money is due the tenant hears about it — with a control on `/admin/settings` and an operator who has already chosen a value. A new column would have been a second knob configuring one intent, which is the accumulation this repo's own first hard-learned rule is about, and it would have arrived with a fifth field in the billing-policy form to keep it honest. **The consequence is stated rather than hidden: an operator who changes their invoice reminder lead time changes their plan reminder lead time too.** That is the right coupling — both answer "how much warning do we give before a payment is due" — but a later item that needs them to differ should split the column, not read this note as permission to guess.

**Once-per-installment comes from the `JobRun`, not from a stamp.** The scheduler holds a unique `(jobName, facilityId, businessDate)`, so a catch-up tick walking five business dates emits each installment's reminder on the one date it is due. That is exactly what `emitDueReminders` has relied on for invoices since B-044, and it is why neither needed a `reminderSentAt` column. **No migration in this item at all.**

**The reminder deliberately carries no autopay skip**, which is the opposite of CN-1's rule for an ordinary invoice and is why CN-24 says so in as many words: a tenant who believes a payment is automatic and is wrong loses the plan over a misunderstanding. The message states which kind of plan it is instead, through `plan.collection_line` — and that line reports D-97's **effective** answer (`isAutoCollecting`: the plan's own opt-in AND autopay on AND a card saved), read fresh at send time. A plan agreed as automatic against a card since removed now says "not taken automatically" in the message, not "we'll take care of it". The three-part expression existed in three copies; it is now one function in `packages/core/payment-plans` used by the plan view, the breach job and the message.

**None of the four skips `tenant_moved_out`, unlike almost every rule above them.** A plan is about ARREARS, which outlive the tenancy. Suppressing the break notice because the lease had ended would reproduce, on the one lease most likely to have one, the exact silence the rule exists to end.

**FR-9a now holds for every templated email in the product, not only these four.** The acceptance criterion named B-084 part 3's standard, which had only ever been met by the *generated* report kind. Every seeded template here ships text-only, so `renderEmail`'s fallback IS the HTML body of essentially every message the product sends — and it was one `<p>` of the entire body with `<br>`s in it, no language, no heading, and the merged values interpolated **raw**: a facility genuinely called "Bob & Sons" emitted broken markup into every message it sent. It is now a language-declared wrapper with the subject as a single `<h1>`, one `<p>` per block, single line breaks preserved inside a block, and every value escaped. Fixed once in the shared function rather than four times in four seeded bodies, which is also what makes it survive a template edit.

**What FR-9a still does not get, and why it was raised rather than half-built.** CN-24 asks for the schedule as a real `<table>` with a `<caption>` and `<th scope>`. That needs an HTML body of its own, and **a seeded `bodyHtml` would be a lie waiting to happen**: CN-16's editor (`lib/admin/templates.ts`) writes `bodyHtml: null` on every save, so the first staff edit of that template would silently downgrade it back to the fallback with nobody told. The schedule ships as a numbered list — "1. September 15, 2026 — $600.00" — in both parts, and the real fix is **B-198**, raised today.

**The dashboard card was wrong in two directions, both towards telling the tenant less the worse things got.** It populated only while `status === 'active'`, so it **unmounted the night the plan broke** — the same hour the hold lifts, dunning resumes, late fees re-arm and access suspension re-arms. And it took the first installment whose status was not `paid` and called it "your next installment", while `installmentViews` marks a past-due uncovered installment `missed`, so it named a payment already failed on a date already gone. `PortalLeaseSummary.activePaymentPlan` is now `paymentPlan`, present for a `broken` plan as well as an active one, with `next` and `missed` as separate facts that are never merged. The card states all three cases in words, never by colour (1.4.1 A), and stays a server-rendered `role="status"` present at page load rather than inserted on change (4.1.3 AA). `completed` and `cancelled` are still null here — a permanent route to a plan's history is B-193's.

**The public accessibility statement gained an exception, and it is a pre-existing gap being declared rather than a new one.** `/portal` has carried a payment-plan card since B-090c in a state no scan has ever reached (it needs a real `PaymentPlan` on a demo lease, which the seed does not create), and unlike the schedule table on `/portal/payment-plan` that state was never named in `STATE_EXCEPTIONS`. This item edits that card, so leaving the gap undeclared would have been the overstating direction. B-196's seed row closes both. `LAST_REVIEWED` does not move.

**Test verification.** Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`) clean; lint clean (7 pre-existing warnings, unrelated); schema-drift check clean (`No difference detected`); production build clean.
