New `tests/payment-plan-comms-db.test.ts` — 10 cases with **the clock pinned** (`vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ['Date'] })`, per CN-24's AC and CLAUDE.md's quiet-hours trap): the catalog wiring for all four events and the deliberate absence of `autopay_covers_it`; the agreed message listing three dated installments, the total and the automatic-charge line, with no internal vocabulary in it; the same plan saying "not taken automatically" once the card is removed; the reminder raised on the lead day and sent **despite** autopay being live; nothing raised on a day no installment is the lead days away; the reminder cancelled at send time when the plan is no longer active (the `Message` row reads `cancelled`); the break notice sent with the balance and a real pay link; the break notice quoting the balance at **send** time, not job time (a counter payment lands in between and the figure moves from $1,800 to $1,000); and the completion message. Four new cases in `tests/comms-render.test.ts` for the FR-9a fallback, one in `tests/portal-dashboard.test.ts` for the card's three states. Full unit suite **3,822 passed, 8 skipped of 3,830** (227 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0, run **three** times against the un-reseeded database.

**One fixture fact worth writing down.** Both sweeps under test are FACILITY-wide, so a plan left behind by one test is picked up by the next one's run — which is a real property of the job, not a fixture quirk. The suite tears plans down between tests rather than assuming its own lease is the only one on the site.

**Left behind.** **The schedule is not a table in the email** — B-198, above. **A declined installment still raises no staff task of its own** (B-189 left it, and it stays with B-191's comms rather than being guessed at): the tenant is now told when the plan breaks, but nobody is told when the charge that will break it declines. **The autopay run's `payment.failed` event is still not emitted for an installment decline** — B-189 named this as the gap "B-191 closes properly", and it is only half closed: the tenant now hears about the *plan* breaking, but B-050's retry reminders still do not fire for an installment decline, because that event's payload is invoice-shaped. Closing it properly needs a plan-shaped failure event and a template, and that is a row, not a footnote. **The messages are email only.** CN-13's `payment_reminders` category governs the installment reminder, so an SMS-preferring tenant gets the email; making any of these SMS-eligible needs a sibling SMS template per key and the quiet-hours discipline that goes with it. **`/portal/payment-plan` still has exactly one way in and shows only the newest plan** (B-193), **the builder's refusals still land page-level and the section still sits where D-95 says it must not** (B-192), and **no report can still say who is on a plan** (B-195).

## B-192 — The payment-plan builder announced nothing, named nothing, and sat where D-95 says it must not

`97491e2`

**What it built.** Six defects on one screen, all in the section B-090c added to `app/admin/tenants/[tenantId]/page.tsx`, plus the schedule column both this row and B-193 asked for.

**(1) B-170's regression, in a new place.** Both `AdminForm`s here are removed by their own success — the `<details>` builder is filtered out the moment a plan is active, the cancel form is gated on `status === "active"` — so each announced into a `role="status"` that React unmounted in the same commit, and focus fell to `<body>` (4.1.3 AA, 2.4.3 A). The page's one `AnnounceRegion` wrapped only the returned-payments list. Both forms now pass `announceOutside` into a second `AnnounceRegion` mounted unconditionally in `Actions`, above both, which is the exact mechanism B-170 built and neither form had opted into.

**(2) Twelve identically-named fields are now six named groups.** Each installment was a `<div>` holding a `<span>Installment N</span>` and two controls labelled "Due" and "Amount ($)" — nothing tied any of the twelve to an ordinal (1.3.1 A, 3.3.2 A). They are `FieldSet`s now, not bare `<fieldset>`s, and that choice is what makes (3) work.

**(3) Refusals reach the installment that caused them.** `actions.ts` joined every `PlanProblem` into one page-level sentence with `fieldErrors: {}`, discarding the `index` each problem already carried (3.3.1 A, 3.3.3 AA). **The re-keying is the part that is not obvious and is why it got a pure function and a test.** `validateSchedule` numbers its problems by position in the array it was handed, and the action compacts that array — a staffer who fills rows 1, 2 and 5 sends three installments, so problem index 2 is form row **5**. Reporting it against `installment_3` would have put the message on an empty group two rows above the field at fault, which is worse than the summary it replaces. `problemsByRow` in `packages/core/payment-plans` maps a problem's index back through the row list the action kept; problems with a null index — the total mismatch, D-98's day cap, an empty schedule — are about the PLAN and stay the summary line rather than being attached to an arbitrary row.

**The error goes on the GROUP, not on one of its two fields.** "Installments must be in date order, one per date" is a fact about the pair, and `FieldSet` exists in this codebase for exactly that — the error on the group rather than on any one control, which is why it was reused rather than a bare `<fieldset>` written.

**(4), (5) and (6).** The cancellation reason was required by the server and marked required nowhere; it carries `required` and says so in its hint. Every plan rendered a button called "Cancel plan" beside a field called "Reason for cancelling", indistinguishable on a multi-unit tenant (2.4.6 AA) — both are named after their subject now, and so is the builder's "Agree plan", which had the same problem for the same reason. And the section sat at `:592` between Leases and Outstanding fees carrying two write forms while `Actions` sat at `:1388`, which **D-95 settled the day before B-090c shipped**.

**What it decided. A settled decision is not reversed by the next item, and the split is where D-95 draws it — reads up, writes down.** The status, the chain sentence and the schedule stay in the read stack, because a plan's state is something a staffer reads with somebody on the phone. The builder and the cancel control moved into `Actions`, each as its own `<details>` named after its unit. **The read section is now gated on there being a plan at all**: with the builder gone it would otherwise render a heading with nothing under it for every tenant who has never had one, which is one more of the seventeen headings D-95 counted.

**No pointer from the read section to `Actions`, deliberately.** The holds banner does not have one either, and D-95's whole claim is that `Actions` is the one place to look for a control; a cross-reference on every read section would restate that seventeen times.

**The remaining-balance column is `plan.totalCents` less the cumulative amount, not the arrears less what has been paid.** It answers "what is still on the plan after this installment", which is what a schedule is read for; what is *outstanding* is D-96's frozen-invoice arithmetic and is already stated above the table as collected-of-deferred. Conflating the two would put a figure in the table that moves when a payment lands and does not match the row beside it. B-193 adds the same column to the portal.

**Test verification.** Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`) clean; lint clean (7 pre-existing warnings, unrelated); no migration, so no schema drift. Four new cases in `tests/payment-plans.test.ts` for `problemsByRow` — the compacted-index-to-form-row mapping with a gap in it, a plan-level problem dropped rather than mis-keyed, two problems on one installment joined rather than one lost, and an index with no row behind it ignored rather than keyed on `undefined`. Full unit suite **3,826 passed, 8 skipped of 3,834** (227 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0. `e2e/admin-tenants.spec.ts`: **34 passed, 6 failed**, and the axe pass that opens the plan builder by name is green on **both** viewports — it now finds the disclosure inside `Actions`, and the six `FieldSet`s introduced no violation. The 6 failures are the same `mobile-chrome`-only set the B-090c, B-186 and B-188 entries above each record (`the tenant ledger`'s two, `lien notices for a lease`'s four), confirmed pre-existing here for the fourth time by stashing this row's whole diff and re-running against unmodified `main`: identical six, identical names, and the same tests pass in under a second on `desktop-chrome`. **This time it is raised rather than only disclaimed — B-199.**

**The recurring six now have a row.** Four items in a row have written "not this row's regression" about the same six tests and moved on, and the underlying defect is real: the profile's leases table is a bare `w-full` seven-column `<table>` with no `overflow-x-auto` wrapper, so on a 375px viewport its Ledger, Notices, Move out and Transfer links sit outside the document — unreachable to Playwright's scroll AND to a thumb, and very likely 1.4.10 Reflow, which axe does not check. **B-199**, raised today with the evidence and with an explicit instruction not to close it by narrowing the tests to `desktop-chrome`.

**One environment fact this session paid for.** The first e2e attempt failed three specs at ~5s each with `The column role.maxPlanDeferralCents does not exist` in the `[WebServer]` output — B-190's migration had never reached the e2e `public` schema. `npm run db:migrate:e2e` fixed it. CLAUDE.md already names this trap; the note here is that the failure surfaced as three *unrelated* specs failing on the tenant SEARCH page, not as anything resembling a missing migration.

**Left behind.** **The `AdminForm` error summary lists each field's message without naming its field** — `Object.entries(state.fieldErrors)` renders `<li>{message}</li>`, so the summary now says "Installments must be in date order" three times over with nothing distinguishing which installment, while the per-group message beside the field is correct. That is pre-existing and product-wide, not specific to this form, and fixing it means passing a label map into every one of the 156 actions or deriving one from the field name — a row, not a footnote. **No plan surface is scanned by axe in the state that matters**: the demo seed creates no `PaymentPlan`, so the schedule table, the filled builder and a refused submit are all unreachable to the pass — **B-196** owns the seed row that closes it, and it is deliberately last in this block. **`/portal/payment-plan` still has one way in and shows only the newest plan** (B-193), and **no report can say who is on a plan** (B-195).

## B-193 — The tenant's plan page had one way in, and it vanished the moment the plan broke

`88f066a`

**What it built.** Four defects on `/portal/payment-plan` and the shell around it, merged from accessibility review finding 8 and UX review findings 4 and 9.

**(1) A second way in, and it is the one that survives the plan breaking.** The page was reachable from the dashboard card alone, and B-191 made that card render for a broken plan but not for a cancelled or completed one — so a tenant whose plan ended had no route to the schedule stating what they agreed, at the hour collections resumed. That is **2.4.5 Multiple Ways (AA)** failing on a page about money the tenant owes. `apps/web/app/portal/layout.tsx` now carries a Payment plan entry whenever `hasAnyPaymentPlan` is true — any plan, live or not. **Conditional rather than permanent for everyone, deliberately**: B-117 cut that row to four top-level links because nine wrapped to four lines at 360px, and a fifth belongs there only for the tenants it is about. It sits in the top row and not behind Manage, because a tenant on a plan is checking it routinely, which is the exact test B-117's ordering comment states.

**(2) Every plan, not the newest one.** `paymentPlansForTenant` called `paymentPlanForLease` — B-190's `findFirst`-shaped survivor — so a tenant on their third plan saw one schedule and had no record of what they paid under the other two. It calls `paymentPlansForLease` now and flattens, which is the tenant-facing half of B-190's chain. Each plan states what it collected of what it deferred, for the reason B-190 gives: a replacement plan is agreed over the arrears that were *left*, so its own progress correctly restarts at zero, and without that line beside it a chain of three reads as three failures.

**(3) The pay button threw the plan away.** It linked to `/portal/pay?lease=…` with no amount, and that page defaults to the whole balance — so a tenant tapping through from an installment schedule was quoted the arrears the plan exists to replace. `?amount=` already existed and already validated. The button now carries the next installment not yet covered (which is a *missed* one where there is one, since that is what has to be paid to keep the plan), and the whole balance sits beside it as a second link. **Both are labelled with their figure**, because either can be the right one and neither should be a guess.

**(4) The status now says what it costs, not only what happened.** "Broken — an installment was missed, so collections have resumed" told a tenant their situation and not their next move. Every status is a sentence naming the consequence — the whole balance being due, late fees and gate access back to normal — and broken and cancelled plans carry a link to pay that balance. A completed one does not: there is nothing to fix.

**And B-192's remaining-balance column**, same arithmetic and same heading as the staff schedule, so the two cannot disagree over the phone.

**What it decided. The empty state was reported missing and is not — that sub-claim is declined on inspection**, as the row itself anticipated. `:37-38` renders "You're not on a payment plan right now" and it is correct; it is left untouched.

**The nav entry is conditional, and that is a real trade against 2.4.5.** A permanent entry would be simpler and would guarantee two routes for everybody — but for the overwhelming majority of tenants it names a page that says only "you are not on a plan", and it costs the four-link row B-117 measured. The criterion is about a page being *findable* by more than one means, and for a tenant with no plan there is no page to find.

**Nothing here writes.** The portal reads what staff and the tenant agreed, the same posture `lib/portal/move-out.ts` takes — B-193 changes what is shown, not who may change it.

**Accessibility.** Two routes in satisfies 2.4.5 (AA). Every status is text and never colour (**1.4.1 A**). The schedule stays a real `<table>` with `<th scope="col">` on all four columns, and its `<caption>` now names the unit **and the date the plan was agreed**, because a tenant with three plans on one unit was otherwise offered three tables with identical captions. Copy is the tenant's language (**D-15**).

**The scan-coverage exception was widened rather than left, and that is the honest direction.** `STATE_EXCEPTIONS` declared the unscanned state as the "active plan schedule"; the page now renders a schedule for every plan a tenant has ever had, and the nav entry renders on *every* portal route in that same state. All of it is behind the one fixture that does not exist — no demo `PaymentPlan` — so it stays one exception, but "active plan" would have implied the other three states were covered when nothing scans them. **B-196** closes it with the seed row, along with its `/portal` twin.

**Test verification.** Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`) clean; lint clean (7 pre-existing warnings, unrelated); `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` reports no difference — no migration in this row. Full unit suite **3,826 passed, 8 skipped of 3,834** (227 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0. Two assertions added to `tests/payment-plans-db.test.ts`'s chain case: the portal reads **both** of a lease's plans in the same newest-first order the staff screen does, and `hasAnyPaymentPlan` is true — filtered to the lease under test, because every case in that file shares one tenant. `e2e/portal.spec.ts`: **128 passed, exit 0**, including B-117's two nav tests, which still pass because the demo tenant has no plan and so gets no fifth link — the same missing fixture that keeps the schedule unscanned.

**Left behind.** **No plan surface is scanned by axe in the state that matters** — the schedule in any status, and now the nav entry too, all need the demo `PaymentPlan` **B-196** owns; this row widened the declaration and did not close it. **A plan on an ENDED lease is invisible here**: `paymentPlansForTenant` filters to occupying leases, so a tenant who moved out mid-plan loses the record of what they paid. Deliberate — the whole portal is scoped that way, and changing it is a portal-wide decision, not a payment-plan one. **Nothing tells the tenant a plan was cancelled by staff** — the page states it once they visit, but no message is sent; B-191 built the send path for broken and completed and cancellation was not in its set. **The move-out and invoice figures are still not tables in email** (B-198), **no report can still say who is on a plan** (B-195), and **the six `mobile-chrome` failures on the staff profile are still open** (B-199) — untouched by this row, which ships no admin change.

## B-194 — Two notice forms discarded the server's refusal, and the screen promised a charge nothing charges

`be9c24b`

**What it built.** Four defects on the off-platform notice B-186 shipped, merged from accessibility review finding 3 and UX review findings 6, 7 and 8.

**(1) Both callers of `recordNoticeGiven` now read what it returns.** It has always returned `{ ok: false, problem: 'future_date' | 'not_occupying' }`, and both callers — the tenant profile's table cell and the move-out screen's form — awaited it, ignored the result and revalidated regardless. Both were plain `<form action={…}>` void actions, so there was no success announcement either: the page reloaded identically whether the date saved or was refused, and a staffer had no way to tell (**3.3.1 A**, **4.1.3 AA**). Both are `AdminForm` + `FormState` now, so a refusal lands on the field that caused it and a save says what it saved. The `max` on the input was always a client-side courtesy, not the check that failed.

**(2) The date field's accessible name was a paragraph about where notice can be given.** `move-out/page.tsx` nested the explanatory `<span>` inside the `<label>`, so the field announced as "Notice given on Off-platform notice — at the counter, by phone, by mail. Leave blank if nobody has confirmed one." It is a `Field` with a `hint` now, which is `aria-describedby` (**2.4.6 AA**, **3.3.2 A**) — the component that already existed for exactly this, rather than a hand-rolled label.

**(3) Two date fields on one screen, and the gap between them is the whole point.** One sentence above the first names both: notice given on is when the tenant told you, move-out date is when the tenancy ends, and the distance between them is what the shortfall measures. That is US-14's "three dates never collapsed into one", said rather than left to be inferred from two similar-looking pickers.

**(4) The overpromised charge — copy corrected, decision untouched.** The screen said a short-notice move-out's "remedy is a charge, not a refusal" and `settleMoveOut` posts nothing: no shortfall input, no ledger entry, no fee. It now says the shortfall is recorded, not blocked, that **nothing is charged for it**, and that a charge — where the lease provides for one — is posted by hand through B-167's "Charge a fee for this unit" control already on that screen (a staffer without `fees:charge` is told that instead of being pointed at a control they cannot use).

**What it decided. The charge itself is D-99 and stays OPEN — this row did not settle it, exactly as B-186 said it would not.** D-99 already existed, raised by this row's own review; it now records what shipped. The copy is written to be *true under option A* (no charge) and to be *replaced under option B* (charge the shortfall), and the comment above the paragraph in `move-out/page.tsx` points at D-99 so a later session replaces the sentence rather than leaving two claims in the product. Whether a short-notice move-out is charged, and on what basis, is a lease-terms and per-state question (**D-10**, Texas default, draft-only, **not legal advice**).

**The redirect went, and that is what makes the announcement possible.** `setNoticeGivenOnMoveOutAction` redirected back to the same URL on every outcome — which is why it could not carry a message, and why it discarded the refusal. The URL already carries `lease` and `date`, so `revalidatePath` re-runs `previewMoveOut` against the same date and the shortfall below still updates; what is new is that the outcome has somewhere to land.

**The refusal copy lives beside the function, not in either action file.** `NOTICE_PROBLEM_COPY` and `parseNoticeGivenAt` are exported from `lib/admin/move-out.ts` because both forms call the same function, and two screens describing the same refusal two different ways is what a staffer and a manager then disagree about over the phone. `parseNoticeGivenAt` cannot be `parseDate`: **blank is a value here**, clearing the field back to "nobody has confirmed a notice", which B-186 built as a state distinct from a date and which `parseDate` refuses.

**Each row's form is named by facility AND unit.** An `aria-label` makes a `<form>` a landmark, so one per lease row means N landmarks on the profile; a tenant renting unit 101 at two sites would otherwise give the page two landmarks with one name (axe `landmark-unique`). The first column of that table already reads the same pair.

**Accessibility.** The two refusals are now reported per-field with a suggestion (3.3.1, 3.3.3), the save is announced in `AdminForm`'s pre-mounted live region (4.1.3, FR-20), the date field is named by its label and described by its hint (2.4.6, 3.3.2), and the shortfall paragraph states a consequence the product actually applies. **Neither refusal is reachable from a browser** — `future_date` is blocked first by the input's own `max`, and `not_occupying` needs the lease to end in another tab between render and save — so they are declared in `STATE_EXCEPTIONS` rather than scanned, with the copy asserted by unit test instead. That is the honest direction: they are defence against a crafted POST, not a state a scan can visit.

**Test verification.** Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`) clean; lint clean (7 pre-existing warnings, unrelated); `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` reports **no difference** — no migration in this row. Full unit suite **3,830 passed, 8 skipped of 3,838** (227 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0 — four new cases in `tests/move-out-db.test.ts`: `NOTICE_PROBLEM_COPY` covering every problem `recordNoticeGiven` can return (a missing key renders `undefined` in the error summary, which is the defect this row exists to fix), and `parseNoticeGivenAt` on blank-as-clear, a date field's value as UTC midnight, and garbage refused rather than stored as `Invalid Date`. `e2e/admin-move-out.spec.ts` + `e2e/admin-tenants.spec.ts`: **50 passed, 6 failed**, with the new spec green on **both** viewports and every axe pass on both screens green — including the tenant profile with a disclosure open, which is what proves the per-row form landmarks did not collide. The 6 failures are **B-199's** known `mobile-chrome` set (`the tenant ledger`'s two, `lien notices for a lease`'s four), identical in name and count to the run of the same two specs before this row's diff; B-199 is open with the cause and the instruction not to close it by narrowing the tests.

**Left behind.** **The charge is not built** — D-99 is open, and B-167 already shipped the fee primitive it would post through, so the build is small once the basis is settled. **The success announcement is not scanned** on either screen: reaching it means writing a notice date to a shared demo lease, and B-120's rule points at a fixture nothing else asserts against rather than an unscoped mutation on Dana's — the new spec reads only. **`AdminForm`'s error summary still lists each field's message without naming its field** (raised in B-192's entry, still product-wide and still a row of its own). **The six `mobile-chrome` failures on the staff profile are still open (B-199)** — untouched by this row, and the fifth consecutive entry to record them.

## B-195 — The aging report's arithmetic was right and said nothing about what was being done

`0ebc3ff`

**What it built.** The one fact the delinquency reports had never carried: whether anybody is chasing the money.

**(1) Every aging bucket splits into being chased and halted.** `agingForFacility` bucketed each lease's balance by `daysPastDue` with **no awareness of holds at all**, so a lease behind a bankruptcy hold nobody had opened in four months and a lease the ladder was actively working summed into one figure describing neither. `arAgingSplit` in `packages/core/metrics/delinquency.ts` partitions the same balances and guarantees `chased + halted = total` in every bucket; the `Total` column is unchanged and still ties out. The delinquency report renders each facility as two rows under one `scope="rowgroup"` header, and the tenant detail table and its CSV gain a **Collections** column naming the halting hold and how long it has been on.

**(2) A plans-and-holds report per facility, with the roll-up.** `/admin/reports/plans-holds` — lease, unit, hold type, plan status, next installment, amount deferred, days halted, **longest halted first**, one `<details>` per facility rolling up to the portfolio, plus a CSV matching the screen's order exactly. It answers "who is on a plan at my site", which no screen in this product could answer before.

**(3) The three figures that say whether plans work.** Amount put on plans, amount collected under them, amount that broke — per facility, per month.

**(4) The halted leases are back on the screen that exists to show them.** `/admin/delinquency` filtered an on-hold lease out of the queue — correctly, the ladder raises nothing for it — and thereby removed it from the only view an operator works. It now lists them below the queue, longest halted first, with the hold and whether a plan was agreed in return. **No money in that section, deliberately:** the queue is gated on `delinquency:execute_step` and a balance is `reports:financial` (B-055), so the figures stay on the report behind that key.

**What it decided.**

- **"Halted" means `halt_dunning`, asked of the catalog and never of the type.** US-42's own AC — "a new hold type is a configuration row, not six code changes" — so a new hold type joins or leaves this split by what it declares in `packages/core/holds/catalog.ts`. Every type in the catalog today declares it, which is why the test fixture for "chased" carries **no hold at all** rather than a narrow one.
- **A broken plan is counted in the month it BROKE, not the month it was agreed.** A plan agreed in February and broken in March belongs to February's `agreedCents` and March's `brokenCents`. Summing them under one month would make both months wrong, and it is the arithmetic a later session is most likely to "tidy".
- **Collected and still-owed are read from the invoices as they stand NOW, even for a month already past** — progress is derived, never stored (D-96), so there is no as-at figure to read. The screen says so rather than implying an as-at-month-end number it cannot produce.
- **The halted list takes an instant and refuses a range (D-65).** Holds and plan status keep no history, exactly like `Unit.status`. Two clocks live on one screen and the page names which governs which — the defect B-131, B-150 and B-183 each found in turn, headed off rather than repeated.
- **`deferredCents` is the lease's ledger balance**, the same definition as everywhere else (PRD 01 §7.3), so this report's total is the aging report's halted total by construction and not by coincidence — asserted, not assumed.

**Two N+1 reads went while they were in reach.** `activeHoldsByLease` is one query for a portfolio's holds and now backs `effectsByLease` as well, so there is one hold query in the codebase rather than two nearly identical ones; `planProgressByPlan` does the same for plan progress, and `planProgressCents` calls it rather than keeping a second copy of the arithmetic (§4.11: "no screen, tile or export computes any of these inline" is only true while there is one implementation to point at).

**Accessibility.** Both new tables are real tables with `<th scope="col">` and `<th scope="row">`; the facility name on the split table is `scope="rowgroup"` spanning its two rows, so the halted row announces as "Cedar Park, Halted, 61–90 days" rather than as figures with no owner. The chased/halted distinction is **carried in words and never by colour** (1.4.1) — a bankruptcy and a payment plan are opposite situations and both are "halted". Each roll-up `<summary>` is named after its facility and carries its count and amount (2.4.6), never one word repeated per site. **Both populated states are declared, not assumed:** the halted table and the queue's halted section render only for a lease under a hold and the demo seed places none, so each is a `STATE_EXCEPTIONS` row naming **B-196** as the seed that closes it — a missing fixture, said as one, rather than a green scan of an empty page taken for coverage. `apps/web/app/(public)/accessibility/page.tsx` is **unchanged and did not need to be**: this row ships nothing a customer touches, and the public page renders `SCAN_EXCEPTIONS` (whole routes) rather than `STATE_EXCEPTIONS`, so no sentence on it moved in either direction.

**Test verification.** Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`) clean; lint clean (7 pre-existing warnings, unrelated); `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` reports **no difference** — no migration in this row. Full unit suite **3,852 passed, 8 skipped of 3,860** (228 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0 — 4 new cases on `arAgingSplit` (each balance in exactly one half, the halves adding back to the unsplit aging bucket by bucket, roll-up by summation, and never inventing a halted figure) and a new `tests/plans-holds-report-db.test.ts` of 16 against real rows, built on the three cases that must never be confused: a lease under a plan hold **with** a plan, a lease under a bankruptcy hold with **no** plan, and a lease under **no** hold. `e2e/admin.spec.ts` + `e2e/admin-reports.spec.ts`: **586 passed, 6 failed**. The new route is green on **both** viewports for all four of the admin loops — axe, reflow at 320px, 200% zoom and forced text spacing — and so is `/admin/reports/delinquency` with its widened split table.

**The 6 failures are pre-existing and are now B-200**, verified by stashing this row's whole diff and re-running `e2e/admin-reports.spec.ts` against unmodified `main`: the identical three tests, on both projects. They are **not** B-199's set — these fail on `desktop-chrome` too. One of them is worth more than its size: `the CSV export matches the screen exactly` reads the screen's `td` index 3 (**sq-ft** occupancy) against the export's field 3 (**unit** occupancy), because the facility name is a `<th scope="row">` and not a `td` — so US-39's named AC has never actually been asserted on the column it names.

**Left behind.** **No demo hold and no demo plan exist**, so `/admin/reports/plans-holds` is scanned in its EMPTY state and the delinquency queue's halted section renders for nobody — the seed row **B-196** already owns closes this along with `/portal/payment-plan` and the admin builder, and B-196's row now names this third surface. **The plan-effectiveness figures are not in the CSV** — the export carries the halted list only, because a file where half the rows answer for a month and half answer for now is a file that will be read wrong; when a period-scoped export is wanted it is its own route. **The three pre-existing report-spec failures are open as B-200** and were deliberately not absorbed here: which side of the duplicate-content expectation is wrong is a UX call about what that report lists first, not a mechanical one. **The six `mobile-chrome` failures on the staff profile are still open (B-199)** — untouched by this row, and the sixth consecutive entry to record them.

## B-196 — The scan contract IV: a waiver earned on one page stopped covering the whole product

`9f7c722`

**What it built.** Four gaps in the accessibility scan contract, and one finding nobody had written down.

**(1) The hand-checked exemptions are no longer global — and two of them were never about the pages they had been checked on.** `e2e/a11y-helpers.ts` held four regexes matched against axe's `failureSummary` on **every route in the suite**. Each was earned properly, by hand, on one element of one screen; each then silently suppressed its whole check product-wide, including over a genuine overlap on a page nobody had looked at.

Three of them are one component on one page and are now keyed to it, the same `[param]`-aware route shape `SCANNED_STATES` uses: B-118's sticky Rent-now bar on the facility page, the `unrentable` badge's hatch gradient on `/admin/units`, the checkout stepper's glyph on `/checkout`. An optional `state` narrows an entry further and is compared against the `state` the caller passes.

**The other two were not a property of a page at all, and finding that out is the substance of this row.** `elmPartiallyObscured` and `shortTextContent` had been hand-checked twice — B-090c on the tenant profile, B-187 on the lead screen — and both times the finding was that nothing was overlapping anything. Walking every route in `ADMIN_SCAN_ROUTES` at phone width found **thirteen more routes firing the same two checks, with zero genuine overlaps among them**: every report with a wide table, plus `/admin/units/types`, `/admin/units/rates` and `/admin/access`. The mechanism is one thing and it is not the page — a wide table inside an `overflow-x: auto` container at 320–412px puts a cell's centre point OUTSIDE the viewport, so `document.elementsFromPoint` returns an empty stack and axe cannot resolve an effective background.

So those two are waived by **performing the hand check on every scan** rather than by remembering it: `nothingOverlaps` runs `elementsFromPoint` at the element's centre and waives only where nothing that is not the element's own ancestor or descendant sits on top of it. A real overlay over a real cell now fails **anywhere in the product**, which a fifteen-route list could not promise and would have rotted on the next admin table.

**(2) Nothing can open a second raw scan.** `tests/a11y-scan-coverage.test.ts` walks `e2e/` and fails any file but `a11y-helpers.ts` that builds its own `AxeBuilder` — and asserts the helper still builds one, so the rule cannot be satisfied by the suite having stopped scanning. Same shape as B-139's route check and B-184's state check: walk the directory, do not trust a list.

**(3) One seed row reaches four surfaces that had only ever been scanned empty.** `/portal/payment-plan`'s schedule and the nav entry beside it, the portal dashboard's plan card, `/admin/reports/plans-holds`'s halted table and `/admin/delinquency`'s halted section all render only for a lease under a hold, and the demo seed placed none — four `STATE_EXCEPTIONS` whose stated remedy was always a fixture. The seed now agrees a three-installment plan over two months' arrears.

**(4) The admin builder's refusal and the schedule it produces are scanned.** The six-installment grid is the densest form in the product and had been scanned only pristine.

**What it decided.**

- **The plan goes on its OWN demo tenant (`pia@demo.example.com`), not on Dana.** An active plan places a `payment_plan` hold, and that hold halts dunning, late fees and access suspension. Dana is the lease the portal past-due banner, the suspended gate-code panel, the delinquency queue and the dunning specs all depend on being CHASED — `admin-tenants.spec.ts` says so in as many words — and the builder's own disclosure is deliberately hidden on a lease that already has a plan, which would have taken the scan of that form with it. Same reasoning that gave `DEMO_POS_TENANT_EMAIL` its own tenant in B-039.
- **Every installment is in the FUTURE.** A missed one would be broken by `payment-plan-breach.ts` the first time the delinquency job ran, so the fixture would show an active plan on Monday and a broken one on Tuesday. A seed whose meaning depends on when the jobs last ran is worse than no seed. `autoCollect: false` for the same reason — no autopay run can retire an installment between sweeps.
- **The two ended-plan states are NARROWED, not merged away.** `/portal/payment-plan`'s broken/cancelled/completed schedules and `/portal`'s two warning card states all need a plan that actually missed a payment, which is exactly what the point above refuses to seed. They stay declared, describing what is genuinely unreached instead of being quietly swallowed by the fixture that closed their siblings.
- **B-090c's `partially obscured` hand check was not re-litigated and not deleted.** Its reasoning was sound and is now checked on every scan instead of once.

**A latent test assumption the new fixture exposed.** `admin.spec.ts`'s "money owed agrees with the report it links to" read the FIRST report row for the facility and passed — because nothing in the demo data had ever been halted, so *being chased* always equalled the total. B-195 split each facility into a chased row and a halted row with no combined row per facility, and this row's plan is the first fixture to make that false. The assertion now sums both halves, which is what it meant all along: a tile that quietly stopped counting money behind a hold fails here rather than agreeing with half a report.

**A real bug found along the way:** none in product code. The two findings are both in the test contract — the global waivers above, and the money-owed assertion that could only pass while nothing was halted.

**Accessibility.** The public statement gets its own sentence, per the rule: one claim on it was **false in the overstating direction**. "They also fail on checks the tool could not decide, everywhere they run" — added by B-184 finding 4, correct about the eight spec files it was written for — was untrue of four checks, which were suppressed product-wide. The page now says that a few undecided checks are hand-checked limits of the tool and that each is waived only on the page it was checked on. `LAST_REVIEWED` is not bumped: the coverage claim and that one sentence were re-checked against the build, the rest of the page was not.

**Test verification.** Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`) clean; lint clean (7 pre-existing warnings, unrelated); `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` reports **no difference** — no migration in this row. The demo seed was run **twice in a row** to prove it is still idempotent: `PaymentPlan` restricts its lease, its hold and the staff user who agreed it, and `LeaseHold` restricts its lease, so teardown deletes both before leases — the same foreign-key trap B-132's auction case hit. Full unit suite **3,853 passed, 8 skipped of 3,861** (228 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0.

Full e2e sweep: **1,249 passed, 10 skipped, 13 failed of 1,272**. Every scan this row added is green on BOTH viewports — the portal schedule and the nav entry beside it, the dashboard plan card, the delinquency queue's halted section, the plans-and-holds halted table with a facility open, the profile's plan schedule, and the refused builder submit — as are the two pre-existing scans the rescoping had been hiding a real undecided check on (`/admin/leads/[leadId]` and `/admin/reports/rent-roll`).

Of the 13: **B-200's three report specs on both projects (6)** and **B-199's six `mobile-chrome` staff-profile tests**, both untouched by this row and unchanged in name and count. The thirteenth is `units (B-116) paginates at 50` on `mobile-chrome`, a **flake** — a `Next` click that did not navigate — re-run on its own immediately afterwards and green (3 passed, exit 0), and green in the sweep before this one.

The route this took is worth recording, because the first sweep is what produced the finding. Rescoping the waivers turned three previously-green scans red — `/admin/leads/[leadId]`, `/admin/reports/rent-roll` and the new plans-and-holds table — each on an undecided check that had been suppressed since B-118. Hand-checking those is what showed the mechanism was `overflow-x: auto`, not the page, and the assertion message now names axe's own phrasing for the limitation rather than only the rule that gave up: "check them by hand" without the phrasing is most of the work missing.

**Left behind.** **No plan in the demo data has ever missed a payment**, so the two narrowed state exceptions above stay open — closing them needs a fixture that can hold a missed installment still against the nightly jobs, which is a seed problem, not a scan one. **`state` is carried by `HAND_CHECKED_INCOMPLETE` and used by no current entry** — the containment pair that needed it became the hit test instead; it is one optional field and the tenant profile still passes its state for the failure message. **The pre-existing failures are untouched and still open:** B-200's three report specs on both projects, and B-199's six `mobile-chrome` staff-profile tests, now the seventh consecutive entry to record them.

## B-197 — The four limits that decide who may give money away were reachable only from a database client

`0be870b`

**What it built.** `/admin/settings/roles` — one org-level screen showing every staff role against the four monetary limits on it (`maxFeeWaiverCents`, `maxRefundCents`, `maxCreditCents` and D-98's `maxPlanDeferralCents`), and the forms that change them. Until this row those four columns were seeded by `packages/db/rbac-catalog.ts` and written by **nothing anywhere in the product**, which made PRD 02 RBAC-2 — "starting values the owner can change in configuration; they are not hardcoded policy" — false in as many words. An operator who wanted their managers to waive $100 rather than $50 had to ring somebody.

Beside role and permission management rather than in facility settings, because the limits live on `Role` and a role is one row for the whole portfolio: there is no per-site version of "what a facility manager may waive" to put on a facility's own page. The gate is therefore `users:manage` asked with a **null facilityId**, the same question `/admin/settings/staff` asks — only an owner, or a manager assigned to every facility, satisfies it. Every save is audited as `role.limits_changed` with all four limits on both sides.

**What it decided.**

- **The ladder check is scoped to the roles that hold the permission, and to the fields the save actually moved.** `nextApproverRole` walks roles above the actor's rank in ascending order and stops at the first whose limit covers the amount — so a lower-ranked role with a bigger limit means every over-limit request escalates to somebody with *less* authority than the person who asked, and the rung above never sees it. `ladderViolation` refuses that at the point of editing. It compares only roles that hold the action's permission, because those are exactly the roles `nextApproverRole` considers; an inert number on a role that cannot waive a fee is not in the chain and cannot break it. And it checks only the actions a save changed: validating all four every time means a ladder that was already crooked when the screen loaded blocks an unrelated field, and the only way to fix it is the database client this row exists to remove.
- **Roles at the same rank are not compared.** Counter staff and the bookkeeper are both rank 10. Neither is above the other, so neither is where the other's over-limit request goes.
- **Blank is unlimited, `0` is no authority, and nothing in the chain may collapse them.** `null` sorts as `Infinity` in the ladder check, not as zero — the two would get the comparison exactly backwards. `parseScaled` is never reached for an empty box (it refuses an empty string by design), and `describe()` is the single place either becomes words, used by the table, the success announcement and the refusal message alike. This is the same `undefined`-is-not-`null` distinction `checkMonetaryAuthority` already carries a paragraph about.
- **Five forms, one per role, rather than inputs inside the table.** A cell-level input would have to reach its `AdminForm` through the `form=` owner attribute (the B-180 pattern), which carries the DOM relationship but not the React context `Field` reads its error from — so 3.3.1 would have been satisfied by a summary at the top of the page and nothing beside the field that caused it. The table stays read-only and says today's figures; the forms sit under it.
- **`LIMIT_FIELD` and `REQUIRED_PERMISSION` are exported from `authorize.ts` rather than re-declared.** Which column carries which limit, and which permission gates it, is one fact — a second copy in the editing screen is a second thing to keep true.

**Accessibility (PRD 02 §5.5).** A real `<table>` with `<th scope="col">` on each limit and `<th scope="row">` on the role name, inside the same focusable `overflow-x-auto` wrapper the staff table uses. Every amount field is named after its role *and* its act — "Fee waiver limit for Facility Manager (dollars)", never four fields called "Limit" on a page carrying five forms (2.4.6) — and each form is labelled for its role for the same reason. Unlimited and "nothing (no authority)" are stated in words in every cell, never by a blank alone (3.3.2). A refusal is keyed to the action, which is the name of the input it belongs beside (3.3.1). A role that does not hold the permission behind a limit says so, in the cell and in the field hint, rather than letting somebody raise a figure that changes nothing.

**No claim on the public accessibility statement changes, and that is deliberate:** every surface here is under `/admin`, which the statement makes no claims about. The route IS added to `ADMIN_SCAN_ROUTES`, so `admin.spec.ts` scans and reflow-checks it like every other admin page — B-139's contract refuses a route that appears in neither list — and the reasoning is written into that page's header so the next reader does not have to re-derive it.

**A real bug found along the way:** none. The defect was the absence itself.

**Test verification.** Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`) clean; lint clean (7 pre-existing warnings, unrelated); `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` reports **no difference** — no migration in this row, because the columns already existed. Full unit suite **3,865 passed, 8 skipped of 3,873** (229 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0. `tests/role-limits-db.test.ts` adds ten: five against real rows (the save and its audit both sides, the ladder refusal writing nothing at all, an unknown role, the org-level gate refusing a single-facility manager, and the listing excluding the non-staff `tenant` role) and five pure ones covering every shape the ladder comparison has to get right — including the two it must **not** complain about. The targeted e2e for the new route passed **10/10** on both viewports.

**A shared-table trap the fixtures had to dodge.** `role` is global to the whole test schema, so a fixture role holding a real permission *and* a real limit is visible to every other suite's `nextApproverRole` for as long as the file runs. Both fixtures therefore sit at $0 throughout — an escalation only ever considers a role whose limit covers the amount, so a $0 rung can never be picked — and the one test that raises a limit above $0 on a role holding `fees:waive` is the test that is **refused**, which writes nothing. The staff fixture is not reclaimed and cannot be: `audit_log`'s RESTRICT foreign key pins its author forever (B-185), and `npm run db:reset-test` is the only cleanup.

**Left behind.** **The ladder is checked on save and never again**, so inserting a role *below* an existing one with a bigger limit still produces a crooked chain that only the next edit of that action reports — creating and ranking roles is not built and **B-004** still owns it. **There is no approval queue for an over-limit action**, which is the same posture `waiveFeeInvoice`, B-167's charge control and B-190's plan builder all already take; B-048 owns it. **Nothing warns that lowering a limit has no effect on what is already approved** beyond the sentence at the top of the screen — no in-flight approval is revisited, by design.

## Demo readiness — the preview-deploy safety net was inert on the only platform this deploys to

`f859549`

Not a backlog row. The session was scoped to demo configuration — a real org phone number, outbound email, the shared password gate — and the second of those turned up a defect that had to be fixed before the configuration it blocked could be applied safely.

**What it built.** One line of behaviour: `isProductionEnv()` in [apps/web/lib/comms/provider.ts](../apps/web/lib/comms/provider.ts) now reads **`VERCEL_ENV`** where Vercel sets it, and falls back to `NODE_ENV` only off-platform.

**The defect.** Four guards exist so a non-production deployment cannot mail or text a real person: the email sandbox redirect (`effectiveRecipient`), the SMS sandbox redirect, and the log-only provider fallback on each (`selectProvider`, `selectSmsProvider`). All four asked `NODE_ENV === 'production'`. **Vercel builds every deployment with `NODE_ENV=production`, previews included**, so on Vercel all four answered "this is production" from a preview, and all four were inert. `RESEND_API_KEY` set at Vercel's default all-environments scope — which is the default, and which is exactly what "add a Resend key so mail sends" would have done — would have sent real mail to real recipients from every preview deploy. `COMMS_SANDBOX_INBOX` would have been read and ignored, because `effectiveRecipient` returns the real address before it looks.

Both `.env.example` and this file asserted the opposite in as many words: "no preview deploy can reach a real tenant" (the B-030 entry). The claim was true off Vercel and false on it, and Vercel is where this deploys. `VERCEL_ENV` appeared nowhere in the codebase.

**What it decided.**

- **The fix is in the shared predicate, not at the four call sites.** All four guards already route through one function; a guard added per-caller would be four things to keep true and would leave the next caller unprotected by default.
- **`NODE_ENV` stays the fallback rather than being replaced.** `VERCEL_ENV` is unset off-platform, where `NODE_ENV` is the correct and only answer — local dev, the CI container, a self-hosted build. Reading `VERCEL_ENV` unconditionally would have made every non-Vercel environment non-production, which is a different bug in the same place.

**What was decided about the configuration itself** (owner, 2026-08-28):

- **`SITE.phone` stays `(512) 555-0100`.** There is no org-level office line to point it at yet, and 555-01xx is the range reserved precisely so it cannot dial a real person. A plausible-looking substitute would be strictly worse — it can ring somebody. The reasoning is now a comment on the field so a later session does not "tidy" it into a fake.
- **`DEMO_ACCESS_PASSWORD` on** for the demo deployment. No code change: the gate, its six exemptions and its production verification have been in place and documented since it was built.
- **Resend goes live, scoped per environment.** `RESEND_API_KEY`, `RESEND_WEBHOOK_SECRET` and `COMMS_EMAIL_DOMAIN` at **production scope only**; `COMMS_SANDBOX_INBOX` on **preview**. `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md` gains an "Email go-live" section stating that scoping as a table and saying why it matters, beside the Twilio one that already existed. This is the step the defect above would have silently undone.

**Twilio was evaluated and deliberately not touched.** It is built and dormant — webhook, signature verification, double opt-in, STOP/HELP, quiet hours, per-facility Messaging Service SID — and blocked on A2P 10DLC campaign approval, which is a carrier wait measured in days to weeks. There is no code to write, and the one step that would prove it works (a round trip from a real handset) cannot run before approval. With `TWILIO_*` unset every SMS rule falls back to email, which is the designed behaviour.

**A real bug found along the way:** the one above, and it is the entry. Nothing else.

**Test verification.** Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`) clean; `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` reports **no difference**. Full unit suite **3,869 passed, 8 skipped of 3,877** (230 files passed, 1 skipped), exit 0 — reconciled, and +4 over B-197 exactly matching the four added here. `tests/comms-provider-env.test.ts` pins the predicate at all four corners: a Vercel preview with `NODE_ENV=production` redirects to the sandbox and falls back to log-only when there is no sandbox; a Vercel production deployment sends to the real address; and off Vercel `NODE_ENV` still decides. **Verified failing before the fix** by stashing `provider.ts` alone — the two preview tests go red, the two controls stay green, which is what shows they are testing the predicate and not the environment.

The test uses `vi.stubEnv` rather than assigning `process.env.NODE_ENV`, which is read-only on `ProcessEnv`. The first draft assigned it, and `npm run typecheck` caught all four lines — the check CLAUDE.md records as having been off for most of this repo's life, doing exactly the job it was turned on for.

**The public accessibility statement was re-read and no claim changes.** It says nothing about email, which its own header already notes deliberately; nothing customer-facing shipped here. `LAST_REVIEWED` is not bumped.

**Left behind.** **`COMMS_SANDBOX_SMS` has the same shape and no test**, because SMS cannot be exercised end to end until the campaign is approved — the predicate it depends on is now pinned, but the SMS side of the redirect is covered only by the shared function. **The three MVP rows are still open**: B-199 (the tenant profile's leases table is unreachable at 375px — a real reflow defect, and the demo will be shown on a phone at some point), B-200 (three stale report-spec assertions, one of which means the occupancy CSV export has never been checked) and B-198 (every email is one `<p>`). None was touched here.

## B-199 — Seven wide staff tables clipped their own action links on a phone, and the reflow test could not see it

`f9a9823`

**What it built.** The `overflow-x-auto` wrapper this codebase already uses for a wide table, on the seven admin tables that did not have one: the tenant profile's leases table (the one the row was about), the billing runs table, the POS deposit-slip table, two report tables, the rent roll, and the tenant search results. On a 375px phone the leases table's last column holds up to four action links — Ledger, Notices, Move out, Transfer — and they sat outside the document, untappable and unreachable by scrolling.

Six e2e tests had recorded it as a `mobile-chrome` flake for four items running. All six now pass on both projects, which is what the row named as its proof.

**What it decided.**

- **The floor is the load-bearing half, and the row did not say so.** `overflow-x-auto` on its own fixes nothing here: `w-full` sizes the table to exactly the wrapper's width, so the wrapper never has anything to scroll and seven columns are crushed into 327px instead. The links become reachable and unusable. The pairing is `w-full` **plus `min-w-2xl`** (or `min-w-max` past eight columns), which is what every already-wrapped table in this repo uses — the pattern was there to copy and copying half of it would have passed the six tests while leaving the screen unusable.
- **Seven tables, not one, and not seventeen.** The row asked for a check across every admin table wider than four columns, and that is an audit rather than a fix of the page the tests named. The first pass counted columns over a fixed line window, which spills into the next table: three genuinely three-column tables were briefly wrapped and given a floor that would have made them scroll sideways for no reason. Counting `scope="col"` between a table's own `<thead>` boundaries is what got it right, and the corrected audit says no wide unwrapped table remains in `/admin` or `/portal`.
- **The scoped exemption list was not touched.** B-196's hand-checked waivers and its `nothingOverlaps` hit test both stand exactly as written. Nothing here re-litigates a hand check somebody already did.

**The real finding, and why four items in a row could honestly call this pre-existing.** `e2e/admin.spec.ts` has asserted 320px reflow over every admin route since B-094, and every one of these seven pages was passing it. `[contain:layout]` on `<main>` — added by B-116, correctly, so a properly wrapped table's own scroll region would stop Chromium's root-level `scrollWidth` walk — stops that walk either way. A table with **no** wrapper overflows inside a containing block the document cannot see past, so `documentElement.scrollWidth` stays at 320 and the assertion passes while the columns are unreachable by any means. That is strictly worse than the sideways scroll the check exists to catch, and it is invisible to the check. The containment is not the bug and was not removed; B-116 measured it and its reasoning holds. What is missing is a check it cannot mask, which is **B-201**, raised rather than absorbed — along with the second half of the same gap: the reflow, 200%-zoom and text-spacing loops run over `ADMIN_SCAN_ROUTES` only, so the seven dynamic routes in `SCANNED_BY_OWN_SPEC` have never been reflow-checked at all. B-199's defect lived on one of them.

**A real bug found along the way, and it is not the one the failure said.** Once the wrapper let the lien-notices tests run at all, one of them failed with a `color-contrast` incomplete naming two nodes — a `Balance` column header and a `$161.00` cell — that **do not exist on that route**. The cause is in the spec, not the page: its `beforeEach` clicked through to the notices page and then waited only for `<main>` to be visible, which the profile's own `<main>` already satisfies. The axe scan therefore raced the client-side transition and scanned the previous page while `page.url()` already reported the new path; by the time the hit test looked for those nodes, the notices page had rendered and they were gone. `nothingOverlaps` treats a missing element as "keep", so a navigation race presented as an accessibility overlap. Fixed with `waitForURL`, and confirmed by scanning the route with the wait in place: **zero incompletes**. Verified pre-existing rather than introduced by stashing the whole diff — against unmodified `main` all four lien-notices tests time out at 30.1s, the axe one included, so it had never run.

`assertNoAxeViolations` now reports the offending target selectors alongside axe's phrasing, and says explicitly when a flagged node is no longer in the DOM. B-196 made the point that a message naming the limitation but not what to look for leaves most of the work undone; this is the same argument one level down — without the selector the hand check begins by re-running the scan under a debugger, which is exactly what it cost here.

**Accessibility.** Each wrapper is `tabIndex={0}`, the established pattern, so the scroll region is reachable by keyboard (2.1.1). No table markup changed: every `<caption>`, `<th scope="col">` and `<th scope="row">` is as it was. The public statement was re-read and **no sentence changes** — it is a statement about the customer site and every screen here is under `/admin`. What had to be checked before leaving it alone was the mechanism rather than the scope: if `[contain:layout]` were anywhere on the public site, that page's own "reflows to 320px" claim would be resting on a check that cannot fail, which is worse than an untested claim because it reads as evidence. It is not — the containment is on `admin/layout.tsx` and nowhere else, verified by grep. `LAST_REVIEWED` does not move.

**Test verification.** Typecheck (including `tsconfig.tests.json`) clean; lint clean (7 pre-existing warnings, unrelated); `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` reports **no difference** — no schema change. Full unit suite **3,869 passed, 8 skipped of 3,877**, exit 0. e2e over `admin-tenants`, `admin`, `admin-reports` and `admin-pos`: **658 passed, 6 failed**, and the six are B-200's three stale report assertions on both projects, untouched by this row and failing identically on `desktop-chrome`. The 116 reflow tests pass. One new spec pins the half the six recovered tests cannot: at 375px the leases wrapper is a real scroll region (`scrollWidth > clientWidth`), the document still does not scroll sideways, and the Ledger link is clickable — a `w-full` table with no floor would satisfy the six and fail this.

**Left behind.** **B-201**, which is the check rather than the defect, and is the reason this went four items unnoticed. **B-200's three report assertions are still red** and still the only check on the facts they name — including an occupancy CSV column that has never actually been compared. **The narrow tables were deliberately left bare:** nine tables of four columns or fewer in `/admin` and `/portal` have no wrapper, and giving them one would add a keyboard tab stop to a region that never scrolls.

## B-198 — The template's second HTML body is deleted, and the schedule became a real table anyway

`cb4e6f1`

**What it built.** `MessageTemplate.bodyHtml` is gone — the column, the schema field, the `checkPublishable` input, both of the unconditional `bodyHtml: null` writes in the editor, and the branch in `renderEmail` that would have used it. Migration `20260828175542_drop_message_template_body_html`, verified beforehand against the dev database: 40 template rows, **0** with a non-null value, so nothing was lost.

In its place, one thing the second body could never have done safely: **a structured merge value.** `MergeValue = string | { text, html }`. Most merged values stay a plain string. A value that is inherently tabular supplies both renderings, built side by side by whoever has the data. `plan.schedule` is the first: the numbered list a tenant reads in the text part, and a captioned table with `<th scope="col">` and `<th scope="row">` in the HTML part, both from the one array of installments — through `tableHtml`, which B-084 part 3 already wrote, reviewed and tested for report emails, now exported rather than re-implemented.

The HTML part of a templated email is now built from the **template body**, not from the already-rendered text: literal text escaped, merged values escaped or contributing their own markup, `<br>` only where the author put a line break. A structured value alone in its own paragraph owns that block unwrapped, because a `<table>` inside a `<p>` is invalid and the browser's fixup for it strands the caption.

**What it decided.**

- **D-102: one body per template, and the HTML part is that body rendered as markup.** The row asked for the deletion to be priced against the build, and the deletion won on evidence rather than taste: the column was null on every row that ever existed, the editor wrote it null on every save, and no message in the product's life ever rendered from it. Reversing this is a migration.
- **CN-24's table was never a body problem.** It is one merge field whose value is tabular. That reframing is the whole item — it turns an M with a second editable document, a second publish gate and a permanent drift surface into a union type and a helper, and it meets the criterion more completely, because two renderings of one array cannot disagree about a date the way two authored bodies can.
- **The deleted column was also an escaping hole.** `renderString` interpolated a `bodyHtml` **raw**. Had anyone ever seeded one, a facility called "Bob & Sons" would have emitted broken markup from the very body an operator had been told was the safer, richer one — the exact bug B-191 fixed on the text path. Nobody found this because nobody could reach the code. It left with the column.
- **`tableHtml` was exported, not copied.** One table implementation in the product, reviewed once. A tenant's schedule and a staff report email are now accessible in the same way for the same reason.
- **The text part keeps the numbered list, deliberately.** `tableText`'s monospace column padding is right for a report a staffer opens and wrong for a tenant's mail client in a proportional font. Same document, two renderings — which is what FR-9a asks for and not the same as "both parts identical".

**Accessibility.** CN-24's email criteria are met in full for the first time: `lang` on the wrapper, the subject as the single `<h1>`, `<caption>` and both header scopes on the schedule, every merged value escaped, and a text part built from the same document rather than by stripping tags. The public accessibility statement gets a new entry and **no claim on it moves** — it says nothing about email in either direction, and it should not start; but the B-191 entry's written statement that the schedule "is a numbered list rather than a `<table>`" had gone false, so it is corrected in place rather than left reading as current. `LAST_REVIEWED` does not move.

**Test verification.** Full unit suite green: **3872 passed + 8 skipped = 3880**, exit 0, 231 files. Typecheck clean including `tsconfig.tests.json`. `prisma migrate diff --exit-code`: **no difference**. `db:migrate:test` and `db:migrate:e2e` both run. Two checks were added where the logic actually is: `tests/comms-render.test.ts` covers a structured value unwrapped in its own block, inline in a sentence, absent from the text part, and empty (which must still throw `RenderError`); `tests/payment-plan-comms-db.test.ts` asserts the caption, both header scopes and the absence of `<p><table` **on a real send**, so the table is checked end to end rather than only in the renderer.

**Left behind.** **The move-out settlement and invoice figures are still prose, not tables.** The row listed them alongside the schedule; they are not CN-24 criteria, no acceptance criterion names them, and each one now costs a `scheduleValue`-shaped helper and nothing else — so they get done when a row asks for them rather than speculatively here. **No template offers rich formatting to an operator**, which is the thing the deleted column looked like it might one day become; D-102 says what would have to be true to revisit it. **B-200 and B-201 are still open** and untouched by this item.

## B-200 — Three stale report assertions, one of which was never checking the column it named

`4ce99da`

**What it built.** Nothing new on any screen except a corrected sentence. Three e2e tests in `e2e/admin-reports.spec.ts` were failing against unmodified `main` on both projects, and B-195 verified that by stashing its own diff. Each one is the only check on the fact it names, so none was closed by deleting it.

**(1) The occupancy CSV test compared the wrong two columns.** It read the roll-up row's `td` at index 3 and compared it to field 3 of `occupancy.csv`. The facility name is a `<th scope="row">`, so `td` 3 on the screen is **Sq-ft occ.** while field 3 of the export is **Unit occupancy %** — different figures that had simply been rounding alike. US-39's acceptance criterion is "CSV export matching on-screen data exactly", and the column it names had therefore never been asserted at all.

The fix went past the index. The test now maps **all six** screen columns to their CSV fields — `[td, field, name]` triples, with `%$,` stripped so `50.2%` and `$1,234.56` compare against `50.2` and `1234.56` — so the export cannot drift on a column nobody is looking at, and a mapping that goes wrong fails with the column named instead of coinciding. It is a map rather than a zip because the CSV carries three columns the table does not show (occupied and rentable sq ft, gross potential).

**(2)+(3) The duplicate-content tests were pinned by position to a row that moved.** They took `getByRole('row').filter({ hasText: 'Austin, TX' }).first()` and expected the rowheader `City page intros`. B-089's per-city/size intros score ~0.94 against each other where the city intros score 0.82–0.85, the report sorts most-alike first, and a size row's label reads `10×10 — Austin, TX` — so it matches the same text filter and sorts above. A shared `kindRow(page, kind)` helper now selects on the rowheader, which says which kind the test meant and stays correct however the pairs re-sort.

**The real defect the row had not named.** Chasing (2) turned up a live bug: the report treated `bothGenerated` as one case, so a **City/size page intros** pair carried "Write copy for one of these cities" linking to `/admin/settings/marketing/cities`. That link cannot fix it — `citySizeIntro` takes no authored override, so following it edits the city page and leaves the size pair exactly as it was. An operator does the work and watches nothing happen. A city/size row now states what D-77 actually did about the page (served `noindex` rather than advertised) and offers no fix link, with a new test asserting the row has exactly two links — the two pages, and no fix.

**What it decided.**

- **D-103: the sort does not change; the advice does.** The rejected option was sorting actionable pairs above unactionable ones, which would have made the positional `.first()` correct again for free. It is the wrong trade: it hides the most-duplicated page in the portfolio below less-duplicated ones, on the one screen whose job is to say how alike things are.
- **Neighbours were checked, and there were none.** The row warned that the same off-by-one is available to every CSV test written against a table whose first cell is a row header. This was the only spec in `e2e/` indexing `td` positionally — the tenant-ledger CSV test reads `.at(-1)` and looks the balance up by its `<dt>`, and the journal tests assert status codes.
- **A test that means a kind selects on the kind.** `.first()` encodes an ordering the test does not own and cannot see change. That is what made this look like a product regression for four items rather than a stale expectation.

**Test verification.** Typecheck clean including `tsconfig.tests.json` — it needed `rm -rf apps/web/.next` first, since stale generated route types under `.next/` fail `tsc` on their own and say nothing about the diff. Lint clean (7 pre-existing warnings, none in these files). Full unit suite **3,875 passed, 8 skipped of 3,883**, exit 0, 230 files passed + 1 skipped. `e2e/admin-reports.spec.ts`: **88 passed** — 43 desktop-chrome, 43 mobile-chrome, 2 setup — exit 0. No schema change, so no migration and no drift check.

**Left behind.** **B-201 is untouched** and is still the reason a defect of this kind goes unnoticed. **B-134 still owns the missing authored city/size copy** — the new row wording says there is nowhere to write it, which is true today and is the sentence that has to change when B-134 lands. **The six columns are mapped by position, not by header text**: a column inserted into either the table or the CSV moves an index, and the test will say so loudly rather than silently — but somebody still has to update the triple.

## B-201 — The reflow check that `[contain:layout]` cannot mask, and the seven defects it found on green routes

`bf21eba`

**What it built.** Two halves of one gap, both named by B-199 and both closed here.

**(1) The seven dynamic routes are checked at 320px, 200% zoom and forced text spacing.** `SCANNED_BY_OWN_SPEC` exists because a route with a `[param]` segment needs a live fixture to render its real content, and B-156 correctly gave each one an axe scan inside its own topic spec. It did that for axe and only for axe: `/admin/tenants/[tenantId]`, its ledger, notices, move-out and transfer, plus `/portal/pay` and `/portal/transfer`, had never been measured at any width by anything. B-199's defect lived on one of them for four items. `e2e/a11y-own-spec-routes.spec.ts` reaches all seven through **one** table of click-throughs rather than seven copies pasted into seven topic files, and a route in `SCANNED_BY_OWN_SPEC` with no entry in that table is a failing test named for the route — so this cannot fall behind the axe coverage again the way it already had.

**(2) The assertion no longer goes through the document.** Every reflow, zoom and text-spacing loop in the suite asked one question of one element, `document.documentElement.scrollWidth > clientWidth`. B-116 put `contain: layout` on admin's `<main>` so a correctly-wrapped table's own scroll region would stop Chromium's root-level scrollWidth walk, and it stops the walk either way — an unwrapped wide table overflows inside a containing block the document cannot see past, so the root reports 320 while the columns are unreachable by any means. `expectNoHorizontalOverflow` asks instead, per element, whether anything is **painted past the right edge of the screen that no scrollbar reaches**. The root comparison is still inside it. All four loop sites — public, portal, admin and the new file — route through the one function.

**The seven defects it found on its first run, on four routes that were green throughout.**

- **Six are one bug, and B-116's own comment names one of them.** `Field`'s wrapper `<div>` is a flex item in `AdminForm`'s wrapping row, so its default `min-width: auto` holds it at its own min-content width — and for a `<select>`, that is the **longest option**. B-116's `max-w-full` on `CONTROL_CLASS` then caps the control at 100% of a parent that is already too wide, and the pair cancels out. `protectionRequired` — the control B-116's comment cites as the reason for `max-w-full` — still ran to 365px on a 320px phone, with that fix present and applied. The others: `autoEnrolProtectionOnLapse`, the promotion minimum-stay and transfer-discount settings, `/admin/rate-increases`' tenant picker, and the transfer wizard's unit picker.
- **The seventh** is `GOOGLE_SEARCH_CONSOLE_CLIENT_EMAIL` on `/admin/reports/indexation`, a token with no break opportunity in it, at 347px. `break-all`, the same fix as B-094's JSON example on `/admin/units/setup`.

**What it decided.**

- **`min-w-0` is prepended to every `Field` wrapper, not written into its default class string** — and that distinction is a finding rather than a style choice. Five files (`admin/pos`, the tenant profile, its move-out and transfer wizards, `/portal/contact`) declare a local `FIELD_CLASS` that is a hand-copy of `Field`'s own default and **replaces** it. The first attempt put `min-w-0` in the default: `/admin/settings` and `/admin/reports/indexation` went green and `/admin/rate-increases` and the transfer wizard did not move, because neither uses the default. One line inside the component reaches all of them whatever they were handed; consolidating the five copies would have been a bigger diff for the same result, and the copies are now merely redundant rather than load-bearing.
- **The check is a right-edge test, not a per-element `scrollWidth` test, and the rejected version is worth recording** because it is the obvious one to reach for next time. Comparing `scrollWidth > clientWidth` on every element is more sensitive and was unusable: 60+ findings over seven routes, not one a defect. `sr-only` is `position: absolute`, and a `div.overflow-x-auto` here is `position: static` — so an sr-only span inside a horizontally scrolled table is **not** clipped by that scroll container, escapes to the nearest positioned ancestor, and by itself pushed `<main>`'s scrollWidth to 675px on the tenant profile, which then looked exactly like the defect the check exists to find on a page that renders correctly. Chromium also lays out `content-visibility: hidden` subtrees, so the portal nav's **closed** "Manage" menu reported six links overflowing a 45px column nobody can see. Both exclusions are named in the helper with the reason; `checkVisibility` covers the second and the `sr-only` clip is matched in both spellings the utility has used.
- **`[contain:layout]` stays.** The row required it, B-116 measured it, and its reasoning holds. What was missing was a check it cannot mask, not the removal of a rule that is doing its job.
- **The alarm was verified against a real failing run before being relied on.** Deleting the tenant profile's `overflow-x-auto` reproduces B-199's exact defect, and the check names it — `table.w-full.min-w-2xl.text-sm — right edge at 696px, screen is 320px — "Leases held by this tenant…"` — then goes green when it is restored. The failure message carries the element's classes, its right edge, the screen width and the first 60 characters of its text, for the same reason B-199 put axe's target selectors in `assertNoAxeViolations`: without them a hand check starts by re-running the scan under a debugger.

**Accessibility.** `/portal/pay` and `/portal/transfer` are customer-facing and had never been reflow-, zoom- or text-spacing-checked; both pass all three. The public statement's reflow sentence is unchanged and no claim on it moves — every defect found was on `/admin`, which the page makes no claim about. What did change is what carries that sentence: B-199's entry on the page argued the public claim was safe because `[contain:layout]` is admin-only and the public assertion could therefore still go red. The public loops now use a check that does not depend on that remaining true. `LAST_REVIEWED` does not move.

**Found along the way, and fixed here.** The full sweep turned up the move-out screen's axe scan failing on a `color-contrast` incomplete naming `.text-left > .text-right` — a **tenant profile** element that is not on that route. It is the race B-199 diagnosed on the lien-notices scan and fixed there only: the click-through leaves the profile, whose `<main>` is already visible, so `await expect(getByRole('main')).toBeVisible()` is satisfied instantly and axe can read the old DOM while `page.url()` already reports the new path. The same two lines were sitting in the move-out scan and the ledger scan the whole time; both now `waitForURL` first. It is worth noting that this diagnosed itself — the "some of these are no longer in the DOM, so this scan probably raced a navigation" note B-199 added to `assertNoAxeViolations` is what turned a contrast finding on nodes that do not exist into a one-line fix, which is exactly the work that message was added to save.

**Test verification.** Typecheck clean including `tsconfig.tests.json`. Lint clean (7 pre-existing warnings, none in these files). Full unit suite **3,875 passed, 8 skipped of 3,883**, exit 0. `prisma migrate diff --exit-code`: **no difference** — no schema change, so no migration. Full e2e sweep **1,288 passed, 10 skipped of 1,298**, exit 0, on both `mobile-chrome` and `desktop-chrome`; the four-file reflow sweep was run green immediately before it against the same un-reseeded database, and the new spec writes nothing at all, so B-120's shared-fixture rule is met by the first of its three disciplines rather than by luck. The `min-w-0` change reaches `/checkout`, `/reservations` and eight portal pages, which is why the whole suite was run here rather than left to CI's own lane.
