**Left behind.** **The five `FIELD_CLASS` copies are still there**, now redundant rather than load-bearing; deleting them is a tidy-up nobody needs to schedule. **Hand-rolled `<label className="flex flex-col gap-1 text-sm">` fields that do not go through `Field` get no `min-w-0`** — there are many, none of them currently overflows, and the check now fails loudly if one starts to, which is the reason not to touch 175 call sites speculatively. **Content clipped by an `overflow: hidden` ancestor is not flagged**: it is unreachable too, but separating deliberate clipping from accidental needs evidence this run did not produce, and no route currently shows it.

## B-129 (part) — The auction lot sheet, and the readiness check that decides what may be advertised

`1350aa8`

**What it built.** The half of US-30's advertising story that does not depend on an unanswered question. **B-129 stays open**; both of its blockers are still blockers.

`/admin/auctions/lots.csv` is a structured lot sheet — lot number, facility name and address, unit number, size and square feet, sale date, terms of sale, case reference — that an operator uploads to a marketplace, hands to an auctioneer, or reads down a phone to a newspaper. `/admin/auctions` gains an **Advertising the sale** section that offers it, and a **Not on the sheet** list. `/admin/settings/delinquency` gains a terms-of-sale form.

**What was deliberately NOT built.** No marketplace driver, no vendor API call, and no `AuctionAdvertisement` row written by exporting. Downloading a sheet is not evidence that an advertisement ran; that row stays typed by the person who placed the ad, with the publication and the tear sheet (B-062). Master PRD §11 OQ-9 — live on-site auctions versus online — is still open, and a CSV is neutral between the two in a way a driver written against one vendor's API would not be.

**What it decided.**

- **D-104: the lot sheet ships while OQ-9 stays open; the driver does not.** The row itself had already named this as the safe first move — "useful whichever way OQ-9 goes and fabricates nothing" — and the owner confirmed it rather than my inferring it from a sentence that also said "when it is unblocked". D-63's no-simulator rule is untouched, because nothing here simulates a third party: every figure on the sheet is a fact this system already holds about its own facility.
- **The selection rule is the item, not the download.** A lot is exportable only if it is `scheduled`, carries a sale date, **and still passes live `auctionReadiness`** — the same function the case screen refuses on. `status` is not the test and cannot be: a sale is scheduled once and then sits for weeks, and the tenant paying, an SCRA or bankruptcy hold landing, or a titled vehicle being recorded all leave `status` at `scheduled` while making the advertisement wrong. The database test for this pays the lien off and asserts the lot drops off the sheet **with the case row unedited** — status still `scheduled` — which is the property no amount of filtering on status could give.
- **Every dropped case is named, with its blockers.** A short CSV nobody realises is short is the failure mode; "three of your five scheduled sales are not on this sheet, and here is why" is the screen. Sold and cancelled cases are silently omitted rather than refused, because nobody is about to advertise them and a refusal line for each would be noise on a list whose whole value is being read to the end.
- **Terms of sale are a facility column with its control in the same item**, per this repo's rule, and it is its **own form** rather than a field on the timeline. Saving the timeline mints a version every governed lease stays pinned to (US-29); editing a comma in the terms of sale must not bump the version each open case's approval screen cites. Terms are current policy, a timeline version is evidence. Null stays a real state — blank column, and the auctions screen says the terms are not set — which is D-63's honest-degradation posture rather than a plausible default becoming a term nobody chose.
- **`facility:settings` was added to one test actor, not to the shared `ALL` list.** That list is used by every actor in `auctions-db.test.ts`, and widening it would quietly weaken whatever refusals the other 40 tests rely on.

**Accessibility.** Everything here is behind `auctions:approve` or `facility:settings`, so nothing a customer touches changed and the public statement gains no claim — the same reasoning as B-197, recorded on the page rather than left implicit. Both screens are already in `ADMIN_SCAN_ROUTES`, so the new markup is axe-scanned and — since B-201 — measured at 320px, at 200% zoom and under forced text spacing. The refusal list is a list of links with the reason as text beside each, so nothing is carried by colour or position.

**Test verification.** Typecheck clean including `tsconfig.tests.json`. Lint clean (7 pre-existing warnings, none in these files). Full unit suite **3,886 passed, 8 skipped of 3,894**, exit 0 — 11 new, eight on `selectListableLots` and three against real rows. `prisma migrate diff --exit-code`: **no difference**; the migration is applied to `storage_test` and to `public` (`db:migrate:test`, `db:migrate:e2e`). Full e2e sweep **1,295 passed, 9 skipped of 1,304**, exit 0, on both projects.

**And an honest note about how that number was reached, because two sweeps before it were red.** Three consecutive full sweeps failed on `mobile-chrome` — two, then twelve tests — on pages this row does not touch, so the work was stashed and the sweep re-run against committed `main`. **The baseline was worse than the working tree**: twelve failures, with individual axe scans recorded at 16.2 and 10.2 minutes and a 32-minute total against a normal 4–9. `uptime` gave load averages of **11 / 45 / 53**. It was the machine, and it was self-inflicted — four full sweeps back to back, each five workers of Chromium against a production server. Waiting for load to fall below 4 and re-running gave 4.2 minutes and a clean pass. **The rule this re-proves is one this repo already wrote down and I did not follow: a wall of failures at implausible durations is an environment symptom, and `uptime`/`lsof` come before the stack trace.** Reading those twelve as twelve bugs would have cost an afternoon.

**Left behind.** **Photographs are not on the sheet, and this is a real gap rather than an oversight.** `recordLockCut` requires a photograph reference on every inventory line, but those references live inside the hashed evidence `Document` it renders — there is no structured per-lot image store, and no `storageRef` on that document. Re-keying them into a CSV would put a second copy of primary evidence beside the hashed original that can disagree with it. Closing this properly means either structured inventory rows or per-lot uploads, and it belongs to a row that asks for one. **The marketplace driver is still blocked** on OQ-9 and a partner agreement, unchanged. **A per-case terms override does not exist** — terms are facility policy, and no acceptance criterion asks for a sale to differ.

## B-218 — `gh pr ready` now runs the e2e lane, which it never has

`6371f1f`

*(Recorded as `94d49de` when built. That commit, and B-202's, were squash-merged into `6371f1f` via PR #17 — the squash collapsed five commits and orphaned every SHA on the branch, which is the same defect the "record the SHA in a follow-up commit, never by amending" rule exists to prevent. Merge with `--rebase`, not `--squash`.)*

**What it built.** One line in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`: `types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, ready_for_review]` on the `pull_request` trigger.

**The bug it fixes, which was in the gate rather than in the code the gate guards.** `on: pull_request` with no `types:` defaults to `opened, synchronize, reopened`. `ready_for_review` is not one of them, so `gh pr ready` fired no workflow event at all — and the `e2e` job, guarded by `github.event.pull_request.draft == false`, kept the `skipping` conclusion it had earned on the last push, back when the PR still *was* a draft. Found by doing exactly what the repo's own "Pull requests" section says to do: marking B-206's PR ready and expecting the heavy lane to run. It did not, and `gh run list --branch` showed no run after the toggle. All sixteen open PRs report `e2e=skipping`.

**What it decided.**

- **`gh run rerun` is not a workaround and must not be offered as one.** A re-run replays the original event payload, in which `draft` is still `true`, so the guard skips the job again. The only things that have ever run e2e on this repo are a merge to `main` and a push while the PR was already non-draft — the first of which is *after* the moment the gate exists to guard.
- **The trigger is fixed rather than the job's `if`.** Loosening the guard to run e2e on drafts would restore the ~30 minutes of Actions time per draft push that splitting the lanes was built to stop spending. The defect is that the ready signal never arrived, not that the condition is wrong.
- **`paths-ignore` is untouched.** Adding `types` alongside it is additive; both filters still apply, so a docs-only push still skips both lanes.

**What it left behind.** **The sixteen PRs already open do not heal retroactively.** For a `pull_request` event GitHub reads the workflow from the PR's merge ref, so each of them picks the fix up on its *next* event — one more draft→ready toggle, or any push. Nothing re-runs on its own. **No test covers this**, and none reasonably can from inside the repo: the failure is in GitHub's event routing, and the check that would have caught it is reading the `types` default in the Actions documentation. The comment above the line is the guard against someone deleting it as noise.

## B-202 — a payment plan now blocks the auction it always should have

`6371f1f`

*(Recorded as `b06b9b5` when built; squash-merged into `6371f1f` via PR #17 — see the note on B-218.)*

**What it built.** One array element: `block_auction` added to the `payment_plan` entry in `packages/core/holds/catalog.ts`. Plus the two operator-facing refusal sentences that enumerate which holds stop a sale — `auctionReadiness`'s `on_hold` blocker and `approveAuction`'s refusal in `apps/web/lib/auctions/service.ts` — which now name payment-plan holds alongside SCRA, bankruptcy, deceased and litigation.

**The bug.** `createPaymentPlan` places a `payment_plan` hold, and that hold carried `halt_dunning`, `halt_late_fees` and `halt_access_suspension` but not `block_auction`. So `blockedByHold` stayed false, `auctionReadiness` returned ready, and `selectListableLots` passed the lot straight onto the sheet. The scenario is selling the goods of a tenant holding a payment agreement this system generated and emailed him, with our own email as the exhibit. B-129's lot sheet made it worse rather than inheriting it: D-104's argument for computing the refusal at export time is precisely that a tenant paying, an SCRA hold landing or a titled vehicle being recorded all leave `status` at `scheduled` while making the advertisement wrong — and a payment plan is that same class of event, the commonest one at the counter, and was the one missing from the list.

**What it decided.**

- **Block, do not cancel.** Whether agreeing a plan on a `scheduled` case should also *cancel* that case is an owner decision and is deliberately still open; it needs its own D-number. Blocking is the safe default and is reversible — a broken plan lifts the hold (`payment-plan-breach.ts`) and the case becomes sellable again on its own, which is the correct behaviour and needed no code.
- **The refusal messages were changed, not just the effect.** They enumerate hold types by name, so an operator refused because of a payment plan would have read a list that did not include payment plans and concluded the refusal was a bug. A block whose stated reason omits the reason it fired invites the workaround the block exists to prevent.
- **One element, no new code path.** Every consumer — `auctionReadiness`, `approveAuction`, `scheduleSale`, the lot sheet, the refusal list, the tenant-profile hold banner — asks the catalog for the effect rather than switching on the type, so all of them picked it up unchanged. This is what US-42's configuration-not-code rule was built for and the first time it has paid out on a bug rather than on a new hold type.

**What it left behind.** **No new test file.** The catalog test that asserted the old behaviour (`hasEffect(payment_plan, 'block_auction')` → `false`) now uses `dispute` for its negative case, and `payment_plan` joined the loop asserting `block_auction` on every type where a sale is unrecoverable — with a comment saying it is there for a different reason than the federal ones. Every layer below the catalog is already generic over the effect and already tested that way, so a per-layer suite would test the catalog three more times. **The cancel-versus-block question is open**, as above.

**An environment note, because the first full sweep was red and none of it was this change.** 18 failures across 8 `*-db` files, 30 occurrences of `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already` in the log, and the three `AssertionError`s downstream of it (a fixture facility that never got created surfacing as `unknown_facility`). Local Postgres is `max_connections=100`; vitest's default worker fan-out times Prisma's per-worker pool exceeds it. Re-running the same 8 files with `--no-file-parallelism` gave 159 passed in 35 seconds. Nothing in the failure set touches holds or auctions. **This is the repo's own rule firing again** — a wall of failures is an environment symptom, and the connection count comes before the stack trace.

## B-203 — a manual payment reaches the plan, not this month's tax

`921822f`

*(The record commit — this entry, the ✅, D-105 and the accessibility re-read — is `302c4a3`. Rebase-merged via PR #4, so both SHAs are the ones that ran and both are reachable from `main`. The branch's third commit was the empty placeholder the draft PR was opened on; the rebase dropped it, which is correct and is why this item shows two commits rather than three.)*

**What it built.** One deferral inside `applyPayment` (`apps/web/lib/billing/allocation.ts`), plus the `coveredByPlan` lookup it needs. A payment that names no invoice and narrows to none — the counter, the portal, a pay link, a re-application after a reversal — now ranks an active plan's frozen `invoiceIds` ahead of every other invoice on the **same lease**, and lets whatever is left over fall through to the rest in the facility's ordinary order. Two database tests in `tests/payment-plan-autopay-db.test.ts`.

**The bug.** Plan progress is measured against the frozen `invoiceIds`, but only autopay's installment charge ever carried `restrictToInvoiceIds` — `settlePayment` passes it only when Stripe metadata names a `paymentPlanId`, which only `collectInstallments` sets. Everything else allocated by the ordinary order, tax first, and **every open invoice's tax share outranks every arrears rent share**. So a tenant on a plan who handed over the exact installment at the counter had this month's tax and protection taken out of it first; `installmentViews` reads partial coverage as uncovered; and three days later the breach job ended the plan, lifted the hold, restarted the ladder and re-armed gate suspension. The tenant had paid, on time, exactly the figure we asked for. Reproduced before the fix: the counter test asserts $300.00 onto the plan and got **$286.00**, the missing $14.00 being September's tax.

**What it decided.**

- **D-105: deferred, not restricted.** `restrictToInvoiceIds` already exists and was the obvious reach, and it is wrong here. Autopay is charging a figure *we* raised — the installment, to the cent. A counter payment is whatever the tenant chose to hand over, so a hard restrict would strand the excess as unapplied credit: a $500 payment against $300 of arrears leaves $200 nowhere, which is a second surprise on top of the one being fixed. Deferring gets both amounts right with one rule, and the second test pins it — it passes with the old code too, on purpose, because its job is to refuse a later session's "simplification" to a restrict.
- **The deferral is scoped to the plan's own lease.** A tenant can hold two leases at one facility, one on a plan and one not. `claimsFor` allocates across everything that tenant owes, so a flat covered-set would drag money handed over for the second lease onto the first's arrears. `coveredByPlan` is keyed by lease for that reason.
- **Fixed once, in the shared function.** `applyPayment` is the single funnel — `pos.ts`, `reconcile.ts` and `reversals.ts` all route through it — so the counter, the portal, pay links and post-reversal re-application were one edit, not four. Guarding only the path the row named would have left the siblings broken.
- **`explicitInvoiceId` still outranks everything**, unchanged: a charge raised for one invoice must settle that invoice (B-045). The deferral runs before that block and is overridden by it.
- **The new tests create their own tenant.** Every lease in that file hangs off one shared tenant nothing cleans up, and these are the first tests in it that allocate *without* naming or narrowing invoices — so they would have landed their money on an earlier test's open invoice. That is the shared-state trap this repo already has written down, not a defect in the code under test, and `newLeaseUnderOwnTenant` is the fix. The `invoice` helper also takes real line-item categories now: the allocation order ranks by category first, so an invoice with no line items behaves as pure rent and cannot show what tax-before-rent does to a plan.

**Accessibility.** Re-read `apps/web/app/(public)/accessibility/page.tsx` and recorded the read there. **No sentence changes, and the reason is not the usual one** — this row *is* customer-facing, a tenant paying in the portal reaches it every time. It is that what changed is where the cents land, not a pixel of markup: no route, no state, no control, no message, no colour. `/portal/pay` was already scanned. `LAST_REVIEWED` does not move.

**Test verification.** Typecheck clean including `tsconfig.tests.json`. Lint clean, exit 0. Full unit suite **3,888 passed, 8 skipped of 3,896**, exit 0 — the two new tests are the whole delta from B-129's 3,886/8 of 3,894. `prisma migrate diff --from-migrations --to-schema-datamodel`: **no difference**; no migration in this row.

**One local-environment note, recorded because it looks like drift and is not.** The CI-form drift check (`--from-schema-datasource`) reports `[-] Removed column auctionSaleTime` on `facility` against this laptop's dev database. The string appears **nowhere in the repo** — not in a migration, not in `schema.prisma`, not in any source file — so it is a leftover in local `public` from an experiment, and the migrations-versus-model diff CI actually runs is clean. Worth knowing before someone writes a migration to "fix" it.

**Left behind.** **The cross-lease case is deliberate and is not a gap being deferred**: a tenant with two leases has only the plan's lease reordered, and money is not steered between leases. **The POS override is not built** — whether a staffer may deliberately send a counter payment to current rent instead of the plan is D-105's open half, and the row's own answer stands: a second control on the POS screen, not the default. No acceptance criterion asks for one yet. **`coveredByPlan` costs one extra indexed query on every un-narrowed payment**, and it exists only because `AllocationTarget` carries no `leaseId`; adding one to the core type would remove the query and is not worth the ripple for a payment path that runs at counter speed.

## B-205 — The lot sheet carries what a lien advertisement has to carry

`18f4b34`, `88cbe59`, `db9432e`

**What it built.** Four defects on one document — `/admin/auctions/lots.csv`, the only file this product generates *for publication*.

1. **The three required elements are on the sheet.** A Texas lien advertisement has to name the person on whose account the sale is held, the time and place of the sale, and a general description of the goods. The sheet carried the place (the address) and nothing else. It now carries **Tenant**, **Sale time** and **Description of goods**. `Facility.auctionSaleTime` is free text with its control on `/admin/settings/delinquency` beside the terms; `AuctionCase.goodsDescription` is per lot with its control on the case screen, above the advertising log because it has to be written *before* a run is placed.
2. **The generated `Lot` column is gone.** It was `index + 1` over whatever passed readiness at that moment, and readiness is deliberately live — so "Lot 3" named a different unit on Wednesday than it had on Monday, on a document whose entire purpose is to be the public advertisement.
3. **A lot the size lookup cannot resolve is named.** It was a `flatMap ... return []` and appeared in neither `lots` nor `refused`, breaking the rule D-104 made load-bearing.
4. **The file is `auction-lots-<slug>-<sale date>.csv`**, the terms field has a worked example, and both time and terms are echoed on `/admin/auctions` beside the download link.

**What it decided.**

- **D-106: the refusal list is about whether the SALE may be advertised at all — a missing advertisement element is a blank column and a gap named on screen, never a dropped lot.** Refusing a lot with no goods description would push it off the sheet on the day it most needs to be on one, and an operator who cannot advertise at all is worse off than one told which sentence to write. So the gaps are named where the operator is standing: the facility-wide ones (time, terms) as one note linking to delinquency settings, the per-lot one as a note naming each unit with a link to the case that fixes it. `no_unit_type` is the one genuine addition to the refusal list, and it belongs there for the opposite reason — it is a lot the sheet cannot *describe*, not a sale whose copy is unwritten.
- **The goods description is not the itemised inventory and does not reopen D-104's photograph reasoning.** That reasoning refused re-keying hashed primary evidence into a CSV where a second copy could disagree with the original. This is a different field with a different job: a phrase written for a newspaper days *before* the lock is cut, at a point when no inventory exists to copy from. The two never overlap. **An earlier pass on this row got this wrong** — it deferred the field and shipped a screen note saying "this system does not hold" a description, justified by D-104. The backlog row had already ruled that out in as many words, and the note was a false statement about the product as soon as the field was cheap to add.
- **`auctionSaleTime` is free text, not a time control.** "10:00 AM, or immediately following the preceding sale" is a real and common phrasing that no time picker holds, and the value is read down a phone to a classifieds clerk.
- **`setGoodsDescription` is gated on `tenants:edit`, not `auctions:approve`.** This is ad copy a manager drafts, not a decision to sell somebody's property; gating it behind the approval permission would mean the one person who has walked past the unit cannot describe what is in it. Audited like the vehicle flag, because "what did the advertisement say the goods were" is a question a wrongful-sale complaint asks.
- **Facility-level time, per-case description.** Every lot in one auction is sold at one sitting, so the time is facility policy the way the terms are. What is in each unit is not.
- **The sale-date filename is the earliest sale on the sheet, not today.** Two downloads for the same sale are the same document and should be named as one.

**Accessibility.** Everything here is behind `auctions:approve`, `tenants:edit` or `facility:settings` — nothing a customer touches changed, so `apps/web/app/(public)/accessibility/page.tsx` gains no claim and `LAST_REVIEWED` does not move. It was re-read anyway and no existing sentence went stale. Both screens are already in `ADMIN_SCAN_ROUTES`, so the new markup is axe-scanned and — since B-201 — measured at 320px, at 200% zoom and under forced text spacing. The per-lot gap note is a sentence with links in it, so nothing is carried by colour or position. **Note for B-215**: that row observes `/admin/auctions`'s populated lot-sheet branch has been rendered by no scan because the demo seed schedules no sale, and this item does not change that — the new note is inside the same unscanned branch.

**Test verification.** Typecheck clean including `tsconfig.tests.json`. Lint clean (7 pre-existing warnings, none in these files). Full unit suite **3,890 passed, 8 skipped of 3,898**, exit 0 — run twice against the same un-reseeded database with identical totals, per this repo's repeatability rule. `prisma migrate diff --exit-code`: **no difference**; both migrations are applied to `storage_test` and to `public` (`db:migrate:test`, `db:migrate:e2e`). `e2e/admin-auctions.spec.ts` **8 passed**, exit 0, with the `[e2e setup]` line present — the full sweep is left to CI's heavy lane.

**Found along the way.** The local `storage_test` database held a column from an abandoned earlier attempt at this row — a migration applied locally and never committed — which made the branch's own migration fail to apply with "column already exists". `npm run db:reset-test` is the documented remedy and it was the right one. Worth recording because the symptom (P3009, a failed migration naming a file that is not in git) reads like a corrupt migration history rather than like local drift from a branch somebody abandoned.

**Left behind.** **Photographs are still not on the sheet**, unchanged from B-129 and for the same reason; the general description does not close that gap and is not meant to. **No per-case time override** — a lot sold at a different sitting from its facility's other lots is not expressible, and no acceptance criterion asks for one. **No sequential lot number**: assigning one properly means storing it on the case at scheduling time and deciding what happens when a lot drops out between the assignment and the sale, which is a decision rather than a default and belongs to a row that asks for it. **B-129 stays open** — the marketplace driver is still blocked on OQ-9 and a partner agreement.

## B-204 — An installment charge honours `halt_autopay`

`3d6b6c4` (`--rebase` merge of PR #19 rewrote the commit; it was `40ee469` on the branch)

**What it built.** `collectInstallments` (`apps/web/lib/billing/autopay.ts`) consulted no hold at all. `runAutopay`'s invoice loop has honoured `halt_autopay` since US-42; the installment half, added by B-189 in the same file, had only three guards — `plan.autoCollect`, `lease.autopayEnabled` and a saved card. `military_scra`, `bankruptcy` and `deceased` all declare `halt_autopay` (`packages/core/holds/catalog.ts`), so a bankruptcy hold placed on the 10th did not stop the 3am charge on the 15th. That is a stay violation committed by the system *after* somebody correctly told it not to, and it is a charge against a real person's card.

The fix is the one the row prescribed: `activePlansFor` now runs before the hold read, both lease populations go into one `effectsByLease` call, and `collectInstallments` takes the resulting set and skips those leases.

**What it decided.**

- **The hold set is read over BOTH populations, and that is the load-bearing half of the fix.** An installment is charged off the PLAN, not off an invoice. A plan lease whose arrears are entirely frozen has nothing in `runAutopay`'s invoice query — nor does one whose tenant has moved out still owing the debt the plan covers, because that query scopes to `OCCUPYING_LEASE_STATUSES`. A set built from the invoice list alone therefore misses exactly the leases `collectInstallments` is about to charge. Passing the existing set through unchanged would have looked like the fix and closed only the easy half.
- **One `effectsByLease` call for both halves, not two.** The same reason `activePlansFor` is read once and shared: two reads are one reordering away from disagreeing about which leases are held, on the question of whether to take money from a bankrupt.
- **The hold check is the first test in the installment loop, ahead of the three manual-pay ones, and it records a skip rather than `continue`ing silently.** A stay, an SCRA protection or a death is not a billing preference, and a plan agreed before the hold landed does not survive it. The three manual-pay reasons pass silently because none of them is an event; this one is, so the run names the lease it stood down on and the message is the same `lease_on_hold` string the invoice loop already uses.
- **No change to the `payment_plan` hold itself.** B-189's reasoning stands: `payment_plan` deliberately does not declare `halt_autopay`, because that effect is all-or-nothing per lease and would turn forbearance on arrears into a rent holiday. This item is about the *other* holds.

**Accessibility.** Nothing a customer touches changed — no route, no markup, no message. `apps/web/app/(public)/accessibility/page.tsx` was re-read per the standing obligation; no sentence went stale in either direction and `LAST_REVIEWED` does not move.

**Test verification.** Two new tests in `tests/payment-plan-autopay-db.test.ts`: a bankruptcy stay stops the installment and the run says so, and a `deceased` hold on a plan lease with **no invoice in tonight's run** (tenant moved out; lease `ended`) is still honoured — the second is the one that fails on a fix that only passes the old set through. **Both were confirmed to fail against `main`'s `autopay.ts` and pass with the change**, rather than being assumed to cover it. Typecheck clean including `tsconfig.tests.json`. Lint exit 0 (7 pre-existing warnings, none in these files). Full unit suite **3,894 passed, 8 skipped of 3,902**, exit 0 — the two new tests are the whole delta from **3,892 passed, 8 skipped of 3,900 measured on `main`** immediately before this change. (B-205's entry above records 3,890/3,898; `main` measures two more, so that figure was written before the last of that row's own tests landed. Noted rather than corrected, since the entry's other numbers stand.) `prisma migrate diff --from-migrations --to-schema-datamodel`: **no difference**; no migration in this row.

**Left behind.** **The sibling defect the row names is B-208, not this one**: `halt_late_fees` and `halt_dunning` are still evaluated per lease rather than per invoice, so a plan still halts the fee ladder on rent it never deferred. That is a separate row with an owner number to settle first. **No backfill of charges already taken** — if a charge was collected under a stay before today, unwinding it is a refund decision a person makes, and nothing here looks for one.

## B-206 — The plan tells the tenant when it ends, and which payment ended it

`48aca48` (the `--rebase` merge of PR #6 rewrote the commit; it was `5d507b3` on the branch)

**What it built.** Two gaps on the same feature, both about a tenant learning that a payment plan is over.

1. **A staff-cancelled plan now says so.** `cancelPaymentPlan` contained no `emitEvent` at all, and there was no `payment_plan_cancelled` template. A regional cancelled a plan on Monday; late fees restarted, the dunning ladder resumed and gate suspension re-armed, and the tenant — holding B-191's email saying we hold off on exactly those three things for as long as they keep to the dates, which they had — found out at the keypad. `payment_plan.cancelled` is the fifth event, with a fifth transactional template carrying the staffer's own words.
2. **The break notice names the payment.** `payment_plan_broken` stated no date and no amount, so a tenant who believed they had paid had nothing to check against, and it carried `links.pay_now` but not `links.plan` — the one message announcing the break could not reach the schedule B-193 built for that moment. It now carries `plan.missed_amount`, `plan.missed_due_date` and `links.plan`, all four required.

**What it decided.**

- **The missed installment comes from the break DECISION, not from a second derivation at send time.** `isBroken` became `brokenOn` and returns the installment it broke on rather than a boolean, and that id rides on the event. The alternative — a `firstMissedInstallment` helper the send path or the emitter calls independently — was written first and replaced, because it re-runs the grace window and the retry ladder to answer a question that was already answered a line earlier, and two computations of "which payment ended this plan" are one reordering away from disagreeing in a message to the person whose money it is. It also cannot return null when a break has actually happened, so the event can never carry `installmentId: null`.
- **`payment_plan.cancelled` is emitted inside the same transaction as the status change.** The hold lift stays outside it, because `liftHold` writes its own audit entry and takes no `tx`. That asymmetry is deliberate and the failure modes are not equivalent: a lifted hold with the plan still `active` is the pre-existing window and is self-healing, since the nightly job re-evaluates; a cancelled plan with no event is silent forever.
- **The cancel reason is read from the plan row at send time, not carried on the event** — the same reason `plan.balance` is. The row is what the audit log and the staff screen show, and a message quoting something different from both is worse than no message.
- **`plan.cancel_reason` is the only staff free-text merge field in the product**, and that changes what the form is. The hint said the reason goes "to the audit log with your name", which was true until it started being emailed; a staffer typing internal shorthand into a field they believe only colleagues read is the whole hazard, so the hint now names the tenant first.
- **Transactional, like `broken`.** It is the end of a financial agreement and the moment three collections mechanisms restart, not a preference a tenant can switch off.
- **The message says "No payment was missed" in as many words** — the difference between a tenant who rings the office and one who believes they broke the agreement.

**Accessibility.** Nothing a customer touches on the site changed — no route, no markup, no control; the one screen edit is the staff cancel form's hint, behind `tenants:edit`. The new email inherits PRD 05 FR-9a through the single `renderEmail` path D-102 left in place, so it gains no markup of its own. `apps/web/app/(public)/accessibility/page.tsx` was re-read per the standing obligation: its claims are about pages, screens and named states on the site and say nothing about outbound email, so this item adds no claim and made no sentence stale in either direction. `LAST_REVIEWED` does not move.

**Test verification.** Typecheck clean including `tsconfig.tests.json`. Lint exit 0 (7 pre-existing warnings, none in these files). `prisma migrate diff --from-migrations --to-schema-datamodel`: **no difference**; no migration in this row. Full unit suite **3,896 passed, 8 skipped of 3,904**, exit 0, run twice against the same un-reseeded database with identical totals per this repo's repeatability rule. The delta from **main's 3,894 passed, 8 skipped of 3,902** is two tests, and only one of them was written here: the new cancellation test, plus one more case in `tests/merge-fields.test.ts`, whose `it.each` runs once per entry in `COMMS_TEMPLATES` and therefore checks the fifth template's required fields against the event catalog without being asked to. Four tests in `tests/payment-plan-comms-db.test.ts` were confirmed to fail with this branch's source reverted and pass with it — the catalog wiring for the fifth event, both break-notice assertions, and the new cancellation message — rather than being assumed to cover it.

**One local-environment note, recorded because it looks like a regression and is not.** The comms catalog is **seeded state**, not read from the constant at send time: `packages/db/prisma/seed.mts` writes `COMMS_TEMPLATES` into the schema, and `npm test` never reseeds. So a working copy whose code is on `main` while the test database still holds this branch's catalog fails both `plan broken` tests — main's `service.ts` cannot supply the merge fields the seeded template now requires, the render guard refuses, and the assertion reads `expected [] to have a length of 1`, which looks exactly like a broken sender. It is neither the sender nor the tests: it is a stale seed. Measuring main's true baseline needs `npm run db:migrate:test` first, and so does switching away from this branch. The same trap will bite any row that edits a template.

**Found along the way — a real bug, and it is not this row's.** `tests/documents-db.test.ts`'s "keeps every document for a subject, newest first" fails **roughly two runs in three on `main`**, measured 2-of-3 both with this branch's changes and with them stashed, so it is neither new nor caused here. The cause is not the test: `documentsFor` sorts on `createdAt` alone and Prisma generates `@default(now())` **client-side at millisecond precision**, so two documents written back to back share an instant and the sort is a coin flip. Left unfixed it would have made this item's own pull request red about two runs in three on an unrelated assertion, so the test was corrected here — it stamps its two rows an hour apart and asserts the ordering `documentsFor` genuinely offers. **The promise itself is still unkept and is raised as B-219**, which also names the real fix (let Postgres generate the timestamp; a `cuid()` tie-break is not it) and the other `@default(now())` models to check. It is a row rather than a defect only because `documentsFor` has no production caller today — it becomes real the moment a lease's document list is rendered, where the order of lien notices is evidence rather than presentation.

**Also found.** PR #6 already carried an earlier attempt at this row, and it **emitted `payment_plan.cancelled` without adding it to the comms consumer in `apps/web/lib/jobs/registry.ts`** — the event would have been written and never delivered, which is the original defect with an extra row in `domain_event` to prove it. Worth recording because the send path is otherwise entirely catalog-driven, so a new event looks complete once its template and rule exist, and nothing fails loudly when the consumer list is the thing that is short.

**Left behind.** **A `payment_plan.broken` event emitted before this deploys carries no `installmentId`**, so during the window between emit and processing it renders as a `Message` row with `status: 'failed'` and the error rather than as a break notice. That is the existing `installment_due_soon` behaviour and FR-9's stated design — a missing merge field blocks the send loudly — but it is a real, if narrow, window in which the most important message in the feature does not arrive, and nothing here retries it. **No backfill**: plans cancelled before today are not told retrospectively, which is a judgement about contacting people about a decision weeks old rather than a gap. **The cross-lease case is untouched**, as B-203 left it.

## B-207 — The chased/halted split reaches the roll-up, the emailed report and the month-end close

`e65e314`

**What it built.** B-195 built `arAgingSplit` — every AR bucket read twice, as money the delinquency ladder is still working and money behind a hold that stopped it — and exactly one screen called it. The four surfaces that actually get forwarded to an owner still reported one undifferentiated figure, because all four read `agingForFacility` and it returned a plain `ArAging`.

1. **`agingForFacility` computes the split**, in one added `effectsByLease(leaseIds, 'halt_dunning', asOf)` alongside the balance query it already ran. Its `aging` is now `split.total`, so the AR table on `/admin/reports`, the dashboard's Money owed tile, the scheduled delinquency email and the accounting close pack all gained the split without any of them asking for it. `delinquencyReport` gained `totalSplit` beside its existing `total`.
2. **The two aging tables are one component.** `ArAgingSplitTable` (`apps/web/components/admin/ar-aging-split-table.tsx`) is rendered by `/admin/reports` and `/admin/reports/delinquency`, replacing two hand-written tables and two copies of the bucket-label map.
3. **The dashboard tile says how much of the money nobody is chasing** — `$X over 30 days · $Y halted`, and the halted clause is omitted when it is zero rather than printed as `$0.00`.
4. **The scheduled delinquency email** is a four-column table (Age, Being chased, Halted, Total) with a sentence saying what halted means, rather than one Amount column.
5. **The close pack freezes the split.** `PointInTimeFigures.arHalted` is written at close and rendered three-column; a month filed before today has no split and the pack says so in a sentence instead.
6. **The delinquency page stopped contradicting itself.** It claimed chased and halted "are never shown added together" and its `<tfoot>` showed exactly that. Each facility now gets a total row on the same footing as the portfolio footer, and the paragraph says what the split is for.
7. **The plans-holds CSV button is named for what it exports** — "Download the halted list (CSV)" — with a line saying it answers for now and that the month picker does not change it. Both were already true and deliberate; neither was on the screen.

**What it decided.**

- **The split is computed in `agingForFacility`, not by each of the four callers.** That is the whole shape of the fix and the reason it is small: B-195's defect was not that the arithmetic was missing, it was that the arithmetic lived one layer above the function every consumer actually calls. Four callers each doing their own hold lookup is four chances to disagree about which holds stop the ladder, on the question of whether anyone is chasing a bankrupt.
- **`halt_dunning` from the catalog, never a list of hold types.** The same reasoning `delinquencyDetail` records: a `do_not_contact` hold stops the sending and a `dispute` stops the fees, and both are still an account nobody is chasing; what would be wrong is counting a hold whose effects leave the ladder running. US-42's rule — "a new hold type is a configuration row, not six code changes" — is what makes that safe.
- **`arHalted` is optional on the close snapshot and `CLOSE_SNAPSHOT_VERSION` is NOT bumped.** This looks like the case the version exists for and is not. The version gates the JOURNAL export, which refuses any snapshot below the current one — and the journal reads no point-in-time figure at all (drift is computed over the period-derived half, and `accounting-close.test.ts` asserts AR is not in it). Bumping would have refused the journal export of every already-filed month over a field the journal never touches. So an old snapshot simply has no split, and the pack says which it is rather than reporting a zero halted figure, which would read as "all of it was being chased" — a claim that month never made.
- **Chased is derived, not stored twice.** The snapshot keeps the total and the halted half; the pack subtracts. Two stored figures that must sum to a third is a reconciliation waiting to fail, and the total is the one that ties out against the ledger.
- **On the tfoot contradiction, the TOTAL stayed and the sentence changed.** The row said "pick one". The total is the figure an accountant reconciles against the ledger, and deleting it to satisfy a sentence would have made the screen worse for the reader who needs it most. What was actually wrong was a promise the page had no reason to make.
- **The CSV was renamed rather than the missing effectiveness export built.** The row offered either; the export is a second table with different columns answering for a different period, which is why the route declined to carry it in the first place. Renaming closes the gap between what the button says and what it does, which is the whole defect a reader hits.
- **`scope="rowgroup"` was moved unchanged.** B-216 has established no screen reader implements it, and that row owns the remedy; fixing it here would leave the two screens disagreeing until B-216 lands. Named in the accessibility statement's log so B-216 is read as covering the shared component.

**Accessibility.** Nothing a customer touches — every surface is behind `reports:financial`. `apps/web/app/(public)/accessibility/page.tsx` was re-read per the standing obligation and a note appended: no route added, no claim moved in either direction, `LAST_REVIEWED` does not move. The note records the two things the shared component changes for future rows — a fix or a defect in it now lands on two screens at once, and it carries B-216's `scope="rowgroup"` with it.

**Test verification.** Six new tests. Four in `tests/reports-financial-db.test.ts` place a `bankruptcy` hold on the fixture's ended lease and assert: the halted balance lands in `halted` and the rest in `chased`; `aging` equals the two halves **bucket by bucket**, not merely on the total, because a mis-bucketed halted dollar would cancel out in a sum; the hold is read as of the date given rather than the wall clock (a February balance is not halted by a hold placed in August); and `delinquencyReport.totalSplit` ties out against `total` and against the per-facility rows. Two in `tests/management-pack.test.ts` cover the three-column pack and the pre-split month. `e2e/admin.spec.ts`'s tile-agrees-with-report assertion was updated for the third row and now asserts the arithmetic (chased + halted = total = tile) rather than summing the group. Typecheck clean including `tsconfig.tests.json`. Lint exit 0 (7 pre-existing warnings, none in these files). `prisma migrate diff --from-schema-datasource --to-schema-datamodel`: **no difference**; no migration in this row. Full unit suite **3,902 passed, 8 skipped of 3,910**, exit 0, run twice against the same un-reseeded database with identical totals. `main` measured immediately before, with these changes stashed: **3,895 passed, 1 failed, 8 skipped of 3,904** — the delta is the six new tests plus the pre-existing failure described below. Full `e2e/admin.spec.ts`: **520 passed**, exit 0.

**Found along the way — a real bug, and it is not this row's.** `tests/delinquency-engine-db.test.ts`'s "resumes at the next step once the grace window is over" fails on `main`, confirmed with these changes stashed. It is not the engine: `reversalGracedLeases` measures the 10-day window from the reversal ledger entry's `occurredAt`, `returnPayment` stamps that with the real wall clock, and the test then runs the timeline at a fixed `2026-09-10`. **The suite was therefore comparing a fixture date against today, and 2026-08-31 is the first day the gap fell under ten days.** The two tests either side of it were passing for the wrong reason — one of them because the bounce was dated five days *after* the business date it was asserted against, so the lease was graced by arithmetic that could not have been intended. Fixed here rather than recorded and left, because it is two lines and it would otherwise have made this row's pull request red about something it did not touch: the helper now pins the reversal to `2026-08-24`, the date the comments have always claimed — two days before the grace-window assertion, seventeen before the resume. This is the same trap the CLAUDE.md rule about marketing quiet hours names, in a place that rule does not reach.

**Also found — a local environment defect, recorded because it reads as a broken app.** `storage_test`'s `public` schema (the one Playwright, `e2e/global-setup.ts` and the app under test all read) held 94 tables, **zero rows and no `_prisma_migrations` table**, so `npm run db:migrate:e2e` refused with `P3005 The database schema is not empty` and every e2e run died in `auth.setup.ts` with `CredentialsSignin` — which looks exactly like broken authentication. Something had built that schema without recording the migrations. `DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE; CREATE SCHEMA public;` followed by `db:migrate:e2e` fixed it in one step; no extension lived in `public` and the `storage_test` SCHEMA the unit suite uses was untouched. Worth writing down because CLAUDE.md warns about *skipping* `db:migrate:e2e` and not about the state where running it is refused.

**Left behind.** **B-208 is untouched and is the sibling defect** — `halt_late_fees` and `halt_dunning` are still evaluated per lease rather than per invoice, so a plan still halts the ladder on rent it never deferred. That row is blocked on an owner number, not on code, and nothing here changes what "halted" means; it only makes the amount visible. **The plan-effectiveness CSV export is still unbuilt** and is now disclosed rather than raised: the halted list is what the button exports and the screen says so. **Months closed before today carry no split**, and there is no backfill — the figure could only have been observed on the day, which is the whole reason the close exists. **`moneyOwedRollup`'s per-facility summary string is still one figure**; the split reaches the tile's hint and the tables, not the facility-switcher roll-up, where a second dollar amount in a one-line summary would cost more than it tells.

## B-208 — A payment plan stops covering for rent it never deferred

`e4276e6`

**What it built.** `halt_late_fees` and `halt_dunning` are evaluated per LEASE, not per invoice (`apps/web/lib/billing/late-fees.ts:88`, `packages/core/delinquency/engine.ts:63`), so a payment plan's hold stood every collections mechanism down on the whole lease — including rent charged after the plan was agreed, which the plan never promised anything about. B-189 narrowed **autopay** to the plan's frozen `invoiceIds` so a card keeps paying current rent; nothing did the equivalent for the fee ladder or the timeline. A manual-pay tenant could therefore keep every installment, pay no rent at all, and for up to ninety days take no late fee, no notice, no access suspension and no lien clock — twice a year at `planMaxPerRollingYear: 2`.

1. **The nightly breach job now also breaks a plan on unpaid post-plan rent.** `overdueRentOutsidePlan` (`apps/web/lib/delinquency/payment-plan-breach.ts`) looks for a `rent` invoice on the lease that is **not** in the plan's frozen `invoiceIds`, is not `void`, still has an outstanding balance, and is past due by at least the facility's own first late-fee day. Oldest first, so what ends the plan is the first bill the tenant let go past. Asked only when the schedule itself is being kept — an installment breach already names the installment and needs no second reason.
2. **N is the facility's own `LateFeeRule` step 1 `daysPastDue` (D-107).** `lateFeeStepsFor` was made exported for it. Falls back to the active delinquency timeline's first `dayOffset` for a facility that charges no late fees but runs a lien clock, and returns null — no rent breach at all — where there is neither.
3. **A sixth payment-plan email, `payment_plan_broken_unpaid_rent`**, on a new `payment_plan.broken_unpaid_rent` event carrying `invoiceId`. It opens by saying the tenant kept to their payments, then names the rent invoice's outstanding amount and due date, then the same restart-of-collections paragraph `payment_plan_broken` carries. Merge fields `invoice.amount` / `invoice.due_date` are **required**, so a break with no identifiable invoice fails loudly rather than mailing a sentence with a hole in it.
4. **The agreement email now states the rule it is about to be enforced by.** `payment_plan_agreed` said "If a payment is missed, the plan ends"; it now says "If a payment is missed, or new rent goes unpaid, the plan ends". It already told the tenant "Rent for each new month is separate from this plan and is still due on its usual date" — this makes the consequence explicit before it is applied.

**What it decided.**

- **No new setting, and that is the load-bearing choice (D-107).** "When is rent late here" is a question this facility has already answered, effective-dated, with a control an operator has used. A `planCurrentRentGraceDays` beside the late-fee ladder would be a second column configuring the same intent — the accumulation this repo's first rule is about — and it would drift from the ladder the moment either was edited. The coupling is also right on its own terms: a lenient ladder buys a lenient plan rule automatically. A flat constant was rejected for the reason D-10 makes compliance per-state configurable.
- **A different fact gets a different message.** `payment_plan_broken` opens "A payment on your plan for unit X was not made" — and this tenant made every payment the schedule asked for. Reusing it would have meant telling somebody who kept to a plan that they did not, in the same email that restarts late fees, notices and gate suspension. That is how a collections message becomes the thing a tenant is angriest about, and this repo already treats false customer-facing sentences as load-bearing (B-211's whole subject). The cost is one template, one event, one resolver.
- **`invoiceId` on the event, not re-derived at send time.** Same rule B-206 established for `installmentId`: which bill ended the plan is a decision this job made against a grace window the send path has no business re-running.
- **Rent only.** A `fee` invoice raised after the plan started should not exist — the hold is stopping the ladder that would raise it — and ending somebody's forbearance over one is not what "current rent stays due" means.
- **The frozen arrears can never trigger it.** `notIn: plan.invoiceIds` is the entire mechanism, and the first new test asserts it: at four days past the post-plan rent's due date the plan is still active with its original arrears invoice unpaid, which is exactly what a plan is for.
- **`void` excluded and nothing else**, matching `arrearsForLease` — the set this asks about is the set a plan would have been agreed over.

**Accessibility.** Nothing a customer touches on the site: a nightly job, one event, one email template — no route, no state, no control. `apps/web/app/(public)/accessibility/page.tsx` was re-read per the standing obligation and a note appended. No claim moves in either direction, and `LAST_REVIEWED` does not move. The note records why a sixth email adds no sentence: B-198 settled that this page says nothing about email in either direction, because a client's rendering of a message is not the site.

**Test verification.** Two new tests in `tests/payment-plans-db.test.ts`, both against a facility given a real `LateFeeRule` step 1 at day 5 (created per test, because every other test in that file is written against a facility with none). The first asserts the plan survives at four days past due and breaks at six, that both hold effects are gone, that the recorded message names rent rather than an installment, and that the `payment_plan.broken_unpaid_rent` event row exists. The second asserts the dangerous direction — paying that rent, named explicitly to its own invoice so it cannot settle the older frozen arrears, leaves the plan active and `halt_dunning` in force. Both were mutation-checked: stubbing `overdueRentOutsidePlan` to return null fails them. Full suite green — 3905 passed, 8 skipped, 3913 of 3913 — with no schema change, so no migration and no drift.

**Left behind.** **The per-lease evaluation itself is unchanged.** `halt_late_fees` and `halt_dunning` still stand the ladder down on the whole lease; what this item adds is that the plan does not survive long enough for that to matter. Narrowing the halts to the plan's invoices would let fees and notices run on current rent *while the plan stands*, which is a different and larger product decision — it would mean a tenant on a plan receiving a dunning letter — and nothing in D-96 or D-98 asks for it. **The break is nightly, not immediate**: rent that goes past the late-fee day at noon breaks the plan at hour 4 the next morning, alongside every other plan decision, which is the same latency the installment breach has always had. **No staff-facing surface names the new reason yet** — the hold's `liftReason` is `payment_plan_broken_unpaid_rent` and the task is the same `payment_plan_broken` type, so the counter reads "plan broken" and has to open the plan to see which kind. **B-209 and B-212 are the next two rows on this screen** and both touch the same builder; whichever runs first should consider surfacing the reason there rather than adding a third pass.

## B-209 — "Collected under plans" counted money nobody collected, and correcting a mistyped plan burned the lease's annual allowance

`5ed47a4`

**What it built.** Two defects the operator review raised against the plans-and-holds report and the plan builder, merged because both are about what a payment plan's arithmetic claims.

1. **`planProgressByPlan` now returns a three-way split, not one number** (`apps/web/lib/admin/payment-plans.ts`). It reads the covered invoices **including voided ones** rather than filtering them out, and returns `PlanProgress { progressCents, collectedCents, waivedCents }`: `collectedCents` is the frozen total less what is outstanding counting a voided invoice's unpaid remainder as *still* outstanding, `waivedCents` is the remainder by construction, and `progressCents` is what D-96 has always meant — the two always add back up to it, including where a bounce has clamped `collectedCents` at zero.
2. **`PlanEffectiveness` gained `waivedCents` beside `collectedCents`**, and `collectedCents` is now allocations only (`apps/web/lib/admin/plans-holds-report.ts`). The defect: `collectedCents` was progress, and progress falls when a manager voids a covered invoice — so waiving $600 of fees to make four plans agreeable read as $600 collected, on the one figure an owner uses to decide whether plans work at all. `brokenCents` deliberately keeps using progress: a waived invoice is genuinely not owed any more, so counting it as still-owed would report money nobody is going to chase.
3. **The screen shows both, and says which is which** (`/admin/reports/plans-holds`): a **Waived** column beside **Collected** in the effectiveness table, with the intro naming waived as arrears a manager forgave by voiding an invoice and stating why they sit side by side. The halted list's per-plan cell and the CSV column were re-worded from "collected" to "cleared", because that figure is `progressCents` — the one `installmentViews` is measured against — and had the same wrong word on it.
4. **A same-day cancellation with nothing collected no longer spends one of the lease's plans for the year** (D-108). `createPaymentPlan`'s rolling-year count subtracts `correctionCount`: plans whose `cancelledAt` falls on the same **facility-local** day as their `createdAt` with no `PaymentAllocation` to a covered invoice between those two instants. It applies to both gates the count feeds — the `too_many_plans` refusal and the second-plan escalation.

**What it decided.**

- **The correction carve-out refines D-98 (3) rather than reopening it (D-108).** Broken plans still count; cancelled-the-next-day plans still count; a plan that collected anything counts however it ended. What is excluded is the one case with no amend path anywhere in the product — a mistyped installment date, spotted and re-entered on a Saturday with the tenant at the counter. It cannot buy a free plan: a plan cancelled the day it was agreed lifts its hold with it and provides no forbearance worth having, and D-98's actual defect (a plan broken last night replaced this morning, for ever, while the lien clock never runs) needs plans that survive days, which this excludes none of. The D-98 row now carries a pointer to D-108, so a later session cannot read "cancelled plans count" alone.
- **The money test reads ALLOCATIONS inside the plan's own few minutes, not its progress.** The obvious implementation — `progressCents === 0` — was written first and is wrong in a way a test caught: progress is a live figure off the invoices, so the *successor* plan's payment retroactively un-corrected the mistype it replaced, and next spring's payment would too. A rule about what happened on one Saturday must not change its mind afterwards. One `paymentAllocation` query, filtered to `[plan.createdAt, plan.cancelledAt]`.
- **Facility-local, not UTC**, matching every other calendar-day rule here: a correction made at 7pm Central is the same day's work as the plan it corrects. `businessDateFor` from `@storage/core/jobs`, the existing helper.
- **`HaltedPlanSummary.collectedCents` keeps its progress meaning and its name.** It feeds `installmentViews` in the same function, so making it allocations-only would let the row's money and its next-installment cell disagree. The screen and the export say "cleared" instead, and the type carries a comment saying why it is not the effectiveness table's figure.

**Test verification.** One new test in `tests/plans-holds-report-db.test.ts` voids the $200 plan's covered invoice — $50 paid, $150 forgiven — and asserts `collectedCents` 5,000, `waivedCents` 15,000, that they sum to the whole, **and** that the halted row still reads the full 20,000 as cleared with no next installment, which is the half that must not move. One new test in `tests/payment-plans-db.test.ts` covers both directions of the carve-out: a same-day cancel and re-entry by the same manager is not escalated, then a payment lands, that plan is cancelled the same day, and the next plan is refused with `priorCount: 1`. The existing D-98 chain test needed a `backdateCancel` helper — it agreed and cancelled in the same second, so every one of its plans was a same-day cancel. Full suite green: 3907 passed, 8 skipped, 3915 of 3915. Touched suites run twice. Lint clean (7 pre-existing warnings), typecheck clean, production build clean, `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` reports no difference — no schema change.

**Accessibility.** Nothing a customer touches. The changed surfaces are `/admin/reports/plans-holds` (staff, `reports:financial`) and the admin plan builder's refusal path; the portal payment-plan page reads `collectedCents` from `paymentPlansForLease`, which is unchanged progress. `apps/web/app/(public)/accessibility/page.tsx` was not edited, and no claim on it moves in either direction. The new **Waived** column is a plain `<td>` in a table that already has its `<caption>`, `scope`ed headers and `overflow-x-auto` wrapper; the caption gained the word.

**Left behind.** **There is still no amend path** — the carve-out makes the workaround (cancel, re-enter) free rather than giving the builder an edit, and B-212 is the row on that screen. **The plan-effectiveness CSV is still unbuilt**, so the waived column exists only on screen; the existing export deliberately carries the halted list only (D-65), and adding a second table with different columns to one file is what that comment refuses. **A void that happens *before* the plan is agreed is invisible to this split and correctly so** — `arrearsForLease` never froze it into `invoiceIds` — but it means "waived" here counts only forgiveness that happened under a standing plan, not fees written off the day before one. **No staff surface names why a plan did not count against the limit**: an operator who corrects a mistype sees the count stay at zero with no explanation, which is the right outcome and an unexplained one.

## B-210 — A tenant one day late was told their plan was dead, and a plan that broke in March still said so in December

`80f7e7a`

**What it built.** Two portal defects the UX review raised, merged because both are the same mistake: the screen states something worse than what the product actually does, to the tenant whose next move is deciding whether it is worth paying.

1. **`installmentViews` gained a fourth state, `late`, and the deadline that goes with it** (`packages/core/payment-plans/schedule.ts`). D-98 (4) gives a missed installment `planGraceDays` (default 3) before the plan breaks, and that number reached exactly one place — `evaluatePaymentPlanBreaches`, which applies it by moving its own clock back. Every other reader marked an installment `missed` the instant its date passed. The function now takes the window and returns `late` for an installment past its date but inside its grace, `missed` past it, with `graceEndsOn` on every view — the day the tenant is actually held to. `graceDays` defaults to `0`, which makes `late` unreachable and reproduces the old two-state behaviour exactly, so no caller changed meaning by being missed.
2. **Three schedules and the halted-leases report pass the facility's window through** — `paymentPlansForLease` (both portal and staff plan tables) and `haltedLeases`, where `missedCount` had been counting installments a day past due as breaches on a report an owner reads. The row renders **"Late — pay by 29 August"** on `/portal/payment-plan` and on the admin tenant profile, in words with a date in them rather than as a colour (1.4.1 A); `missed` keeps its red "Missed".
3. **The portal dashboard card tells late and missed apart** (`apps/web/lib/portal/dashboard.ts`, `apps/web/app/portal/page.tsx`). `late` is its own fact beside `next` and `missed`, carrying `payByDate`: *"A payment on your plan is late. $306.24 was due on 26 August. Your plan carries on if you pay it by 29 August."* Both the late and the missed paragraphs now link to `/portal/pay` **with the installment amount on the link**, the correction B-193 already made on the plan page — an installment schedule that quotes the whole arrears offers the tenant the figure the plan exists to replace.
4. **The card goes quiet once the lease owes nothing.** It rendered for `status === 'broken'` with no time bound and no balance test, so "Your payment plan has ended… the full balance above is due now" was permanent — printed directly under a $0.00 balance — for every tenant who broke a plan and then paid it off. It is now gated on the lease's ledger balance being positive. The plan itself stays on `/portal/payment-plan`, which is where a record of something finished belongs.
5. **Both plan emails state the rule they are about to be judged by**, through a new `plan.grace_line` merge field (`packages/db/comms-catalog.ts`, `apps/web/lib/comms/service.ts`). `payment_plan_agreed` and the installment reminder both said the plan ends the day a payment is missed — which is not what the job does, and a tenant told the plan is already gone has no reason to pay by the date that would in fact save it. The line is composed at send time from the facility's own setting, so it cannot go stale when somebody edits it.
6. **The plan builder quotes the same rule at the counter** (`apps/web/app/admin/tenants/[tenantId]/page.tsx`): "an installment still unpaid 3 days after its date lifts it automatically", not "missing an installment".

**What it decided.**

- **`late` is a state, not a shade of `missed`.** Folding it into `missed` with softer wording was the smaller diff and it loses the only thing the tenant can act on — the deadline. Telling somebody their plan has ended when it has not is the same class of harm D-97 names in the other direction (telling them a payment is taken care of when it is not): both are a reason to stop trying.
- **The breach job is unchanged, and the two must land on the identical boundary.** It still shifts its own clock rather than passing `graceDays`, because it measures B-189's retry ladder against the *unshifted* due date in the same call and the two windows must never be netted against each other (D-98 (4) says so outright). That makes boundary agreement a real risk — a plan that breaks on a night the portal says it is alive is this same defect facing the other way — so a test asserts the two agree day by day across the window rather than trusting that `dueDate + grace < asOf` and `dueDate < asOf - grace` are the same inequality.
- **The window is stated as a number, not described.** "You have a few days" is not a rule a tenant can keep. It is read fresh from the facility on every send and every render for the same reason: a sentence with "three days" typed into it goes quietly false the day an operator edits the setting.
- **Zero grace is a real configuration and gets the old sentences back**, in the emails and in the builder copy — where the plan does break that night, there is no catching up to describe.
- **The dead card is suppressed on the BALANCE, not on a time bound.** A "hide it after 30 days" rule would still be wrong on day 29 for a tenant who paid, and still lying on day 31 to one who has not. What made the sentence false is that nothing is due, and that is exactly what the test is.
- **No new decision row.** D-98 (4) already settles the number and its separateness from the retry ladder; what was missing was that anything other than one nightly job knew about it. PRD 01 §4.7 and PRD 02 US-25 carry the AC.

**Test verification.** Four unit tests on `installmentViews` (`tests/payment-plans.test.ts`): `late` inside the window with `graceEndsOn` on it, the flip to `missed` the day after the grace ends, the boundary-agreement test above across five dates, and one asserting the zero-grace default is byte-for-byte the old behaviour. `tests/portal-dashboard.test.ts` now asserts the card at one day past due (`late`, with `payByDate`, `missed` null) as well as at five (`missed`, `late` null), and that a broken plan's card disappears the moment the ledger balance reaches zero and no other plan state moved. Two existing db tests in `tests/payment-plans-db.test.ts` that asserted `missed` at +2 while breaking at +5 — with a comment calling that two separate windows, which it never was — now assert `late` at +2 and `missed` at +5, the same day the job ends the plan. Two comms tests assert the emails carry "3 days to catch it up". Full suite green: **3911 passed, 8 skipped, 3919 of 3919**. Lint, typecheck, production build and `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` clean — no schema change, so no migration.

**Accessibility.** Customer-facing, and it adds a state to two portal screens. Both new states are told apart by **words** (1.4.1 A) — "Late — pay by 29 August" is a sentence with a date in it, not an amber cell — and the dashboard card is still a server-rendered `role="status"` present at page load rather than inserted on change (4.1.3 AA). `apps/web/app/(public)/accessibility/page.tsx` was re-read per the standing obligation and a note appended; `LAST_REVIEWED` does not move, because no claim on it was re-checked against the build and none changed. **Two `STATE_EXCEPTIONS` were widened in the understating direction**: the `/portal` card exception named "the two warning states" and there are now three, and the `/portal/payment-plan` exception covered only ended plans while the late and missed ROW states of a live one had never been named at all.

**Left behind.** **Neither new state is scanned**, and that is declared rather than closed: both need an installment whose date has actually gone by, which the demo seed deliberately does not create — a past installment would be broken by the nightly job on a schedule nobody controls, so the fixture would show a different thing depending on when the jobs last ran (B-193's entry settled that). **`isBreached` in `packages/core/payment-plans/schedule.ts` still has no grace argument and no production caller** — only tests reach it — so it is correct today and would be wrong the moment somebody used it; it wants deleting, not fixing. **The halted-leases CSV and the staff plan card still say "Missed" for a count**, now a correct count, but nothing on those screens names the grace window the way the tenant's schedule does. **No SMS equivalent**: `plan.grace_line` is on the two email templates that stated the wrong rule, and the SMS catalog has no plan messages to correct.

## B-211 — Three screens described behaviour the product does not have

`fd3ea9e`

**What it built.** Copy only, no logic: three statements the product makes about itself that were false, and — for the first one — the two places the false statement came from rather than only the screen it was read on.

1. **`/admin/settings/roles` told the owner that over-limit work escalates.** The words were *"Over the limit does not fail: it escalates to the next role up that can cover the amount"*. Nothing escalates. B-190 shipped a hard refusal that **names** the lowest role above whose limit covers the amount, and there is no queue behind it: nothing is routed, nobody is notified, and the person named has to perform the action themselves. The screen now says that, and says the ordering rule is what keeps the refusal honest — a role left more generous than the one above it would send staff to somebody with *less* authority than the person just turned down.
2. **The same sentence was fixed where it originated, not only where it was read.** `ladderViolation`'s own refusal (`apps/web/lib/admin/role-limits.ts`) told an owner editing the limits that the role above "is who an over-limit fee waiver escalates to"; it now says the refusal *sends staff to* them. And the comment on `checkMonetaryAuthority` (`apps/web/lib/rbac/authorize.ts`) said over-limit "routes to the next role up… the approval workflow itself lands with refunds in **B-048**" — B-048 shipped, without it. That comment is where the screen's sentence came from, and leaving it would have re-grown the copy.
3. **`invoiceLeadDays` configures two things and its label named one.** `emitInstallmentReminders` reads it to decide how far ahead a plan-installment reminder goes out (B-191 chose it deliberately, rather than adding a second column configuring the same intent), while the control said only "Invoice this many days ahead". Shortening invoice lead time silently moved every installment reminder — on the population that most needs the warning. It now carries a hint saying so.
4. **The `plan.schedule` merge-field help described a rendering D-102 replaced.** It read "Every installment, one per line, with its date and amount", which was true until B-198 made the field a `MergeValue` — a numbered list in the text part and a captioned table in the HTML one. **The template editor prints `description` verbatim** (`/admin/settings/templates` renders it as the `<dd>` of the field list beside the box), so that sentence is the only guidance an operator gets, and an operator who wrote the field inside a sentence dropped a table into the middle of a paragraph. It now says it is a block and to keep it on its own line.
5. **PRD 02 RBAC-2 asserted the routed approval request too**, and was corrected in the same pass — it is the line the screen was faithfully implementing.

**What it decided.**

- **No new D-number.** D-98 already settled the posture — "escalation by naming the next role, the same posture as a fee waiver, **with no approval queue behind it**" — so this is the PRD and three surfaces catching up with a decision that was already recorded, not a decision being made.
- **A routed approval request stays unbuilt, and now says so out loud.** RBAC-2 has asked for one since the beginning and no backlog row owns it. Inventing the row was tempting and is product-owner work, not a copy item's; what the copy item can do is stop the product claiming the feature exists. The PRD line names the gap explicitly so the next person reading RBAC-2 sees an unbuilt requirement rather than a built one.
- **Fixed at the source, not at the symptom.** Three of the five edits are not the screen the row named. A false sentence in a doc comment beside the function is how the same false sentence gets written on the next screen.
- **`invoiceLeadDays` keeps its one number.** The alternative — a second setting for the reminder — is exactly the accumulation this repo's first rule is about, and B-191 rejected it on those grounds. The defect was never the sharing; it was that only one of the two meanings was written down.

**Test verification.** Nothing executable changed: five strings, one PRD line. No test asserted any of them (a comment in `tests/role-limits-db.test.ts` used the old word and is unchanged, being a comment). Full suite green — **3911 passed, 8 skipped, 3919 of 3919** — with lint, typecheck, production build and `prisma migrate diff --exit-code` clean. No schema change.

**Accessibility.** Nothing a customer touches: `/admin/settings/roles`, `/admin/settings`, and the merge-field list on `/admin/settings/templates` are all staff screens behind `settings:manage`. `apps/web/app/(public)/accessibility/page.tsx` was not edited and no claim on it moves in either direction. The one new element is a `hint` on an existing `Field`, which the component already wires into that input's `aria-describedby` (3.3.2 A) rather than leaving as adjacent text.

**Left behind.** **Two refusals still say "Ask a manager to approve it" with the word hardcoded** — the fee-waiver and refund paths in `apps/web/app/admin/tenants/[tenantId]/actions.ts` — while the payment-plan and fee-override refusals beside them use the data-driven `escalateTo` name and say what happens when nobody above can cover it either. On a portfolio whose roles have been renamed, or where no manager's limit reaches, "ask a manager" is the same class of false sentence this item was about; it wants the same treatment and did not get it here. **The approval queue itself has no row.** **`tenant-rate-increases.ts:237` still says "escalates to the next role that can carry it"** in a comment — accurate in its own terms, since it is describing where the refusal points, but it is the wording that produced this item and would be better said the other way.

## B-212 — The payment-plan builder is offered where it cannot work, and where it can, it demands cent-exact arithmetic across twelve fields

`14904be`

**What it built.** Two halves, both about the same form on `/admin/tenants/[tenantId]`.

**Not offering a control that cannot succeed.** The disclosure rendered for every non-ended lease with no active plan and no arrears test, so on a current tenant it opened to "$0.00 is past due" over twelve fields and refused every submit — `validateSchedule` returns *"There is nothing past due on this lease to put on a plan"* before it looks at anything else. It is now gated on `arrearsCents > 0`. The rolling-year cap was the same failure one step further in: D-98's `planMaxPerRollingYear` is checked by `createPaymentPlan` **before** the schedule, so a staffer at the limit filled in six dates and six amounts for nothing. The profile now renders that refusal in place of the form, in the server's own words including where the limit is changed.

**Doing the arithmetic the refusal demands.** Where a plan can be agreed, the builder gained an **even split** — installment count and start date, one button — and a **live "still to allocate" figure**. Up to six date/amount pairs had to sum to the arrears to the cent, by hand: $1,837.42 over six months is 5 × $306.23 + $306.27, computed in somebody's head, in front of a tenant, with nothing on screen keeping score. Both are suggestions, not constraints: every field stays editable and `validateSchedule` remains the only thing that decides whether a schedule may be agreed.

**Naming the two money figures.** The leases table's balance and the builder's past-due total are different numbers for the same lease, and a staffer who typed the first was refused with nothing saying why. The column header is now **Total balance**, and the builder says the difference in one sentence — but only when the two actually differ.
